0.title: The King Has Come
0.overview:
Matthew begins where the Old Testament ends — with promises. His opening genealogy is not a genealogy at all; it is a theology compressed into names. Abraham to David to the exile to Jesus: the whole arc of Israel’s story, told in three movements, arriving at the one name toward which every other name was pointing. Matthew’s first word is biblos geneseos — the book of origins, the book of genesis. A new creation has begun.

Matthew wrote for Jewish Christians, probably in Antioch, in the decades after the destruction of Jerusalem. His readers knew the Old Testament. They had grown up with the promises of a coming King from David’s line, a new Moses who would deliver God’s people, a suffering servant who would bear the sins of many, a son of man who would receive an everlasting dominion. Matthew’s argument, sustained across twenty-eight chapters, is that all of these promises find their yes in Jesus of Nazareth (2 Cor. 1:20). The fulfillment formula — that it might be fulfilled — appears again and again like a refrain, stitching the Old Testament to the New until you cannot see the seam.

The great theme of Matthew is the kingdom of heaven. Where Mark asks who is this man? and Luke traces the universal reach of grace, Matthew announces the arrival of a reign. Heaven’s rule has broken into earth’s disorder in the person of the King. He teaches with authority (not as the scribes). He heals with a word. He calms the sea. He feeds the multitude. He raises the dead. And then he goes to the cross not as a victim of circumstances but as the King who lays down his life to ransom many (20:28) — the supreme act of royal authority disguised as utter weakness.

Matthew’s Jesus is the new Moses, but greater. Moses gave the law from Sinai; Jesus gives the new law from the mountain (chapters 5–7). Moses delivered Israel through the Red Sea; Jesus passes through death and comes out the other side. Moses saw the promised land from a distance and died; Jesus enters it, conquers it, and invites all nations to follow him in. “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them” (5:17). In Jesus, the Old Testament does not end — it arrives.

The name given to him in chapter 1 is the key that unlocks the whole: Emmanuel — God with us. And the Gospel ends with the same promise, spoken now in resurrection glory: I am with you always, to the end of the age (28:20). Matthew is bracketed by the presence of God. What began in a manger in Bethlehem does not end at a tomb in Jerusalem. It ends with a commission that will reach every tongue and tribe and nation — because the one who sends is the one to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given.

Read Matthew as someone meeting the King for the first time. Let the authority of his teaching arrest you. Let the tenderness of his healing move you. Let the cross unmake your comfortable religion. And let the resurrection send you — into all the world, making disciples, baptising, teaching. The Gospel of Matthew is not a story that ends; it is a commission that begins.

1.title: Emmanuel — God With Us
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. <sup>2</sup>Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, <sup>3</sup>and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, <sup>4</sup>and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon, <sup>5</sup>and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, <sup>6</sup>and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, <sup>7</sup>and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, <sup>8</sup>and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, <sup>9</sup>and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, <sup>10</sup>and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah, <sup>11</sup>and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. <sup>12</sup>And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, <sup>13</sup>and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, <sup>14</sup>and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, <sup>15</sup>and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, <sup>16</sup>and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. <sup>17</sup>So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations. <sup>18</sup>Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. <sup>19</sup>And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. <sup>20</sup>But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. <sup>21</sup>She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” <sup>22</sup>All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: <sup>23</sup>“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us). <sup>24</sup>When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, <sup>25</sup>but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
1.overview:
Matthew opens not with a manger scene but with a list of names — and the list is the point. Every name in the genealogy is a promise kept. From Abraham, through whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. 12:3), to David, whose throne would endure forever (2 Sam. 7:16), to the exile and back: the whole history of Israel’s faithfulness and failure, strung together like beads on a single cord that ends at the name Jesus. God’s covenant faithfulness spans every generation, including the dark ones. Especially the dark ones.

The genealogy contains surprises that Matthew intends. Four women appear — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and “the wife of Uriah” — each associated with scandal, foreignness, or irregularity. Matthew is signalling from the first page that this King comes not for the respectable but for the broken, not only for Israel but for the nations. Grace does not run through clean lines; it runs through history as it actually happened, mess and all.

Then the birth narrative proper, and its two names. Jesus: he will save his people from their sins (v. 21). The name carries the whole gospel in four letters — Y’shua, the LORD saves. And Emmanuel: God with us (v. 23). The fulfilment of Isaiah’s sign (Isa. 7:14) is no longer a child born in the eighth century BC as a near-term reassurance to Ahaz; it is the Son of God entering human flesh, the Creator wearing the creature’s nature, the infinite becoming finite — without ceasing to be infinite. This is the doctrine of the incarnation, announced in a single breath in a single verse, and it changes everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew opens not with a narrative but with a name-list, and in doing so announces that the gospel is rooted in real history. The genealogy traces Jesus' legal descent through Joseph from Abraham and David, grounding him in both the Abrahamic covenant (promise of blessing to all nations, Gen. 12:3) and the Davidic covenant (promise of an eternal throne, 2 Sam. 7:12–16). Three groups of fourteen generations form a theological argument, not an exhaustive record: Jesus is the divinely appointed culmination of redemptive history. Four women — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — appear unexpectedly, each associated with scandal or Gentile origin, signaling that this King's grace reaches beyond the expected.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy establishes Jesus as Messiah (Christ = Anointed One), Son of David (royal heir), and Son of Abraham (heir of the covenant). The 14-14-14 structure — possibly reflecting the numerical value of David's name in Hebrew — underscores divine superintendence: God has been ordering history toward this moment across centuries of faithfulness, failure, exile, and return. Providence is not the absence of scandal; it is the sovereign use of all things toward the appointed end.
verseByVerse.examples: This genealogy reminds us that salvation is not a timeless philosophy but a historical event rooted in a long chain of real covenantal faithfulness. God's promises survived murder, adultery, exile, and foreign domination to arrive at their fulfillment. What he has promised, he performs — across generations, across continents, across every human failure. The God who kept his word to Abraham keeps his word to you.

verseByVerse.quote: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers,
verseByVerse.commentary: The opening line is a deliberate echo of Genesis: "the book of the genealogy" (biblos geneseos) recalls Gen. 2:4 and 5:1, announcing that what follows is a new Genesis, a new creation story. Two titles define Jesus before a single deed is narrated: Son of David (messianic heir to the throne) and Son of Abraham (heir of the covenant of grace). Matthew's Jewish audience would feel the weight immediately. The order is significant — Son of David comes first, then Son of Abraham, because Matthew is presenting Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's royal hope before expanding to the universal blessing promised to all nations through Abraham's seed.

verseByVerse.quote: and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon,
verseByVerse.commentary: Tamar appears first among the four women in this genealogy — a Canaanite woman who secured the covenant line through an act of desperate subterfuge (Gen. 38). Her inclusion is not a scandal to be explained away but a testimony to be proclaimed: grace does not require moral perfection as its precondition. God wove his redemptive purposes through Tamar's transgression, through Judah's failure, and through unexpected channels. The line runs through Perez — the child of that union — toward David and ultimately toward Christ. What human schemes corrupt, sovereign grace overrules.

verseByVerse.quote: and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah,
verseByVerse.commentary: Rahab the harlot of Jericho and Ruth the Moabitess both enter the messianic line by grace, not by birth. Rahab's faith (Heb. 11:31) overcame her origin; Ruth's loyalty overcame her foreignness. Both point to a King whose lineage is built on faith received, not merit earned. Then comes the darkest entry: Solomon was born "by the wife of Uriah" — Matthew does not write Bathsheba's name, forcing the reader to remember Uriah and the sin that took his life. David the king, the man after God's own heart, is also David the adulterer and murderer. The covenant line runs through that sin too, unbroken.

verseByVerse.quote: and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah,
verseByVerse.commentary: The royal line through the divided kingdom passes through kings who ranged from the faithful (Jehoshaphat) to the wicked (Joram, who killed his brothers). Matthew's genealogy makes no distinction — good kings and bad kings, faithful and faithless, are all in the chain. The covenant does not depend on the moral quality of its custodians. God's purposes are not held hostage to human fidelity. This is perhaps the most quietly staggering feature of the genealogy: that God would bind himself to such a people, and keep every promise made to them despite everything.

verseByVerse.quote: and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah,
verseByVerse.commentary: Ahaz was one of Judah's most faithless kings, importing Assyrian idolatry and closing the temple. Manasseh was worse — he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and led the nation into depths of idolatry unparalleled in Judah's history (2 Kings 21). Yet here they are, in the unbroken chain between Abraham and Christ. The genealogy is not a hall of fame; it is a demonstration of grace operating through the most unlikely vessels. Hezekiah and Josiah, the reforming kings who turned the tide, appear in the same list. God uses both the faithful and the faithless to accomplish his purposes — though he is never the author of the sin.

verseByVerse.quote: and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel,
verseByVerse.commentary: The deportation to Babylon is the pivot-point of the genealogy's second third — the great national catastrophe that seemed to end the Davidic line forever. The covenant appeared broken, the promises void. But the name Zerubbabel — the governor who led the first return from exile (Ezra 3) — signals that God had not forgotten. The covenant did not die in Babylon. It went into exile with the people and returned with them. Matthew's structuring of history around the exile says: even the worst judgment in Israel's history was not the end of the story. God's purposes are indestructible.

verseByVerse.quote: and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud,
verseByVerse.commentary: The post-exilic names are largely unknown to history — no chronicles record them, no psalms celebrate them. They lived and died in obscurity, ordinary people in an occupied land. Yet each was a link in the chain of divine promise. The covenant line passed through them invisibly, carried not by fame or power but by ordinary human generation under divine sovereignty. God's purposes do not require spectacular vessels. Most of redemptive history has been carried by ordinary, unknown people who simply lived, married, and had children — while the promise traveled forward toward its fulfillment in their Descendant.

verseByVerse.quote: and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final verse of the genealogy contains the grammatical key to the whole: "Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born" — the "of whom" is feminine singular in Greek, referring to Mary alone, not to Joseph. Matthew is carefully signaling the virgin birth before he explains it: Jesus is legally in the Davidic line through Joseph, but physically born of Mary without a human father. He is the Christ — the Anointed One — the one toward whom all forty-two generations were moving. The genealogy ends not with a triumphant king but with a carpenter's wife and a name that means Salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations.
verseByVerse.commentary: The three fourteens are a mnemonic and a theological statement, not an arithmetic claim (Matthew omits several kings to achieve the pattern). If 14 encodes the name David in Hebrew gematria (D=4, W=6, D=4), the triple repetition says: this whole history is about David's greater Son. But the structure also says something about time: Abraham to David (promise received), David to exile (promise endangered), exile to Christ (promise fulfilled). History is not random; it has been shaped by divine intent toward a single point. That point is Jesus. Every generation was a step closer to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Birth of Jesus Christ: God with Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew tells the nativity through Joseph's eyes. He discovers Mary's pregnancy, intends to divorce her quietly (sparing her public disgrace), and is then visited by an angel who reveals the child's supernatural origin. Joseph's response is exemplary and immediate: he did as the angel commanded. Two names define the child — Jesus (he will save his people from their sins) and Immanuel (God with us). The birth fulfills Isaiah 7:14, establishing the pattern of scriptural fulfillment that runs through Matthew's entire Gospel.
verseByVerse.theology: The virgin birth is not incidental decoration but theological necessity. If Jesus is to be the sinless substitute for sinners, he cannot enter the world through ordinary generation under fallen Adam. The Holy Spirit's agency in the conception ensures both his full humanity (born of woman, Gal. 4:4) and his freedom from the entail of the first Adam's sin. The two names capture the whole gospel: he is God who has come to be with us (Immanuel), and in being with us he saves us from our sins (Jesus). Doctrine and salvation are inseparable from the first moment.
verseByVerse.examples: Joseph's obedience is one of Scripture's quietly great acts of faith. He received no applause, no public vindication, no explanation beyond the angel's word. He obeyed at enormous personal cost — accepting social suspicion, raising a child not his own, surrendering his right to defend his reputation. In an age that demands visible proof and public validation before any commitment, Joseph's silent, costly fidelity is a rebuke and a model. God still calls his people to act on his word before the full picture is visible.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly.
verseByVerse.commentary: Betrothal in first-century Judaism was legally binding — only divorce could dissolve it, and unfaithfulness during betrothal was treated as adultery. Joseph's discovery of Mary's pregnancy placed him in an impossible situation: the law permitted public accusation; justice seemed to require it. But Joseph was a just man who chose mercy. He resolved to divorce her quietly — to absorb the shame himself rather than expose her to public disgrace. Even before the angel spoke, Joseph's character was formed by a justice that expressed itself in compassion. This is what biblical righteousness looks like: not the rigid application of rights, but the merciful restraint of power.

verseByVerse.quote: But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, "Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel addresses Joseph as "son of David" — a reminder that the legal Davidic lineage passes through him, and that this child needs Joseph's adoption into the royal line. The command "do not fear" meets the genuine terror of Joseph's situation: fear of social ruin, of misunderstanding, of an inexplicable pregnancy. The angel does not minimize the difficulty; he provides the truth that overcomes it. The name Jesus (Greek form of Joshua, meaning "the LORD saves") is not a hope but a declaration: he will save his people from their sins. Not from Rome, not from poverty — from sins. This is the most radical and necessary salvation.

Do not pass over four small words: that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. No human father stands behind this child — and that is everything. Every other son of Adam is conceived in the ordinary way and so inherits Adam's fallen nature; "in sin did my mother conceive me" (Ps 51:5). But this conception is a fresh act of God: the same Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation (Gen 1:2) overshadows Mary, so that "the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God" (Lk 1:35). Hence Jesus is fully man — truly Mary's son, real flesh and blood — yet without the sin every other child of Adam carries. And only such a Savior can save: a Redeemer tainted by Adam's guilt would need redeeming himself. Mark the deeper wonder too — salvation comes wholly from God's side. Mary is the willing soil, but the life within her is the Spirit's gift, not man's achievement; grace from the very first breath. The virgin conception is no decorative miracle. Pull this thread and the whole gospel unravels.

And weigh what Matthew means by "save his people from their sins." To a first-century Jew, "his people" meant Israel, and "salvation" meant rescue from Rome — a throne restored, the pagan boot lifted. Matthew gently overturns both. The enemy is not Caesar but sin; the exile that truly grieves God is the exile of a sinful heart from himself. And "his people" will prove wider than Israel — by the Gospel's last verse it reaches "all nations" (28:19), the true Israel of Jew and Gentile together, everyone the Father has given him. The name itself already preaches this, echoing Psalm 130:8: "he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities." And Matthew tells us how it will be done — at the table, on the night he was betrayed: "this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (26:28). The manger aims straight at the cross.

But what is it, finally, to be saved "from their sins"? Reach for the old threefold answer and feel its sweep. He saves his people from the penalty of sin — the guilt and condemnation we had earned were nailed to his cross, so that "there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1). He saves them from the power of sin — no longer its slaves, for "sin will have no dominion over you" (Rom 6:14); the chains are struck off and the daily war of grace begins. And he will save them at last from the very presence of sin — the day comes when "nothing unclean will ever enter" the city (Rev 21:27), when we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is (1 Jn 3:2). Penalty, power, presence; past, present, and future — sin's guilt cancelled, sin's grip broken, sin's shadow one day gone altogether. All of that is folded into a single name: Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel" (which means, God with us).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew's formula "all this took place to fulfill" rings out ten times in his Gospel. It is not proof-texting but fulfillment-theology: the events of Jesus' life complete Israel's whole story.

Hear first what the prophecy meant in its own day. Isaiah 7:14 was spoken around 734 BC to faithless King Ahaz, white with fear as Syria and Israel marched on Jerusalem. God offered him a sign; Ahaz refused it; so God gave one anyway — a child would be born, and before the boy was old enough to know right from wrong, the two kings Ahaz dreaded would be swept off the map (Isa 7:16). In its own moment the sign preached one thing: God has not abandoned his people. He is with us.

Now the famous controversy over that one word, "virgin." The Hebrew Isaiah used is almah — a young woman of marriageable age, and in the Old Testament always an unmarried one, so a virgin is naturally in view (the narrow, technical word for virgin is betulah). Critics charge that Matthew over-read it. But here is the quiet wonder: nearly two centuries before Christ was born, Jewish scholars translating their own Scriptures into Greek (the Septuagint) rendered almah with parthenos — which means a virgin, plainly and unmistakably. The "virgin" reading was no Christian invention smuggled in to prop up a doctrine; it was already sitting there in the Jews' own Greek Bible. Matthew, carried by the Spirit, simply unveils the depth that had always been sleeping in the words.

What it signifies we have already tasted at verse 20: the virgin conception means this child is truly man, yet without Adam's sin, and truly God come in our flesh — the only kind of Savior who could ever save. Isaiah's sign of "God with us in our crisis" outran its first fulfillment by seven centuries, waiting for the day God would be with his people not by sending help from afar, but by coming himself.

And then the name: Immanuel, "God with us." Something here surprises many a careful reader — no one in the entire New Testament ever actually calls Jesus by this name. He is named Jesus, never Immanuel. So how is the prophecy fulfilled if no one uses the word? Because Immanuel was never a label to be pinned on him; it is a confession of who he is. The name is not on his papers — it is the truth of his very being, and the reality of it floods every page. Matthew makes it the great bracket around his whole Gospel: it opens here with Immanuel, God with us (1:23), and closes on the lips of the risen Christ, "behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age" (28:20). Everything in between is God, with us.

Do not hurry past this. The God who flung the stars into space, whom the highest heaven cannot contain, drew near — wrapped himself in our flesh, was laid in a feed-trough, "and dwelt among us" (Jn 1:14, literally, pitched his tent among us). Not a note of encouragement mailed from a safe distance. God himself, with us — and he has never once left. Read that again, slowly, until it lands.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph's obedience is total and immediate: "he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him." No negotiation, no condition, no delay. He woke from the dream and acted. And the naming of Jesus by Joseph carries legal weight — by giving the child his name, Joseph formally adopts him into the line of David.

Now that odd old phrase, "knew her not." It sounds strange to our ears, but it is simply the Bible's gentle, modest way of speaking about a husband and wife coming together as one. Scripture has talked this way since the very beginning — "Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived" (Gen 4:1). There is real beauty in the word: the joining of husband and wife is not treated as a mere act of the body but as two people truly knowing each other, becoming one flesh. So when Matthew says Joseph "knew her not until she had given birth," he is telling us, plainly but reverently, that Joseph did not come together with Mary as a husband until after Jesus was born. He guarded her, kept his distance, so that no one could ever whisper that this baby was his doing. The child was God's alone.

And do not trip over that little word "until," as some have. It does not hint at anything before the birth; it simply fixes our eyes on the one thing that matters here — that Jesus was conceived of a virgin, with no human father. Joseph's naming of the child is the last we hear of him acting in the story: quietly faithful, publicly unrecognized, essential to it all, content simply to serve.

1.theology:
The Incarnation and the Hypostatic Union. Matthew 1:23 is the first New Testament statement of what the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) would define as the hypostatic union: Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. Emmanuel — God with us. The one born of Mary is not a divine being wearing a human costume, nor a human being elevated to divine status. He is the eternal Son of God who took to himself a true and complete human nature, remaining what he was while becoming what he was not.

Reformed theology has insisted on both sides of this confession with equal force. Against those who diminish the humanity (docetism), the reformers affirm: he was born of a woman, grew in wisdom, wept, hungered, died. Against those who diminish the divinity, the reformers affirm: he is the Lord who saves, the one who forgives sins, who raises the dead, who will judge the living and the dead. The incarnation is not a compromise between deity and humanity; it is the union of both in one Person, the only foundation on which salvation is possible.
1.examples:
Then: The women in the genealogy — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — represent the scandalous grace of God that runs through broken and foreign vessels to accomplish his purposes. The rabbis of Matthew’s day would have found their inclusion in a royal genealogy offensive. Matthew includes them precisely because the gospel offends the self-righteous and welcomes the unlikely. The same grace that wrote Rahab the harlot into the ancestry of the Messiah writes sinners into the family of God through faith.

Now: We live in a world that determines worth by background, achievement, and social position. The genealogy of Matthew 1 demolishes every such calculation. The line of the King runs through exiles, foreigners, adulterers, and the forgotten. If your story has chapters you would rather not name in public, you are in good company in this genealogy. The God who included Rahab and Ruth and Tamar in the ancestry of his Son includes broken people in his family — not despite their stories but through them, weaving even the darkest threads into the tapestry of his redeeming purpose.

2.title: The King and the Nations
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.” <sup>3</sup>When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; <sup>4</sup>and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. <sup>5</sup>They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: <sup>6</sup>‘And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’” <sup>7</sup>Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. <sup>8</sup>And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, “Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him.” <sup>9</sup>After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. <sup>10</sup>When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. <sup>11</sup>And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. <sup>12</sup>And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another route. <sup>13</sup>Now when they had departed, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him.” <sup>14</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt <sup>15</sup>and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, “Out of Egypt I called my son.” <sup>16</sup>Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men. <sup>17</sup>Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: <sup>18</sup>“A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.” <sup>19</sup>But when Herod died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, <sup>20</sup>saying, “Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead.” <sup>21</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. <sup>22</sup>But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee. <sup>23</sup>And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is a chapter of contrasts. From the east, pagan Magi travel hundreds of miles to worship a Jewish king they have never met, guided by a star and driven by a longing they cannot fully name. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes know exactly where the Messiah is to be born — they can quote the prophecy from memory — and do not move a single step toward Bethlehem. Knowledge without seeking is useless; seeking without knowledge leads to Jerusalem first and then to the star. The Magi needed both, and they found the King.

The flight to Egypt is Matthew’s second great fulfilment: Out of Egypt I called my son (Hos. 11:1). What Hosea said of Israel, Matthew applies to Jesus — because Jesus is the true Israel, recapitulating the nation’s story in his own person. Israel went into Egypt to be preserved; Israel came out of Egypt to receive the law at Sinai. Jesus goes into Egypt as an infant; he comes out to receive baptism at the Jordan and give the new law on the mountain. He is not just a figure from Israel’s history; he is Israel’s history compressed and completed.

The massacre of the innocents is the chapter’s darkest moment, and Matthew does not diminish it. Rachel weeping for her children (Jer. 31:15) — the ancient lament of exile reactivated by Herod’s paranoid terror. Children died because the King had come. This is not a comfortable note, and it should not be. The incarnation provokes powers that kill to protect themselves. And yet those children are the first martyrs — the first to die because of the King who would die for all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Visit of the Magi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wise men from the East arrive in Jerusalem following a star, seeking the one born King of the Jews. Their arrival triggers the first of Matthew's great ironies: Gentiles travel from afar to worship the Jewish Messiah, while the Jewish king plots his murder and the religious establishment is unmoved. Herod's response — feigned interest concealing murderous intent — foreshadows the opposition that will culminate at Golgotha. The magi's worship, their gifts, and their Spirit-warned departure set the pattern: the nations come to the light while those who hold the Scriptures remain in darkness.
verseByVerse.theology: The magi's journey is the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision: the nations streaming to Zion's light (Isa. 60:1–6). Their gifts — gold for a king, incense for a priest, myrrh for one destined to die — have long been read as prophetic of Christ's three offices. Herod represents all who will acknowledge Christ's kingship only to oppose it: knowing who he is changes nothing if the heart is not transformed. The Scripture the chief priests quote accurately (Micah 5:2) but do not obey is a standing rebuke to knowledge without submission.
verseByVerse.examples: The magi traveled perhaps a thousand miles, following light they only partially understood, to bring costly gifts to a child. Their worship was costly, inconvenient, and preceded by great uncertainty. Many who have never left their town have more theological knowledge than these men had — and far less devotion. The question the magi's story presses: what are you willing to travel, spend, and risk to find and worship Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying, "Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bethlehem of Judea is named not for geography but for prophecy: the city of David, the place where the Messiah must be born (Micah 5:2). The wise men's question — "Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?" — is the right question asked in the wrong place. They come to the palace in Jerusalem looking for a newborn king and find only Herod. The star brought them as far as Israel; only Scripture would carry them the last few miles to Bethlehem.

It helps to know who this Herod was. History calls him Herod the Great — great as a builder (it was he who lavishly rebuilt the temple in Jerusalem), but monstrous as a man. He was not even a full Jew but an Idumean, a descendant of Esau, handed the title "King of the Jews" by Rome. Forever clutching at his throne, he murdered his favorite wife, three of his own sons, and many besides; the emperor Augustus is said to have joked that it was safer to be Herod's pig than his son. So when word arrives of a child "born King of the Jews," the old tyrant's terror — and the slaughter that follows in verse 16 — is grimly in character. Two kings of the Jews now stand face to face in the story: one crowned by Rome and drenched in blood, one born of God and worshiped by strangers.

And the wise men — the "magi" — were learned men from the East, most likely Persia or Babylon: royal counselors who studied the heavens and weighed the signs of the times. They were Gentiles, outsiders to the covenant, and yet they are the first in this whole Gospel to seek the King and bow down. Where would such men get a hope of a Jewish Messiah? Perhaps from the long memory of the East, where centuries earlier Daniel had been set over the wise men of Babylon (Dan 2:48), and where an old prophecy still glimmered: "a star shall come out of Jacob" (Num 24:17). Scripture never calls them kings and never numbers them — the three crowns and the names Caspar, Melchior, and Balthasar are later legend, the "three" merely guessed from the three gifts. What matters is the picture: the nations streaming to the light of Israel's King, gold and frankincense in their hands, exactly as Isaiah foresaw (Isa 60:3, 6).

But what did these star-gazers actually have in mind? Three of their words can puzzle us. First, "king of the Jews." They were not hunting for some petty local ruler; they had somehow grasped that a King was coming out of Judea whose birth the very heavens would mark — a King of the Jews, yet plainly One who mattered to the nations, or why travel so far? (The Roman writers Tacitus and Suetonius both record that exactly such an expectation, a world-ruler arising from Judea, was in the air across the East in those years.) Second, "his star." We are not told precisely what it was, and we should not pretend to know; but notice that it later moves ahead of them and halts over a single house (v.9), which no ordinary star does. The humbler and truer thought is simply this: God met these men inside their own trade, the reading of the skies, and used a light they could not ignore to draw them to his Son — perhaps with the old word echoing behind it, "a star shall come out of Jacob" (Num 24:17). Third, "to worship him." At the least they meant to do a king honor, to bow before royalty as the custom was; but Matthew means us to see more, for at the house they fall on their faces and pour out their treasures (v.11), rendering to this child what belongs to God alone. And here is the wonder that should jolt us awake: Gentiles travel a thousand miles to worship the King, while Jerusalem, holding the very Scriptures that name his birthplace, will not walk the five miles to see him.

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born.
verseByVerse.commentary: Herod's disturbance and Jerusalem's with him: the city that should have erupted in joy at the announcement of its King's arrival instead trembles. Herod's trouble is the trouble of threatened power; Jerusalem's trouble is the crowd's anxiety about what Herod might do in response. The chief priests and scribes are summoned not for worship but for information — they are treated as a reference library by a man who has no intention of bowing. Knowledge of Scripture does not equal submission to Christ. The religious establishment had every text and no intention. This is Matthew's first portrait of a Judaism that knows its own Scriptures better than it knows its God.

verseByVerse.quote: They told him, "In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: 'And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Micah 5:2 is quoted with precision and obeyed not at all. The chief priests know exactly where the Messiah is to be born — and not one of them makes the six-mile journey to Bethlehem to check. This is the deepest irony of the infancy narrative: pagan foreigners travel a thousand miles to worship; Israel's own scholars travel zero miles to investigate. The text they quote calls the coming ruler a shepherd — a word that evokes David, Moses, and ultimately the one who will say "I am the good shepherd." He came to shepherd his people, and the shepherds of his people refused to go and find him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, "Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod's secrecy is the first mark of his murderous intent — he does not want Jerusalem to know what he is planning. The ascertaining of when the star appeared will become the data for the massacre: "two years old or under" (v. 16) corresponds to the star's timing. Herod's claim to want to worship is among history's most transparent lies — and yet it has been repeated by every power that has ever tried to co-opt Christ for its own purposes. True worship dethrones the worshiper; Herod wanted information to eliminate a rival. The difference between Herod's "worship" and the magi's is the difference between murder and adoration.

A word on the star itself, since Herod fastens on "what time the star had appeared." In the ancient world — and above all in the East, the magi's home — it was simply taken for granted that the heavens spoke: that the birth and death of kings, the rise and fall of empires, were written in the sky for those trained to read them. Astrology was the respected science of that day, and the magi were its scholars; so in watching for a royal star they were doing exactly what their culture had taught them. Yet we must be careful here, for the Bible itself forbids God's people to steer their lives by the stars (Deut 4:19; Isa 47:13 mocks the helpless "stargazers"). How then does God use one? In sheer grace he stooped to meet these outsiders where they were, speaking to them in the one language they knew, the language of the sky — not to bless astrology, but to draw them up out of it and onto the road to Bethlehem. And mark this: the star carried them only as far as Israel; it was the Scriptures that brought them to the King (vv. 5–6). God will often call a man through the dim light he already has, but he never leaves him there — he leads him on to his Word. We are not to scan the heavens for messages; "we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed" (2 Pet 1:19), and the true Morning Star (Rev 22:16) has already risen.

Pause over the sheer blackness of it: Herod wraps the murder of a child in the language of worship. "That I too may come and worship him" — and he means, that I may find him and kill him. It is hard to imagine a fouler use of words. Yet Scripture helps us name what we are looking at. To weld lying and murder together in one breath is the devil's own signature; Jesus said of him, "he was a murderer from the beginning... a liar and the father of lies" (Jn 8:44). Herod is doing the serpent's work — and John later shows us the picture behind the picture: a great dragon crouching before the woman, "so that when she bore her child he might devour it" (Rev 12:4). Here is the lesson that should make us tremble: the deadliest hatred of Christ rarely comes snarling; it comes dressed in the clothes of devotion. The same evil that here says "I will worship" will later kiss him in a garden and quote Scripture at his trial. But mark how the lie ends. God need only warn the wise men in a dream, and Joseph in another, and the child is gone before the swords arrive. The cradle the tyrant meant to empty, God himself was guarding; and the King whom Herod could not kill would one day lay down his life of his own accord — and take it up again.

verseByVerse.quote: After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy.
verseByVerse.commentary: The star's resumption after the consultation in Jerusalem is a small miracle that carries enormous theological weight: God is guiding these Gentiles directly to his Son, bypassing the institutions that should have led the way. "They rejoiced exceedingly with great joy" — Matthew piles up superlatives because ordinary language cannot contain what they felt. To have sought for so long, traveled so far, and now to see the destination confirmed: this is the joy of arrival. It is the prototype of every conversion, every moment when the long-sought Christ is suddenly, unmistakably near. The star had led them through uncertainty; now it led them home.

verseByVerse.quote: And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way.
verseByVerse.commentary: They found not a palace but a house; not a king enthroned but a child with his mother. And they fell down and worshiped. This is authentic worship: it does not require the trappings of majesty to recognize the reality of it. Gold (fit for a king), frankincense (used in priestly temple worship), myrrh (used in burial) — whether intended as prophetic by the magi or by Matthew's narration, these gifts speak of one who is King, Priest, and sacrificial victim. The divine warning that reroutes them away from Herod is the first of several dream-interventions in this chapter: God actively protects his Son from those who would destroy him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Flight to Egypt and the Return to Nazareth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy family flees to Egypt to escape Herod's massacre of Bethlehem's infant boys, returns after Herod's death, and settles in Nazareth — each movement fulfilling a specific Old Testament text. Matthew sees in these events not merely historical geography but the recapitulation of Israel's story: Jesus relives the Exodus (out of Egypt), the Exile (the weeping of Rachel), and Israel's wilderness sojourn (settling in a despised region). The Son of God is doing in himself what Israel failed to do: he is the true Israel, perfectly faithful where the nation was not.
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew's three fulfillment quotations here (Hos. 11:1; Jer. 31:15; and possibly Isa. 11:1 or Judg. 13:5 for "Nazarene") reveal his typological reading of history: Israel's great narrative events were not merely past occurrences but prophetic templates waiting for their ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Jesus does not merely happen to visit Egypt; he is the true Son whom God calls out of Egypt. The slaughter of the innocents does not merely echo Rachel's weeping; it is the event that makes the older weeping fully intelligible. This is not proof-texting but fulfillment theology.
verseByVerse.examples: The massacre of Bethlehem's infants is the event that silences easy answers about suffering. Matthew does not explain it; he quotes Jeremiah's lament and moves on. Rachel weeping for her children who are no more: there are moments when the only honest response to evil is grief, not explanation. The Messiah's birth caused suffering for the innocent. His death would be the answer to that suffering — not by explaining it away, but by entering it and overcoming it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, "Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him." And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt
verseByVerse.commentary: Joseph obeys immediately — "by night," without waiting for morning's reassurance or daylight's practicality. The urgency is real: Herod will move quickly. Egypt, the land of Israel's ancient bondage, now becomes the place of the Messiah's refuge — a reversal rich with symbolic freight. The one who will lead the new exodus must first reenact the sojourn in Egypt. Joseph's role in these chapters is entirely reactive to divine commands: he is told, he does. His is the faith that acts without arguing, that obeys without understanding the full plan. It is a form of faith harder than heroism — the faith of silent, sustained obedience to a voice only he has heard.

verseByVerse.quote: and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, "Out of Egypt I called my son." Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hosea 11:1 originally referred to the Exodus — God calling Israel, his corporate son, out of Egypt. Matthew sees Jesus as the true Son who fulfills that type: where Israel as God's son repeatedly failed in the wilderness, Jesus the true Son will succeed. The recapitulation is intentional, not coincidental.

This raises a fair question that troubles many an honest reader: Hosea was not even predicting the future — he was looking back at Israel and the Exodus. So is Matthew bending his words to fit Jesus? Here is the sound and simple answer. The word "fulfill" does not always mean "a prediction has come true"; often it means "filled full" — brought at last to the completion God always intended. For God himself wrote a pattern into Israel's history: Israel was his "son" (Ex 4:22), carried down into Egypt and led out again. That pattern was no accident but a shadow cast ahead, waiting for the true Son who would walk the same road and, unlike Israel, never once fail. Matthew is not playing loose with Hosea; he is reading the Old Testament exactly as the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it — as one story, by one Author, about one Savior (Lk 24:27). Two rules keep this honest, and we must hold them both: first, we never erase what a text meant in its own day (Hosea truly did mean the Exodus); second, we read every text in the light of the whole Bible, whose center is Christ. That is no license to make a verse say whatever we please — it is learning to see the Author's single design running from Genesis to the manger.

Then comes the massacre: Herod's fury at being "tricked" reveals that he knew he was pursuing a child, not an army — and killed infants anyway. The slaughter of the innocents is history's first Golgotha-shadow: the powers of this world respond to the presence of Christ with violence against the most vulnerable.

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: "A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah 31:15 was originally the voice of exile — Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, mourning as her descendants were led into Babylonian captivity past her grave at Ramah. Matthew hears that ancient lament finding its ultimate utterance in the weeping of Bethlehem's mothers. Matthew does not soften this or provide an explanation — he simply names the grief. The gospel does not protect the innocent from all suffering; it enters human suffering and redeems it from within. These children died because Christ was born; they are the first witnesses to the fact that his coming brings not comfort but a sword (Matt. 10:34) — before it brings the peace that passes understanding.

The same kind of fulfillment is at work here as in verse 15: not a bare prediction ticking over, but an ancient pattern in the life of God's people brought to its deepest point (see the note there). Yet Jeremiah's words carry a buried comfort that Matthew surely means us to find. That cry of weeping stands in the most hope-filled chapter the prophet ever wrote — the very next breath is, "Keep your voice from weeping... there is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children shall come back" (Jer 31:16–17), and a few lines on comes the promise of the new covenant itself (Jer 31:31–34). So even Bethlehem's tears are quoted from a page drenched in promise. Rachel weeps — but not forever, and not without hope.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying, "Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead."
verseByVerse.commentary: Herod dies, and the word comes: return. The phrasing echoes Moses' call to return to Egypt after those who sought his life were dead (Exod. 4:19) — another deliberate typological link. Jesus is the new Moses; his infancy recapitulates the great lawgiver's story. But Jesus is more than Moses: Moses led Israel out of Egypt; Jesus will lead a new humanity out of bondage to sin and death. The connection between the two deliverers is not coincidence but the plan of the one author who inspired both Testaments. Matthew's Gospel is saturated with this sense: the old story was always pointing here.

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joseph's fear of Archelaus is historically well-grounded: Archelaus was as brutal as his father, later deposed by Rome for his cruelties. Divine guidance does not override prudence; here the dream confirms what ordinary wisdom already suspected. The withdrawal to Galilee is divinely directed, not merely circumstantially determined. God's providence operates through human fears, political realities, and family decisions — not only through dramatic angelic interventions. He is equally sovereign in the ordinary as in the spectacular. Joseph acts on both the dream and the danger, and God honors both.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
verseByVerse.commentary: No single Old Testament verse uses the word "Nazarene" — Matthew writes "prophets" (plural), suggesting a thematic rather than verbatim fulfillment. The most likely background is Isaiah 11:1, where the Messiah is called a neser (branch/shoot) from Jesse's stump, with a possible wordplay on Nazareth. Nazareth was a despised village — "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" (John 1:46). That the Messiah would be identified with such a place fulfills the prophetic pattern of the Servant who had no form or majesty, who was despised and rejected (Isa. 53:2–3). Jesus was rejected before he preached a word. His address was scandal enough.

2.theology:
Typology and the Unity of Scripture. Matthew 2 demonstrates the Reformed doctrine of the unity of the two Testaments through typological fulfilment. When Matthew reads “Out of Egypt I called my son” as fulfilled in Jesus, he is not wresting Hosea from its context. He is reading with the grain of Scripture’s own logic: Israel was God’s son (Exod. 4:22), whose history was a pattern that pointed forward to the Son of God. The Old Testament is not a collection of proof texts waiting to be claimed; it is a single story moving toward a single climax.

Reformed biblical theology, developed through scholars like Geerhardus Vos and continued by Edmund Clowney, has called this “redemptive-historical” interpretation: reading every text in the light of its place in the one story of God’s redemptive purpose. Matthew 2 is a masterclass in this method. Every Old Testament quotation is not forced but organic — the story was always moving here, toward the child in Bethlehem, the flight to Egypt, the return to the land, the settlement in Galilee of the nations (Isa. 9:1–2).
2.examples:
Then: The Magi represent the first fruits of the Gentile mission that will be formally commissioned in Matthew 28. They come from outside the covenant, guided by general revelation (the star), and are brought to special revelation (the Scriptures) and to the King himself. This is the pattern of mission throughout Acts: Cornelius, the Ethiopian eunuch, the Philippian jailer — each guided by a mixture of seeking and sovereign orchestration to the one who is the answer to every longing.

Now: In our world, the contrast of chapter 2 repeats daily: people with no theological background travelling great distances (literally and metaphorically) to find Jesus, while those with full access to Scripture never move toward him. Church membership without worship, theological knowledge without seeking — this is Jerusalem troubled but not travelling. The question Matthew 2 poses is not “how much do you know?” but “are you moving toward the King?” The Magi found him because they went. That remains the condition of finding him today.

3.title: The Voice and the Voice
3.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, <sup>2</sup>“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>3</sup>For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” <sup>4</sup>Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey. <sup>5</sup>Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, <sup>6</sup>and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>7</sup>But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup>Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. <sup>9</sup>And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>10</sup>Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>11</sup>I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>12</sup>His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>13</sup>Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. <sup>14</sup>John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” <sup>15</sup>But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented. <sup>16</sup>And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; <sup>17</sup>and behold, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a chapter of two voices. The first voice is John’s: rough, wilderness-forged, prophetic, urgent. He wears the clothes of Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:8) and preaches with Elijah’s directness. Repent. The kingdom is not arriving on your terms. Your ancestry will not protect you. Bear fruit — now, because the axe is already laid to the root. John’s preaching is the sound of the law doing its proper work: exposing the bankruptcy of religious privilege and the urgency of genuine turning.

The second voice is the Father’s: tender, declarative, public. This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. It comes from heaven, over the Jordan, spoken not to John or the crowd but to Jesus himself — or perhaps through Jesus to the whole watching world. The Father is not waiting to see how the ministry goes before rendering his verdict; he speaks it before the first sermon, before the first miracle, before the temptation is overcome. The approval is unconditional, grounded not in performance but in person and covenant.

Between the two voices stands the baptism — and the question it raises: why does the sinless one need a baptism of repentance? Jesus answers it: to fulfil all righteousness. He is not confessing sin; he is identifying with sinners. The one who needs no baptism submits to it on behalf of those who need it most. This is the logic of substitution, enacted in water before it is enacted in blood. The baptism of Jesus is the first act of the atonement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness preaching repentance, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a voice preparing the way. His ministry draws crowds from Jerusalem and all Judea, but he reserves his sharpest words for the Pharisees and Sadducees — those who came for baptism without repentance. Jesus then comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, and at his baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." The Trinity is present at the inauguration of the Son's public ministry.
verseByVerse.theology: John's baptism is a baptism of repentance, anticipating the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. He is the last of the old-covenant prophets and the first herald of the new. His insistence on fruit worthy of repentance cuts against every form of religious privilege — ancestry, tradition, institutional membership. You cannot inherit faith; you must repent. Jesus's baptism is not a baptism of personal repentance (he has no sin) but an act of identification and consecration: he enters the waters of judgment on behalf of sinners and emerges declared righteous by the Father. The Spirit's descent and the Father's voice confirm him as the inaugurator of the new age.
verseByVerse.examples: John confronted the religious establishment with their false security: "Do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.'" The same temptation runs through every tradition — to substitute membership for repentance, heritage for faith, attendance for transformation. John's question to each worshiper is still the right one: is there fruit? Not feeling, not knowledge, not ancestry — fruit. The tree is known by what it produces.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's first word is repent — not "God loves you" or "you are enough" but a call to a complete turning of direction. Repentance (metanoia) is not mere remorse or behavioral adjustment; it is a change of mind so fundamental that it reorients the whole life. The reason given is the nearness of the kingdom: the rule of God in the person of his King is arriving, and the appropriate response to the arrival of the holy King is not celebration but self-examination. John does not soft-pedal the entrance requirement. He announces the kingdom as good news — but good news that demands an honest reckoning with who you are before the King you are about to meet.

But what did that turning actually look like for the people standing on the riverbank? To a Jew, repentance was an old and weighty word — the Hebrew teshuvah, a "returning," coming home to the LORD they had wandered from. The prophets had thundered it for centuries: "Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God" (Hos 14:1); "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:12–13). It was concrete, never sentimental: confession of sin, often with fasting and ashes, and a real forsaking of idols. Yet John pressed it to a shocking edge. There was in his day a baptism for Gentiles converting to the God of Israel; John now made Jews — sons of Abraham, temple-going, law-keeping — come down into that same water, as though they too were outsiders who needed to come in. Repentance meant letting go of every proud "but I have Abraham as my father" (v. 9) and turning with the heart. And John demanded proof: "bear fruit in keeping with repentance" (v. 8) — share your coat, deal honestly, stop your extortion (Lk 3:10–14). A turning you could see.

And today? The heart of it has not changed an inch. Repentance is still a Spirit-given change of mind that turns from sin to God and from self-trust to Christ — not a single tearful moment but the daily set of a whole life (it was Luther's very first thesis that the believer's entire life is one of repentance). Our temptation is just the old one in new dress: we lean on our churchgoing, our baptism, our decent name, our Christian family — our own "child of Abraham." John's word still falls like an axe at the root (v. 10): none of that is the turning itself. Yet hear the sweetness in it — this is no demand to earn God's favor. It is the "godly grief" that "produces a repentance that leads to salvation" (2 Cor 7:10), the homeward turn of a heart that grace has already begun to thaw. We repent not to make the King draw near, but because in Christ he already has.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'" Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 40:3 announced a voice that would prepare the way of the LORD — the divine name, Yahweh — for his coming. Matthew applies it to John preparing the way for Jesus, a staggering identification: Jesus is Yahweh coming to his people. John's clothing and diet identify him as a prophet in the tradition of Elijah (2 Kings 1:8), whose return before the great day of the LORD was promised in Malachi 4:5. John is not wearing prophet's clothes as a costume; he inhabits the prophetic calling with his whole life, refusing comfort, refusing the establishment, living in the wilderness as a sign that the old order is passing and something wholly new is coming.

And what did "prepare the way... make his paths straight" mean to those who first heard it? It is, indeed, the language of a royal arrival. In the ancient East, before a great king set out, crews went ahead to ready the road — filling in the valleys, cutting down the hills, clearing the rocks, straightening the bends — so the king's procession could sweep through unhindered. Isaiah's very next verse paints it plainly: "Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low... and the rough places a plain" (Isa 40:4). But the King in view is no earthly monarch; it is the LORD himself. Isaiah 40 opens the great book of comfort to a people in exile, and its promise is a new exodus: God coming in person to lead his people home across the desert, like a shepherd-king at the head of the march (Isa 40:10–11). The "highway in the wilderness" was that homeward road (cf. Isa 35:8).

By Jesus' day the verse had become a watchword of hope. The wilderness community at Qumran, beside the Dead Sea, took these very words and withdrew into the desert "to prepare the way of the LORD," certain God was about to act. So when John appears in that same wilderness crying Isaiah 40:3, every devout ear caught the freight of it: the King is coming — ready the road. And the road-work, then as now, is the heart: the proud hills of self-righteousness brought low, the sunken valleys of despair filled with hope, the crooked dealings made straight. Repentance is simply how a sinner levels the ground for a holy King.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds streaming to John in the wilderness is itself a fulfillment of prophetic pattern: the people going out to meet God's word in the wild places, as Israel had once done at Sinai. Baptism in John's context was not a new rite but a well-known practice: Gentile converts to Judaism underwent ritual washing as a symbol of cleansing from their old life. John applies it to Jews — a radical provocation. He is saying: you need to be cleansed too. You are no cleaner before God by birth than any Gentile. The confession of sins was the necessary accompaniment — there is no point to the washing without the honesty it symbolizes.

What sins would those people have confessed as they went down into the water? We are not left to guess, for John himself named some when the crowds pressed him, "What then shall we do?" To ordinary folk he said: you keep two coats while your neighbor shivers and goes hungry — that tight-fisted selfishness is sin (Lk 3:11). To the tax collectors, who fattened their purses by charging more than Rome required: your greed and extortion (Lk 3:13). To the soldiers: your bullying, your false accusations, your grumbling discontent with your pay (Lk 3:14). And to the Pharisees and Sadducees who came, his word was sharper still — their pride, their hypocrisy, their smug trust in being "children of Abraham" (vv. 7–9). Behind it all lay the sins the prophets had forever exposed: dishonest scales and withheld wages (Mal 3:5), worship that was all lips and no heart (Isa 29:13), the quiet idolatry of loving money and reputation more than God. Run the list down the Ten Commandments and you meet every one of them. And if we are honest, we meet ourselves there too — their sins were not strange and ancient relics; they were ours.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit in keeping with repentance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's sharpest words are for the most religious. The Pharisees and Sadducees were theological opponents of each other — John addresses them as a single brood. "Vipers" evokes the serpent of Eden: they are children of the deceiver, carrying poison under religious clothing. "Who warned you?" — John is skeptical of their motives. They may be coming for social reasons, political reasons, curiosity — but without genuine repentance. The test is fruit: repentance that produces no change in behavior is not repentance. John refuses to process them through the rite without pressing the reality. A baptism received without repentance is just getting wet.

Single out that command — "bear fruit in keeping with repentance" — for it is the very thing John is after. The picture is an orchard: a tree shows what it truly is by what hangs on its branches, not by its leaves. It is an old image; Israel was God's vineyard, planted and tended and looked to for a harvest of justice (Isa 5:1–7). So John is saying, in effect: do not show me your pedigree or your ceremonies; show me a changed life. Concretely that meant what he would soon tell the crowds — share your coat, deal honestly, stop your extortion (Lk 3:11–14); and Paul would later echo the very phrase, pressing men to "do works worthy of their repentance" (Acts 26:20). But notice the order, for it is everything. Fruit does not make a tree good; a good tree bears good fruit. John is not telling these men to manufacture good works in order to earn their standing — that was the Pharisees' whole mistake; he is telling them that real repentance always shows, that a turning no one can see is no turning at all. And the branch bears fruit only by staying joined to the vine (Jn 15:5): the change John demands is one only the Coming One can work in a heart.

A word on these two parties, for they could hardly have been less alike. The Pharisees were the great lay movement of the common people — their name likely means "the separated ones." Zealous for the Law, they hedged it round with a vast "tradition of the elders," the oral rules meant to guard every commandment, and they were scrupulous about tithing, ritual purity, and the Sabbath. They believed firmly in the resurrection of the dead, in angels and spirits, in a coming judgment and Messiah. Devout and admired by ordinary folk, they were undone by the very thing they prized: their religion curdled into the self-righteous show Jesus would later lay bare (Matt 23). The Sadducees were the opposite number — the wealthy priestly aristocracy who ran the temple, the high-priestly families and their circle. They held only the five books of Moses as binding and flatly denied the resurrection, angels, and any life beyond this one (Acts 23:8); worldly, here-and-now men who kept comfortable terms with Rome to guard their power. When the temple fell in A.D. 70, they vanished with it.

Bitter rivals, then — yet here they walk down to the Jordan together, and one day they will conspire together to kill the Lord. Nothing unites enemies like a shared threat to their religion. John sees through the unlikely alliance in an instant, and will not flatter it: "You brood of vipers."

And what did they hear in "the wrath to come"? Not a new idea at all, but one straight from their own Scriptures. The prophets had long spoken of "the Day of the LORD" — a coming day when God would pour out his anger on sin, judge the wicked, and set the world right: "a day of wrath... of distress and anguish" (Zeph 1:15), the day that "comes, burning like an oven" (Mal 4:1), of which Malachi asked, "who can endure the day of his coming?" (Mal 3:2). Amos had warned that for the complacent it would be darkness and not light (Amos 5:18–20). By John's day this expectation had ripened, sharpened further by the rabbis and the apocalyptic writers into a settled hope of a great Day of Judgment when Messiah would come, the dead would rise, and God's wrath would fall. But here lay the deadly assumption John meant to shatter: the Pharisee and Sadducee took it for granted that this wrath was for Gentiles and sinners — that they, as sons of Abraham, would stand safe among the spectators. John's question lands like a thunderclap: "Who warned YOU to flee from the wrath to come?" The fire is not only for pagan Rome and the obvious sinner; it is for every unrepentant heart, the religious ones first of all. And the only shelter is not ancestry but repentance — and, as the next verses will show, the Coming One who himself will pass through the fire for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not presume to say to yourselves, "We have Abraham as our father," for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The appeal to Abrahamic descent was the deepest form of Jewish religious security — covenant membership by birth. John demolishes it: God could make Abrahamic children from the pebbles underfoot if he chose. The covenant is not a biological inheritance; it is a gift received through faith and evidenced by fruit. The axe already at the root signals eschatological urgency: this is not a gentle warning but an imminent verdict. The tree that produces no fruit is not warned again — it is cut down. John is announcing judgment as the context in which repentance must occur. Grace is real, but so is the ax.

This is the place to pause, for verse 10 can sound like salvation by works: bear fruit, or be cut down and burned. Hear the Reformed answer plainly. We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone; our works add nothing to the verdict, for we are justified not by what we do but by what Christ has done, received by faith (Eph 2:8–9). Yet — and this is the hinge — the faith that justifies is never a faith that stays alone. A living faith bears fruit as surely as a living tree does; "faith apart from works is dead" (Jas 2:17). So John is not saying that fruit earns life; he is saying that fruitlessness exposes death. The barren tree is cut down not because it failed to earn its place, but because its barrenness proves it was never truly alive. When Scripture speaks of a judgment "according to works" (Rom 2:6), it means our works are the evidence brought into the court, not the price paid at the bar — they reveal the root, they do not become it. The old summary holds: we are saved by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone.
