And even the fruit is grace, for God must first make the tree good; an axe never yet turned a dead tree into a living one. That making-alive is the Coming One's work, not ours.

verseByVerse.quote: I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's self-description is striking in its humility: he is not worthy to carry the sandals of the one coming. Carrying a master's sandals was a task too degrading for a Jewish disciple to perform for his rabbi — and John says he is not even at that level. The contrast between water-baptism and Spirit-and-fire baptism is the contrast between the outer symbol and the inner reality. The Spirit transforms; the fire purifies or judges. The winnowing image makes the point concrete: the coming one will separate the genuine from the counterfeit — not eventually, not symbolically, but finally and completely. There is no third category between wheat and chaff.

Single out the three things John says here. First, his water baptism: "I baptize you with water for repentance." The water was a sign, no more — an outward washing that pictured the inward cleansing the people sought, and sealed their turning from sin as they made ready for the King. It could wet the body and mark the confession, but it could not change the heart; it pointed beyond itself to One who could. (Ezekiel had long before married the two: clean water sprinkled, and a new heart and Spirit given — Ezek 36:25–27.)

Second, the contrast. John is the greatest of the prophets, yet he says he is not fit even to carry the sandals of the Coming One — the task of the lowest slave. He gives the sign; Jesus gives the substance. John can lower you into the river; only Jesus can baptize you in the Spirit. The forerunner washes the outside; the King transforms the inside.

Third, that baptism "with the Holy Spirit and fire." The Spirit-baptism is the great gospel promise: the Coming One pours out God's own Spirit to give new birth, to indwell and transform — poured out in full at Pentecost (Acts 2). But what of the fire? Here readers differ. Some take it as the Spirit's refining warmth on believers, recalling Pentecost's "tongues as of fire." The better reading, though, is fire as judgment, and the context settles it: the same passage has the fruitless tree "thrown into the fire" (v. 10) and the chaff burned "with unquenchable fire" (v. 12) — and one does not refine wheat with unquenchable fire. John speaks to a mixed crowd, and the one Messiah's coming divides it in two: he baptizes the repentant with the Spirit unto life, while the impenitent he meets with the fire of judgment. And here is the wonder for all who are his — the reason the wheat need never dread that fire is that the Coming One would himself pass through it for them at the cross.

Single out that last picture, for John's whole message lies inside it once you see the farm behind it. Picture an ancient threshing floor — a flat, hard patch of ground out on a breezy hilltop. The cut grain is spread there and trodden until the kernels break loose from their dry husks. Then the farmer takes his winnowing fork, a broad wooden shovel, and tosses the whole mass up into the evening wind. The heavy, solid grain drops straight back to the floor; the light, empty chaff is caught by the wind and blown aside. He gathers the good wheat into his barn to keep, and sweeps up the useless chaff to burn.

Now hear what John is telling them. The Coming One is not only the Savior who gives the Spirit — the winnowing fork is already in his hand, so he is also the Judge. Until he comes, wheat and chaff lie mingled on the one floor, and to the eye they look like a single heap: the truly repentant and the merely religious stand side by side in the crowd at the Jordan, much alike. But his coming is the wind that sorts them. What has real weight — a heart truly turned, a faith that bears fruit — falls safely to the floor and is gathered in; what is hollow husk is swept away. There are only two heaps and only two destinations: the barn or the fire, and "unquenchable fire" means the verdict is final. And the fork is in his hand now — not a distant threat but a present summons (the prophets had long used the image; "the wicked are like chaff that the wind drives away," Ps 1:4). So the metaphor puts one plain question to every heart: when the wind blows, will I prove wheat or chaff? And the gospel answer is just as plain — the chaff is not bad wheat but empty husk, and the way to be found wheat is not to be impressive in oneself but to come to the Coming One in repentance and faith, the very One who took the fire in his people's place.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. John would have prevented him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus comes from Galilee — the despised north, far from Jerusalem — to submit to baptism by his own forerunner. John's protest is theologically precise: the baptism is a baptism of repentance, and Jesus has nothing to repent of. The logic runs the wrong direction: the sinless one should not be washed by the sinner; the one who baptizes with the Spirit should not be baptized with water. John understands more about Jesus than most of Israel does. His protest is not false modesty but accurate theological reflection. The question he raises — "why would you come to me?" — is the right question, and Jesus's answer is astonishing.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered him, "Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." Then he consented. And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Fulfill all righteousness" is one of Matthew's key phrases: Jesus came not to bypass the law's requirements but to meet them all on behalf of his people. His baptism is not personal repentance but solidarity — he enters the waters of judgment as the representative of sinners, identifying with the people he came to save. The opening of the heavens signals the end of the silence between God and his people that had lasted since Malachi. The Spirit descending as a dove echoes the Spirit hovering over the waters of creation (Gen. 1:2) — a new creation is beginning. At the inauguration of Jesus's ministry, all three persons of the Trinity are present and active.

Was the Spirit not already with Jesus before this moment? Indeed he was — fully, and from the very first. This child was conceived by the Holy Spirit (1:20); as the eternal Son he was never for one instant without the Spirit, never less than fully God, never touched by sin. So we must not picture the Spirit arriving where he had been absent, nor imagine (as some old errors taught) that Jesus only now became the Son or the Christ. Nothing changes in his person at the Jordan.

What happens, then, is two things at once, and both are true. First, it is his anointing. "Christ" means "Anointed One," and here the Father visibly anoints him with the Spirit to begin his public work as Messiah — Isaiah's long-promised Servant: "Behold my servant... I have put my Spirit upon him" (Isa 42:1; cf. Isa 61:1; Acts 10:38). The Spirit who had always dwelt in him now equips the incarnate Son, in his true humanity, for the ministry that begins this very day. Second, it is a sign for others to see. John himself tells us he did not know for certain who the Messiah was until he watched the Spirit descend and remain on him — that was the appointed sign (Jn 1:32–34). So the dove was no empty show; it was God's own testimony, pointing out his Son to John, and through John to us. And mark the sweetness: the Spirit comes to rest, to abide — not to flutter off again as he had with the prophets of old. The very One on whom the Spirit now settles is the One who will pour that same Spirit out on all who are his (v. 11). He is anointed as Head, that the oil might run down to the whole body.

verseByVerse.quote: and behold, a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Father's voice at the Jordan combines two Old Testament texts: Psalm 2:7 ("You are my Son") and Isaiah 42:1 ("my servant... in whom my soul delights"). Psalm 2 is the royal psalm of the messianic King; Isaiah 42 is the first Servant Song of the suffering Servant. From the beginning, the Father defines his Son's identity in both categories: he is the triumphant King and the obedient Servant who suffers. The words "with whom I am well pleased" are spoken before Jesus has done anything in his public ministry — before a sermon, before a miracle, before the cross. The Father's delight is not earned; it is given. This is the fountain from which all of Jesus's ministry flows: he acts out of a secure identity, not toward an uncertain approval.

3.theology:
The Trinity at the Jordan. Matthew 3:16–17 is one of the clearest Trinitarian texts in the New Testament. The Son stands in the water; the Spirit descends upon the Son; the Father speaks from heaven. Three distinct persons, one divine act. Reformed theology has always insisted that the doctrine of the Trinity is not a late addition to Christian thought but the grammar of the gospel itself — the structure of reality that makes salvation possible.

The baptism of Jesus is a Trinitarian event. The Father approves; the Spirit empowers; the Son obeys. This pattern runs through the whole New Testament: the Father sends, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies. The atonement is Trinitarian (the Father gave, the Son died, the Spirit regenerates); the church is Trinitarian (baptised in the name of Father, Son, and Spirit, Matt. 28:19); the Christian life is Trinitarian (praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit). The Jordan reveals the shape of everything that follows.
3.examples:
Then: John the Baptist stands in a long line of prophets who prepared the way for God’s action: Moses before Joshua, Elijah before Elisha, Isaiah before the return from exile. Each was a voice, not the Word; each pointed away from himself. John is the culmination of this pattern — the last and greatest of the preparers. His greatness lay precisely in his self-effacement: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Every faithful preacher, teacher, and leader stands in John’s tradition: making straight the way, getting out of the way.

Now: The Father’s declaration over Jesus at the baptism — This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased — is the word every human being is searching for. We spend our lives seeking approval: from parents, employers, social media, achievement. The gospel announces that in Christ, the deepest possible approval has already been given — not because of what we have done but because of who he is and what he has done. The restless search for significance ends not in achievement but in adoption: we are accepted in the Beloved. That is the word the Father spoke at the Jordan, and it is addressed to everyone who is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3).

4.title: The Tested King
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. <sup>2</sup>And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup>And the tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.” <sup>4</sup>But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” <sup>5</sup>Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple <sup>6</sup>and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>7</sup>Jesus said to him, “Again it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>8</sup>Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. <sup>9</sup>And he said to him, “All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.” <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>11</sup>Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him. <sup>12</sup>Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew to Galilee. <sup>13</sup>And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, <sup>14</sup>so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: <sup>15</sup>“The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles — <sup>16</sup>the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned.” <sup>17</sup>From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>18</sup>While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>19</sup>And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” <sup>20</sup>Immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. <sup>22</sup>Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. <sup>23</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. <sup>24</sup>So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them. <sup>25</sup>And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the axis on which the Gospel turns. The Spirit who descended at the baptism immediately drives Jesus into the wilderness — not as abandonment but as commission. The forty days echo Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, where God’s people failed at every test. Jesus succeeds at every one, and he does it using the same weapon available to Israel and to us: the written Word of God. Three times the devil attacks; three times Jesus answers with Deuteronomy. The true Israel passes where the nation failed.

Each temptation targets a specific aspect of Jesus’ identity and mission. Turn stones to bread: use divine power for personal comfort. Throw yourself from the temple: leverage God’s promises for public spectacle. Bow to me: gain the kingdoms without the cross. Every temptation is a shortcut past suffering to glory — and Jesus refuses every one. There is no crown without the cross, no glory without the grave, no kingdom without Calvary. Satan offers the destination without the path; Jesus insists on the path.

Then the ministry begins — in Galilee of the Gentiles (Isa. 9:1), the region of mixed ethnicity and questionable reputation, the last place a respectable rabbi would choose as his base. The people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light. The light does not go to the well-lit; it goes to the dark. And the first disciples he calls are working men with nets and boats — not scribes with scrolls. The kingdom of heaven is staffed from the margins, then and now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Temptation of Jesus in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. The forty days echo Israel's forty years in the wilderness; the three temptations echo Israel's great failures — bread, testing God, idolatry. But where Israel fell, Jesus stands. He defeats each temptation not by miraculous power but by the word of God alone, quoting Deuteronomy three times. The temptations are not trivial: they are the offer of the kingdom by a shortcut — bread without suffering, glory without the cross, dominion without death. And he overcomes not merely as our example but as our champion — the last Adam and true Israel, whose perfect obedience is reckoned to all who are his, so that we now resist temptation not to win God's favor but from within the victory he has already won for us.
verseByVerse.theology: The temptation of Jesus is not merely a test of personal willpower but a cosmic conflict at the hinge of redemptive history. The devil who succeeded in Eden now faces the second Adam in a wilderness, and loses. Jesus is revealed as the true Israel — obedient where the nation failed — and the true Adam — resisting the serpent where the first man did not. His weapon is the word of God alone: not angelic power, not divine fiat, but the Scripture he has internalized and believes. This models the Christian's resource in temptation: not mystical experience but the word of God believed and obeyed.
verseByVerse.examples: The devil's three temptations all contain a kernel of legitimate desire: food is not evil, protection is real, authority over the nations is Jesus's ultimate inheritance. The temptation is in the shortcut — get the good thing the wrong way, on the wrong timetable, from the wrong source. This is how temptation almost always works: it offers real goods through illegitimate means. Jesus refuses not because the ends are bad but because the path bypasses the Father's will and the cross's necessity.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit who descended at the Jordan now leads Jesus into the wilderness — not away from God's will but deeper into it. The temptation is not an accident or an ambush; it is a divinely appointed trial. Forty days and forty nights deliberately echoes Moses on Sinai (Exod. 34:28) and Elijah's journey to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), as well as Israel's forty years in the wilderness. Jesus recapitulates these great prophetic patterns in himself. He was hungry — genuinely, physically hungry after six weeks without food. The temptation begins at the point of real need. The devil is shrewd enough not to waste his best offer on someone who has everything; he waits for the moment of vulnerability.

verseByVerse.quote: And the tempter came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread." But he answered, "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The "if" is not genuine doubt — the devil knows exactly who Jesus is. It is a provocation: use your divine power for your own comfort. The temptation is for Jesus to act as Son of God independently of the Father's provision and timetable, to bypass the suffering and take the sustenance. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3 — God's word to Israel after he fed them with manna: the lesson of the manna was that physical bread is not the deepest need; the word of God is. Jesus applies Israel's lesson to himself: he will not use divine power for personal comfort when the Father has not provided. The Son of God chose to be hungry rather than to be satisfied outside the Father's will. This is the shape of his whole mission.

But how do we know it was the Father's will for Jesus to stay hungry rather than make bread for himself — can we be sure that is the right reading? Three things make it firm. First, the Spirit had just led him here on purpose: "Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted" (v. 1). The hunger is no accident of the road; it is a God-appointed ordeal. Second, weigh what the devil is really urging. There is nothing wrong with bread, nor with Jesus' power — he will later multiply loaves for thousands (14:19). The poison is in the "if": prove your sonship by serving yourself, snatch relief at my suggestion, step out from under your Father's hand and timetable. Third, and most decisively, Jesus tells us himself how he reads the moment by the very text he reaches for. He answers with Deuteronomy 8:3, a verse about God deliberately letting his people hunger to teach them dependence. In choosing that verse Jesus names his own situation: this is a God-ordained hunger, and the faithful response is trust, not self-supply. We are not imposing a guess on the scene; we are reading it exactly as he read it. (It remains an inference — no line says "the Father commanded him to stay hungry" — but an inference anchored in the Spirit's leading and in our Lord's own Scripture.)

It helps, too, to stand back in Deuteronomy 8 itself. Moses is on the plains of Moab, looking back over forty years, and he explains why God led Israel the long, hard way: "that he might humble you, testing you... and he... let you hunger and fed you with manna... that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone" (Deut 8:2–3). God himself emptied their hands — no crops in that desert — and then sent bread from heaven they had never seen and could not make, bread to be gathered fresh each morning in simple trust. The whole aim was to wean them off the lie that life is secured by what we can provide for ourselves, and to teach them that they lived by the word and provision of God, day upon day. Israel, sadly, mostly failed the lesson, grumbling and craving and demanding bread on their own terms (Ex 16; Num 11). Now see why Jesus reaches for these very words. He is the true Son, the true Israel called out of Egypt (2:15), reliving their wilderness test — forty days for their forty years, hungry in the same kind of waste. Where Israel said in effect, "give us bread or we perish," Jesus says: my life rests not on bread I can conjure but on every word from my Father's mouth — including his word that I be here, and wait, and trust. He renders in obedience the very lesson Israel would not learn.

So what is the deep message of this temptation — and of all three? It is, first and gloriously, this: Adam was tempted in a garden where every tree was good, and fell; Israel was tested in the wilderness, and fell; Jesus, in a far harsher wilderness, starving and alone, was tempted at every point — and prevailed. He is the last Adam and the true Israel, the obedient Son who keeps the covenant we all broke, and he keeps it as our representative, our champion. His victory is not merely admirable; it is reckoned to us, the spotless obedience that becomes our very standing before God. Thank you, Lord, indeed — he won the battle we never could. Yet that bedrock holds up a second word as well. Because he triumphed for us, and now lives in us by his Spirit, his way becomes our way: when we are tempted we resist as he did — not by willpower or cleverness but with "it is written," trusting the Father's word and bowing to his will. And here is the comfort that keeps this from curdling into a crushing demand — the Christ who was tempted in every way is able to help those who are tempted (Heb 2:18; 4:15). The order is everything. We do not climb up to God's acceptance by fighting temptation like Jesus; we fight temptation because in Jesus we are already accepted, and never once alone in the fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, 'He will command his angels concerning you,' and 'On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.'" Jesus said to him, "Again it is written, 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second temptation is subtler: the devil quotes Scripture. Psalm 91:11–12 promises angelic protection to the one who trusts God. The temptation is to force God's hand — to manufacture a situation that requires divine intervention, thereby proving sonship through a spectacle rather than through obedience. Throwing himself from the temple pinnacle would have been the ultimate public demonstration, drawing a crowd and commanding instant recognition. But it would have been faith demanding proof rather than faith resting in promise. The devil can quote the Bible accurately and use it to tempt. Knowing the text is not the same as submitting to its intent.

Deuteronomy 6:16 — "You shall not put the LORD your God to the test" — was given in the context of Israel's demand for signs at Massah. Jesus applies it to the devil's proposal: manufacturing a crisis to force God's response is not trust but presumption. Real faith does not require God to prove himself on demand. Jesus refuses to use Scripture as a lever to compel God, choosing instead to trust the Father without proof.

Stand for a moment at the place Deuteronomy 6:16 points back to. The verse runs in full, "You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah." At Massah (Ex 17:1–7) Israel had no water, and instead of trusting the God who had just split the sea and rained down manna, they turned on Moses and snarled, "Is the LORD among us or not?" They demanded that God prove himself on the spot, on their terms — and Moses named the place Massah, "testing," a byword ever after for the sin of cornering God (Ps 95:8–9). To "put God to the test" is to refuse to trust him until he performs a proof on demand. Now watch the straight line to the pinnacle: the devil invites Jesus to do exactly that — to fling himself down and make the Father dispatch angels, a manufactured emergency to force a divine rescue. It is Massah all over again, only now wrapped in a Bible verse.

But notice the sharp twist, for it teaches us much. Israel tested God out of open unbelief: "Is he even here?" The devil dresses the very same sin as its opposite — as daring faith: "You trust your Father? Then prove it — leap, and let him catch you!" Jesus sees through the costume. A faith that must have a spectacle to lean on is not faith but presumption; a trust that demands proof has already stopped trusting. Where Israel said, "Make God show he is with us," Jesus answers, in effect, "I will not put my Father in the dock; I already rest in his care, and need no stunt to secure it." The weak and starving Son trusts the promise without forcing the promise — the very thing Israel, with full bellies and water from the rock, would not do.

And the application? As with the first temptation, the first note is praise: where Israel failed the Massah test, and where we fail it still, the true Israel stood firm, and his unwavering trust is counted as ours — rejoice, he passed the exam we keep failing. Yet there is a real lesson here for the Christian too, and a needed one: beware of testing God. We do it whenever we treat his promises as levers to pull, manufacturing a crisis and then calling our recklessness "faith." Picture a man who stops taking the medicine his doctor prescribed and announces he is "trusting God to heal him," or who makes some rash, ruinous leap with his money and assumes God is bound to catch him. That is not the faith that rests in God; it is the presumption that dictates to him. Real faith uses the means God provides and waits on him without demanding he prove his love on cue — and we can walk that road, because the One who walked it perfectly now lives in us and helps us walk it (Heb 4:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." Then Jesus said to him, "Be gone, Satan! For it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third temptation then broadens in scope: from personal need (bread), to public recognition (the temple), to global dominion (all kingdoms). The devil escalates toward what Jesus actually came to possess.

And the offer is staggering: everything he came to win — the kingdoms of the world — held out at the price of one act of worship. This is the kingdom without the cross, global authority without Gethsemane, inheritance without suffering. That the devil could offer "all these" requires that he has some genuine, if temporary and delegated, authority over them (John 12:31; 2 Cor. 4:4). Jesus does not dispute the offer's reality; he refuses its terms. "Be gone, Satan!" — the only point at which Jesus directly commands the tempter. The worship of God alone is not negotiable, not for any conceivable reward. Jesus will receive the kingdoms — but through the cross, not around it. The path of obedience cannot be bypassed.

Two angles open here for our own hearts. The first is to lift our eyes and worship the Conqueror. The deepest pull of this third temptation was the shortcut — the crown without the cross, the kingdom for the bargain price of one compromised act of worship. Jesus would indeed inherit the nations; the Father had promised, "I will make the nations your heritage" (Ps 2:8). But he would not take them from the devil's hand on the devil's terms. He chose Gethsemane over the easy throne, obedience over the bypass, and with a single word he bound the strong man: "Be gone, Satan!" And mark the glory of it — he won. By the long road of the cross and the empty tomb he could at last stand on another mountain and say, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me" (28:18). He gained the very kingdoms Satan dangled, but gained them rightly, and gained them for us. Here is our song: the world had a rightful King who could not be bought, who conquered where Adam and Israel and every one of us has failed.

The second angle is closer to home. This same temptation comes to us in a hundred ordinary disguises, and underneath it is always a question of worship: the prize you long for, offered at the price of a small bow to something other than God. The promotion is yours if you will fudge the figures. The comfort, the security, the applause you crave can be had if you will quietly serve money, or status, or self, and give God only your leftovers. Satan's oldest trick is unchanged — he shows you the kingdoms and hides the bill. The lesson of the mountain is to answer as Jesus answered: refuse the shortcut, worship God alone, and trust that his costly road is the only one that leads to a kingdom that lasts. The crown still comes by way of the cross; the servant is not above his Master (16:24). And we can say our own "be gone" not in raw willpower but as people already joined to the Victor — for in him we are "more than conquerors" (Rom 8:37), and every shortcut we turn down was only ever a path to a kingdom that crumbles.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The devil departs — not defeated forever (Luke adds "until an opportune time," Luke 4:13) but defeated here. The angels who would have been summoned by a dramatic leap from the temple now come quietly, without spectacle, to minister to the exhausted Son of God. This is the pattern of the kingdom: the glory that comes through suffering, the service that follows faithfulness rather than preceding it. The angelic ministry after the temptation echoes Elijah's experience at Horeb (1 Kings 19:5–7): God provides for those who trust him, in his time and by his means. Jesus had refused supernatural bread from his own power; now the Father provides bread through angels. Obedience is always vindicated — though rarely on our timetable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — The Beginning of Ministry in Galilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After John's arrest, Jesus withdraws to Galilee and settles in Capernaum, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy about light dawning in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali. He begins preaching the same message as John — "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" — and immediately calls his first disciples: Peter, Andrew, James, and John. They leave their nets and their father without delay and follow him. Matthew concludes with a summary of Jesus's ministry: teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and affliction, drawing crowds from all of Syria and the surrounding regions.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus's settlement in Galilee of the Gentiles fulfills Isaiah 9:1–2: the regions most despised in Israel — the northern territories given first to Assyrian darkness — receive the first light of the kingdom. This is the pattern of the kingdom: light to the edges, hope to the marginalized, the first shall be last and the last first. The calling of the disciples is not recruitment but sovereign summons: "Follow me" is a command, not an invitation to consider. Their immediate response models discipleship — not eventual obedience after weighing options, but the abandonment of everything for the one who calls.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples left their nets immediately. They left their boats. James and John left their father. The commentaries note what Matthew stresses: the immediacy and totality of their response. Jesus did not give them time to consult, calculate, or negotiate terms. He called; they followed. This is the New Testament pattern of conversion — not gradual warming to the idea of Jesus but the decisive moment of abandonment and allegiance. The question the passage presses: what are your nets? What would obedience cost you to leave behind?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,
verseByVerse.commentary: John's arrest is not explained here — it will be in chapter 14 — but it is the trigger for Jesus's public ministry to begin. The withdrawal to Galilee is not retreat but fulfillment: Jesus goes to exactly the place Isaiah said the light would dawn. Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee becomes his ministry headquarters — a fishing town, not a religious center, in a region considered by southern Jews to be half-Gentile and fully suspect. That the Son of God chose to base his ministry in Galilee of the Gentiles rather than Jerusalem is itself a statement about who the kingdom is for. He goes to the margins, not to the center.

verseByVerse.quote: so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles —"
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah 9:1 originally spoke of the reversal of the shame brought on the northern territories by the Assyrian invasion of 733 BC — the regions of Zebulun and Naphtali, which suffered first, would be "honored" in the day of the Messiah's coming. Matthew sees that promise fulfilled in Jesus's choice to minister there. The phrase "Galilee of the Gentiles" is important: even in Isaiah's day, the north was ethnically mixed. That the Messiah brings his first concentrated ministry to this mixed region anticipates the Great Commission's universal scope. The kingdom begins at the edges of Jewish respectability and moves outward.

verseByVerse.quote: "the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 9:2 — one of the great promises of the Old Testament — reaches its fulfillment not in a Jerusalem spectacular but in a Galilean teacher walking along a lakeshore. "Darkness" and "shadow of death" are not mere metaphors for ignorance; they describe the human condition before God — estranged, condemned, without hope. The "great light" is not an idea or a movement but a person. Jesus is the light that Isaiah promised: not a lamp that illuminates part of the darkness, but a light that dawns — changes the whole condition, makes the night itself into day. The image is of sunrise: total, irreversible, making everything visible at once. In Isaiah's own day the promised dawn was first the daybreak after the Assyrian night — a real but partial relief for the broken northern tribes; in Jesus the true Sun rises at last over a far deeper darkness, the night of sin and death itself, and not for Zebulun and Naphtali only but for the whole Gentile world those border lands had long been mingled with.

And mark what kind of light this is, for here the wonder deepens past words. A lamp only shows you the room; this Light does what no lamp can — it saves. It does not merely expose the shadow of death; it breaks it. Malachi had promised, "the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings" (Mal 4:2), and Zechariah sang of "the sunrise from on high" that would visit us "to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace" (Lk 1:78–79). This is light that warms the frozen and heals the wounded, light that speaks life into the dead as it once spoke a world out of nothing — "Let light shine out of darkness," the God who "has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6). To sit in darkness is to be lost and condemned; but when this Sun rises on a soul, the night does not merely become visible — it is over. The dead man blinks, and breathes, and lives. That is what dawned on Galilee. That is what can dawn on you.

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus's inaugural message is identical to John's (3:2), but the context has changed: John announced the coming one; Jesus announces the arrival of the kingdom in his own person. "From that time" marks a turning point in Matthew's narrative. Jesus does not settle in and develop a ministry gradually; he begins immediately to preach and immediately to call.

But what is this "kingdom of heaven" Jesus announces? (Matthew, with reverent Jewish caution about uttering the divine name, says "heaven" where Mark and Luke say "of God"; they mean one and the same thing — the kingly rule of God.) When the average Jew heard the word "kingdom," his heart leapt to a long-cherished hope: that God would at last act in power to throw off the pagan boot of Rome, restore the throne of David, regather his scattered people, judge the wicked, and reign in peace and justice from Zion. It was a hope soaked in the prophets — "your God reigns" (Isa 52:7), the everlasting dominion given to the Son of Man (Dan 7:13–14), the kingdom that shall never be destroyed (Dan 2:44). But for most it was a largely earthly, national dream: a Messiah on a war-horse and Israel's golden age restored.

Jesus takes up that ancient hope and both fulfills and transfigures it. The kingdom he brings is God's saving reign breaking into history in his own person — yet it comes first not against Rome but against sin, Satan, and death; not by the sword but by a cross; not in one blaze of glory but quietly, like a buried seed taking root in repentant hearts before it fills the earth. "If it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (12:28) — it is already present in him; yet its full and visible glory still awaits his return. So the kingdom is deeper, wider, and more glorious than they dreamed, and it asks not for revolution but for repentance.

This is the key to the much-debated phrase "at hand." The word means "has drawn near," and it has been read in a few ways — as a kingdom merely soon to come, as one that has actually arrived in Jesus, or, best, as both at once. The historic Reformed reading is exactly this "already and not yet": in Christ's first coming the kingdom has truly and powerfully arrived, present now and advancing through the gospel, the Spirit, and the church, and it will be consummated in fullness only when the King returns. Here, in love and honesty, is where this reading parts from the dispensational understanding many dear brothers and sisters hold (perhaps your own fellowship). On that view, Jesus offered Israel a literal, earthly, Davidic kingdom; when the nation's leaders refused him it was postponed, the present church age came in as an unforeseen interval, and the promised reign will be set up only in a future thousand-year kingdom centered on Israel and Jerusalem. The Reformed conviction is different: the kingdom was not postponed but inaugurated; the one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, is the true Israel; and the Old Testament promises of throne and land are not shelved but fulfilled in Christ and, at last, in the new heavens and new earth. We hold this clearly — and hold it humbly, remembering how much we share with those who differ: that Christ is King, that his promises are sure, and that he is coming again in glory. On those great certainties every believing heart stands together.

verseByVerse.quote: While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene is deliberately ordinary: two working men ankle-deep in fish and routine. The kingdom does not come through unusual people in unusual places; it breaks into the ordinary and calls it to something greater.

"Follow me" is the whole of the call — no exam, no conditions. And "I will make you fishers of men" promises transformation through following, not before it: Jesus makes them what they cannot make themselves, and their part is simply to come. Their response is the word Matthew loves for true discipleship — immediately. Not "after I settle my affairs," but at once. The nets were their livelihood and identity; they left them. To follow Christ has always cost something real; a discipleship that costs nothing is not discipleship.

What does following look like for us, who cannot walk Galilee at his side? Notice that Peter and Andrew left their nets — but not everyone Jesus called did; many followed him right where they were. So following is less about which job you quit than about who now owns your life: Jesus as Lord of the very boat you are in — your work, your family, your ordinary Tuesday. In practice it means hearing his voice in his Word and obeying; turning from sin and trusting him afresh each morning; loving him above all; taking up your cross daily (Lk 9:23) — which is not bearing life's random troubles but dying each morning to self-rule, saying no to your own will and comfort for his sake, as a condemned man once shouldered the beam to his own execution; and abiding in him as a branch in the vine (Jn 15:5) — staying so joined to Christ that his life flows into you, for "apart from me you can do nothing"; the fruit grows from the union, not from your striving. And it looks like being made a "fisher of men," an ordinary person through whom he quietly draws others to himself.

But perhaps you wonder whether you are doing it well — and here the gospel speaks tenderly. Following is a direction, not a flawless performance. These first followers argued over greatness, slept when he needed them, scattered at his arrest; Peter denied him three times — yet they were following still, and Jesus did not cast them off but restored Peter and made him a rock. Remember his promise here: "I will make you." He does the making; you do the coming — not transform yourself and then follow, but follow and let him transform you. So if your heart is turned toward him, grieving sin, longing to obey, and rising again after every fall, you are following, however stumbling it feels. Your standing rests not on the quality of your following but on the strength of the One you follow, "who began a good work in you" and "will bring it to completion" (Phil 1:6). Keep near him; he will keep you.

verseByVerse.quote: And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John left not only their nets but their father — a detail Matthew adds to sharpen the cost. Zebedee is not abandoned carelessly; he apparently had hired servants (Mark 1:20) and could manage. But the point stands: the call of Jesus takes priority over family obligation, over the father-son bond that was the foundation of ancient society. Jesus himself will say "whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" (Matt. 10:37). This is not cruelty but clarity about ultimate allegiance. The kingdom of God does not abolish family; it reorders priorities. Zebedee remains; the sons go. The call was absolute, and so was their response.

And here is a sweeter truth, easily missed: though Christ must come before family, in the end he comes for the family's good as well. The son who loves Jesus first becomes a truer son, the father a better father; love rooted in God loves rightly — not clutching the other as an idol but receiving them as a gift. Often the Lord even uses the one who follows him to draw the rest home: Zebedee's own wife would later follow Jesus all the way to the cross (27:56), and the gospel would sweep through whole households (Acts 16:31). To put Christ first is not to lose your family but to love them at last with a love that can bless them forever. (The cost can be real — sometimes following him brings a sword between kin (10:34–36) — yet even then the disciple holds out to his household the one thing of everlasting worth.)

verseByVerse.quote: And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew's first ministry summary presents Jesus in three simultaneous roles: teacher (in synagogues), herald (proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom), and healer (of every disease and affliction). These are not separate departments of his work; they are the unified expression of who he is and what the kingdom does. Teaching illuminates; proclamation announces; healing demonstrates. Word and deed are inseparable in Jesus. The spread of his fame to "all Syria" signals already what will be made explicit in chapter 28: the kingdom cannot be contained within Israel's borders. The nations were already coming, drawn by the reality of what he was doing.

It is worth pausing on what the healings meant, for they were never mere kindness — real and tender though they were. First, they were the King's credentials. Isaiah had foretold that when God came to save, "the eyes of the blind shall be opened... the lame man shall leap like a deer" (Isa 35:5–6); so when John the Baptist later sent to ask, "Are you the one?", Jesus simply pointed to exactly these works (11:4–5). Every healing announced: the kingdom is here, and here is its King. Second, they were a window into a deeper healing. Sickness is one of the bitter fruits of the fall, and in mending broken bodies Jesus was showing in the flesh what he had ultimately come to do for the soul — to heal our lostness, to forgive, to make whole. "With his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:5). He touched the symptom to point us to the cure.

But what of now, when, as a rule, we do not see such healing in the church? The great tide of miracles clustered around Jesus and his apostles to authenticate the gospel once for all; we are not promised that abundance today, and we should be wary of any who guarantee it. Yet God remains free to heal, and still does as he wills in answer to prayer (Jas 5:14–15). And here is the deeper comfort: these healings were the firstfruits of a coming world, the future leaking into the present — a kingdom already begun though not yet complete. For a day is surely coming when God "will wipe away every tear," and "death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore" (Rev 21:4). Every blind eye Jesus opened in Galilee was a crack of that dawn. The believer's healing is therefore never finally denied — only, for a while, delayed; and the empty tomb has made it certain. The King who healed the sick of Syria will one day heal the whole creation, and close the last grave forever.

verseByVerse.quote: And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary: The five regions named — Galilee, Decapolis (the ten Greek cities east of the Jordan), Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan — map the whole of the land of Israel and its surrounding territories. Matthew is showing that Jesus's ministry immediately attracted a pan-regional response. The crowds "followed" — the same word used for the disciples, though the crowds will prove less committed. Following and discipleship are not the same thing: the crowds want healing and teaching; the disciples have left everything. Both are drawn to Jesus, but differently. Matthew will spend the rest of his Gospel exploring the difference between those who follow and those who truly follow.

4.theology:
Active Obedience and the Imputed Righteousness of Christ. The temptation narrative is crucial to the Reformed doctrine of imputed righteousness. Jesus does not merely die for our sins (removing the guilt of our disobedience); he also lives in perfect obedience (providing the positive righteousness that we lack). This is called his active obedience — the life of perfect faithfulness to the Father from baptism to cross.

At each point of testing in the wilderness, Jesus does what Adam failed to do in the garden and what Israel failed to do in the desert: he trusts God’s word over his own need, refuses to demand signs, and worships God alone. This perfect obedience is credited to everyone who trusts in him. We are justified not only by the forgiveness of our sins through his death but by the clothing of his righteousness through his life. The temptation narrative is the biography of our justification — the record of the obedience that is now ours by faith.
4.examples:
Then: Israel’s forty years in the wilderness is the extended backstory of Jesus’ forty days. Every test Jesus faces has a corresponding failure in Israel’s wilderness narrative: bread (the manna crisis, Exod. 16), testing God (Massah, Exod. 17), worship (the golden calf, Exod. 32). Jesus passes where Israel failed, using the very Scriptures that Israel was given at Sinai. He is the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who finally does what the nation was always called to do.

Now: Every temptation we face follows one of Satan’s three patterns: use what you have for immediate gratification (stones to bread), demand that God prove himself (test the promise), or compromise your worship for immediate reward (kingdoms without the cross). Jesus’ answers are our weapons too: It is written. The Scripture that armed the Son of God in his temptation is the same Scripture available to every believer in theirs. The difference between victory and defeat in temptation is often simply whether we know the word well enough to wield it in the moment.

5.title: The New Law from the Mountain
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. <sup>2</sup>And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: <sup>3</sup>“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>4</sup>Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. <sup>5</sup>Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. <sup>6</sup>Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. <sup>7</sup>Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. <sup>8</sup>Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. <sup>9</sup>Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. <sup>10</sup>Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>11</sup>Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. <sup>12</sup>Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. <sup>13</sup>You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet. <sup>14</sup>You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. <sup>15</sup>Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. <sup>16</sup>In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven. <sup>17</sup>Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. <sup>18</sup>For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. <sup>19</sup>Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. <sup>20</sup>For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. <sup>21</sup>You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ <sup>22</sup>But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. <sup>27</sup>You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ <sup>28</sup>But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart. <sup>38</sup>You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ <sup>39</sup>But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. <sup>43</sup>You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ <sup>44</sup>But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, <sup>45</sup>so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. <sup>48</sup>You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
5.overview:
Jesus goes up on a mountain to teach — and every Jewish reader of Matthew’s Gospel would have heard the echo: Moses went up on Sinai. But this is not a repetition; it is a surpassing. Moses received the law and gave it; Jesus gives the law with his own authority: But I say to you. No prophet ever spoke like this. The prophets said “thus says the LORD”; Jesus says “I say.” He does not claim to relay a message from God; he speaks as God.

The Beatitudes are the charter of the kingdom — and they invert every human expectation of what blessed looks like. Poor in spirit, not rich in confidence. Mourning, not celebrating. Meek, not powerful. Persecuted, not applauded. The kingdom of heaven belongs to people the world dismisses. This is not a programme for self-improvement; it is a description of those who have been broken of self-sufficiency and have learned to receive everything from God’s hand. The Beatitudes describe Jesus perfectly — and they describe every person who has been conformed to his image.

The antitheses (“You have heard… but I say”) press the law deeper than the scribal tradition imagined. It is not enough not to murder; the anger that murders in the heart is already culpable. Not enough not to commit adultery; the lust that adultery in the imagination is already a violation. The law reaches inward. And this inward reach is not only a demand; it is a diagnosis. No one can meet the standard of verse 48 — “be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect” — by their own effort. The Sermon on the Mount is the X-ray that shows us the fracture and sends us to the only Physician who can heal it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Beatitudes and the Call to Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes up the mountain — deliberately evoking Sinai, where Moses received the law — and sits to teach, the posture of a Jewish rabbi. His first words are the Beatitudes: nine declarations of blessedness that systematically invert the world's value system. The poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the hungry — these are not character traits to develop but descriptions of those who know their need before God. The section closes with the salt and light metaphors: disciples are to be world-preserving and world-illuminating, not by withdrawal but by visible, costly presence.
verseByVerse.theology: The Beatitudes are not a moral ladder to climb but a portrait of kingdom citizens in their native condition. They describe the same person from different angles: the one who is poor in spirit mourns their sin, is meek before God, hungers for righteousness, shows mercy, is pure in heart, makes peace, and bears persecution gladly. This is not nine different types of Christian but one Christian seen fully. Crucially, the blessings are not rewards for achieving these qualities; they are the condition of those who have already received the kingdom. Grace precedes the beatitudes; they describe those who know it. And before they are a portrait of the Christian, they are a portrait of Christ: he alone was perfectly poor in spirit, mourning over sin, meek, hungering for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, the peacemaker, the persecuted — he kept every blessing flawlessly, and that whole beatitude-life is reckoned to all who are united to him. This is the lens that keeps the Beatitudes from crushing the believer. We do not read them to measure ourselves and despair; we read them resting in the One who fulfilled them for us and who is now, by his Spirit, slowly forming them in us. So the struggler need not flee: the very ache of falling short — the grief over sin, the hunger to be made clean — is itself the first Beatitudes already at work, the early evidence of grace rather than the proof of its absence. Here law and gospel meet: the Beatitudes show us a righteousness we cannot produce, and then point us to the Christ who both gives it freely and grows it within.
verseByVerse.examples: Salt in the ancient world was a preservative — it slowed decay. Light is simply visible; it cannot be hidden without ceasing to be light. Jesus calls his disciples both: agents of preservation in a decaying world, and bearers of visible testimony that draws glory to the Father. Neither metaphor allows for invisible, privatized Christianity. The Christian life is inherently public — not in the sense of performance (that will be condemned in ch. 6) but in the sense of witness. The question is not whether your life will be seen, but what people will see when they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ascent of the mountain is not incidental geography. Matthew has crafted a deliberate Sinai-echo: Moses went up the mountain to receive the law; Jesus goes up the mountain to interpret and fulfill it. That Jesus sits to teach (the posture of authoritative rabbinic instruction) and his disciples come to him establishes the relational context: this teaching is addressed first to those who have already begun to follow, not to the general public as entry requirements. The Sermon on the Mount describes the life of the kingdom from the inside — it assumes the regenerating work of God has already begun. "He opened his mouth and taught them": what follows is the fullest sustained teaching of Jesus in any Gospel.

Before we climb into the Beatitudes one by one, take this to heart, or they will crush rather than bless. They are not eight entrance exams you must pass to earn God's favor. Notice that every "qualification" is really a disqualification in the world's eyes — poor, mourning, hungry, persecuted. This is grace from the very first word: a blessing pronounced not over the strong and accomplished but over the empty-handed. The Beatitudes are not a ladder you climb up to God; they are a portrait of the people God has already stooped down to bless.

And they are, before they are anything else, a portrait of Jesus himself. He was the truly poor in spirit, the one who mourned over sin, the meek, the one who hungered and thirsted for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemaker, the persecuted — he lived every line you and I cannot keep, and his flawless beatitude-life is credited to all who are his. So read them first as the face of your Savior, and then as what his Spirit is slowly making you. If "pure in heart" stings because you are still battling your thoughts, do not despair: that very sting is poverty of spirit, that grief is the mourning, that ache to be clean is the hunger for righteousness — the first Beatitudes already at work in you. The struggler who keeps running to Christ is not shut out of these blessings; he is the very person they describe. "Blessed are" is God's word spoken over you now, in Christ, even as he conforms you to the picture across a lifetime — finished only on the day you see him face to face (1 Jn 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Poverty of spirit is not low self-esteem but theological honesty: the recognition that before God one has nothing to offer, no claim, no merit — total dependence on his grace. The tax collector in Luke 18 is the portrait: he cannot name a single achievement, only beat his breast and say 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner.' That posture — empty hands held out to God — is poverty of spirit. It shows itself in specific moments: in prayer, the poor in spirit have nothing to produce before God, only need; in success, they cannot take the credit; in conflict, they do not reach for the card of their own righteousness; in moral failure, they have no deflections available. The kingdom belongs to such people — not eventually or conditionally, but now — because they are precisely the ones who know how to receive what the kingdom gives: everything, as sheer gift.

It is the patient who admits he is ill who finally calls the doctor; the man who insists he is fine stays sick. The poor in spirit are simply those who have stopped pretending they are well before God — and so they are the only ones who let the Physician in.

Take heart: this first blessing asks not for a virtue you must produce but for the empty hands you already have — for he who was rich became poor for your sake (2 Cor 8:9), that beggars might be made heirs.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mourning flows directly from poverty of spirit: those who see their condition clearly before God will grieve it. This is not depression but the godly sorrow of 2 Corinthians 7:10 — the grief that turns from self toward the Savior, the grief that leads to life. The comfort promised uses Isaiah's great consolation word (Isa. 40:1 — 'Comfort, comfort my people') spoken to a people who have passed through judgment and know they deserved it. The mourning is real; the comfort is more real still.

Picture the man who, after years of shrugging off his sharp tongue or his wandering eye as "just how I am," at last truly grieves it before God. He finds, to his surprise, that the tears are not a pit but a doorway — for God draws near to the brokenhearted, never to the self-satisfied.

And the comfort is certain because it was purchased: the Man of Sorrows (Isa 53:3) wept our tears and bore our griefs, so that ours now have an end appointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meekness is not weakness or passivity — it is strength held in submission to God's timing rather than deployed for self-vindication. The meek person does not lack power; they choose not to exercise it for their own defense. When someone publicly humiliates you in a meeting, meekness is not having nothing to say — it is having something to say and choosing not to say it, because you have entrusted the vindication to God. When someone takes credit for your work or dismisses your contribution without cause, meekness does not agree with their verdict; it entrusts the accounting to the One who keeps perfect records. Psalm 37:11, quoted here, embeds this promise in a longer command: 'Trust in the LORD and do good... commit your way to the LORD... he will act' (Ps. 37:3–5). Meekness is precisely this trust made visible — the refusal to take God's work of vindication into your own hands. Jesus universalizes the promise from Canaan to the earth itself: all of renewed creation belongs to those who received it from God rather than seized it.

We learn this not from a rule-book but from him who said, "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (11:29) and stood silent before his accusers; his meekness is credited to us, and in him the meek inherit everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hunger and thirst for righteousness are bodily images of desperate urgency — not a mild preference for improvement but the drive of someone who has gone without and cannot stop seeking. The one who hungers for right standing before God and right living in the world will be fully, finally satisfied — because God himself, not a system or a reward, is the satisfaction.

Picture the gap between idly wishing you were a little fitter and the gasping thirst of one lost in a desert. God blesses not the casual wisher but the soul that aches to be made right — and this is the one appetite he promises always to fill.

And the righteousness we hunger for is first a gift, not a wage — Christ himself is the bread and the living water (Jn 6:35), and his perfect righteousness is reckoned to all who come empty and hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mercy given and mercy received are linked — not as a transaction (you earn mercy by showing it) but as a pattern: those who have genuinely received God's mercy cannot withhold it from others, and those who withhold it reveal they have not truly received it (cf. Matt. 18:23–35).

The forgiven heart forgives. Picture someone carried for years by the patience of God, who then meets a friend that has wronged him — and chooses not to send the bill he has every right to send, because he remembers how vast a debt was once torn up in his own name.

We do not work up mercy to earn God's; we pass on what we have drunk deeply of. The mercy you show is the overflow of the mercy that found you at the cross, never its price.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Purity of heart — singled out by Kierkegaard as "willing one thing" — is the undivided, unalloyed devotion of the whole inner person to God. The promise is breathtaking: they shall see God. The beatific vision — direct knowledge of the divine presence — is the ultimate human destiny, promised here not to the theologically sophisticated but to the single-hearted. Complexity of mind is no substitute for simplicity of devotion.

Think of a man who worships on Sunday with one eye always on his money, his image, his comfort; his heart is divided, the water cloudy. The pure in heart is the one whose loves have been simplified, who wants God more than the gifts of God — and only such clear water can mirror the face of heaven.

If your heart feels anything but pure, look away from it to him: the only truly pure in heart gives us his own cleanness now (1 Cor 1:30), washes us day by day, and will make us spotless when we see him (1 Jn 3:2). The fight to be pure is itself a fruit of grace, not a bid for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peacemakers are not peacekeepers — they do not merely avoid conflict but actively work to reconcile what is broken. The title "sons of God" reflects the character of the Father, who is himself the great Reconciler (2 Cor. 5:18–19). To make peace is to participate in the divine work.

Picture the friend who, when two others fall out, refuses to take a side and instead walks back and forth between them, bearing the awkwardness and even the blame, until clenched fists become clasped hands. That costly go-between work is the family likeness of God, who in Christ stepped between heaven and earth to make peace by his blood (Col 1:20).

We can only make peace because peace was first made with us: Christ "is our peace" (Eph 2:14), reconciling us by his blood (Col 1:20) before ever sending us out to reconcile others.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final beatitude closes the bracket: the kingdom of heaven belongs to the persecuted just as it belongs to the poor in spirit (v. 3). Persecution for righteousness' sake is not random suffering but the suffering that comes specifically from kingdom allegiance. The world does not persecute the harmless; it persecutes those whose righteousness exposes its darkness. The blessing of the persecuted is that they are in good company.

It need not be a prison cell. It may be the colleague quietly sidelined for refusing to fudge the figures, or the teenager frozen out for not joining the cruelty in the group chat. When obedience to Christ costs you something at others' hands, you are not unblessed — you stand exactly where the citizens of the kingdom have always stood.

And the persecuted are blessed because they suffer with the One who was cast out for them; in him the kingdom is already theirs, untouchable by any who revile them.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eighth beatitude shifts from third person ("they shall") to second person ("you") — it becomes personal. Persecution "on my account" identifies Jesus as the issue: it is allegiance to him, not merely being good, that draws the world's opposition. The command to rejoice is not false cheerfulness but eschatological perspective: the reward is in heaven, where no moth destroys and no thief breaks in. The link to the prophets is crucial: persecution does not mark the disciple as having failed; it marks them as standing in the line of those who faithfully proclaimed the word of God to a resistant generation. To be persecuted for Christ is to be in the best possible company.

Such suffering is no sign of God's frown but a mark of union with his Son, who was reviled first and in your place; the great reward is grace upon grace, not wages owed.

verseByVerse.quote: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet. You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary: Both metaphors are declarative — "you are" — not aspirational ("you should become"). The identity precedes the calling. Salt in the ancient world was the primary preservative: before any form of refrigeration, packing fish or meat in granular salt drew out moisture and inhibited bacterial growth, extending the useful life of food by weeks or months. The Galilean fishing industry that employed Peter and Andrew depended entirely on this process — salted fish from the Sea of Galilee were traded through markets across the empire. Salt was so valuable it was sometimes used to pay wages; the Latin salarium (salary) derives from sal, salt. Disciples function as salt in exactly this way: they slow moral and social decay by their presence in the world. A community of truthful, faithful, just people in a neighborhood does not transform it by force or noise but by the quiet, persistent influence of transformed lives — the way salt works through meat: slowly, thoroughly, from the inside. Tasteless salt is useless — the warning is against a Christianity so fully assimilated into its culture that it has nothing left to preserve or season. Light is simpler still: it is inherently visible. A city on a hill cannot choose to be hidden; its very existence makes it seen. The Christian life is unavoidably public — not in the sense of performance but in the sense of testimony. The question is not whether to be visible but what the visible life will say about the one who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary: The lamp on a stand gives light to all in the house — not selected people, not just those who deserve it. The purpose of good works is not self-promotion (chapter 6 will condemn that) but the glory of the Father. The distinction is crucial: works done to be seen by others for their praise are hypocrisy; works done before others so that God is praised are witness. The same deed — giving to the poor, visiting the sick, speaking truth — can be either, depending on whose glory it seeks. Jesus calls his disciples to a visible, costly life whose visibility is always directed upward: not "look at me" but "look at my Father." Light points beyond itself to its source.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–48 — The Law Fulfilled: A Righteousness That Exceeds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses the relationship between his teaching and the law of Moses: he has not come to abolish but to fulfill. He then gives six antitheses — "You have heard... but I say to you" — in which he does not contradict the law but penetrates to its interior logic. Murder begins in anger; adultery begins in the look; divorce fractures the covenant; oaths corrupt speech; retaliation perpetuates violence; hatred divides what love should unite. The section climaxes with the demand: "You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." — a standard no one reaches by effort, which is exactly why it drives us to the Christ who fulfilled the law in our place and to the Spirit who reshapes us from within.
verseByVerse.theology: The antitheses reveal that the law was always concerned with the heart, not merely the external act. Jesus does not introduce a new, stricter morality; he discloses the full depth of what God always intended. The Pharisees' righteousness was wide but shallow — it covered the surface of behavior without reaching the roots of motive and desire. The righteousness Jesus requires exceeds theirs not by adding more external rules but by going deeper into the same terrain. This is why grace must precede the Sermon on the Mount: no one can produce this righteousness by effort; it must be worked in us by the Spirit of the one who fulfilled the law perfectly. To "fulfill" the law (v. 17) is not to abolish it but to bring it to its goal: by his flawless obedience Jesus meets its every demand, in himself he embodies the types and shadows that pointed forward, and at the cross he bears its curse. And the righteousness that "exceeds" the Pharisees comes in two layers — first the perfect righteousness of Christ credited to us through faith, the only righteousness that truly opens the kingdom, and then the real if imperfect righteousness the Spirit grows in a regenerate heart. So the very law that drives the unbeliever to Christ by exposing his sin becomes, for the believer, the shape of a Spirit-empowered life of love. Read this way, the towering standard of verse 48 humbles without crushing: it sends us to Christ for a righteousness we cannot produce, and then to the Spirit who produces it in us.
verseByVerse.examples: The demand for perfection (v. 48) has driven interpreters in two directions: some make it an impossible ideal that drives us to grace; others read it as a call to wholeness or completeness (the Greek teleios can mean "complete" or "mature"). Both are partially right: the standard is God's own character, which we cannot reach by effort, but which the Spirit progressively conforms us to (2 Cor. 3:18). The sermon is both a mirror that shows us our need and a map of the life the Spirit produces in those who have received the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus flatly denies that he has come to abolish the Law or the Prophets — that is, the whole Old Testament. He has come to fulfill them, and that word means far more than merely to obey. He fulfills the law in every dimension at once. He fulfills its demands, keeping perfectly by his own obedience what Israel and all of us have broken. He fulfills its types and shadows, for the sacrifices, the temple, the priesthood, and the feasts all pointed forward to him, and he is the reality they foreshadowed (Lk 24:44). He fulfills its penalty, bearing on the cross the curse the law pronounces on those who break it (Gal 3:13). And he fulfills its true meaning, pressing its commands to their full inward depth, as the rest of this chapter will show. The law prescribed and demanded a righteousness no sinner could ever produce; Jesus is the one who at last produced it, embodied it, and is himself its goal (Rom 10:4).

That is the key to the next line. Not the smallest letter (the iota, the Hebrew yod) nor the tiniest pen-stroke of the law will pass away — it stands utterly secure — "until all is accomplished."
