The law is not scrapped; it is carried to its appointed completion, and that completion is reached above all in Christ: in his perfect life, his atoning death, and his resurrection, with the final consummation still to come when heaven and earth themselves pass away. This is why Paul can say the believer has "died to the law" and is no longer under it (Rom 7:4–6). He does not mean the law was a mistake; he means that, now that Christ has accomplished it and borne it for us, we are released from it as a covenant of works — no longer under its demand to "do this and live," and no longer under its condemnation, because Jesus met the demand and absorbed the curse in our place.

What, then, is our relationship to the law now? It still has vital work to do — but different work for different people. For the one not yet in Christ, the law is God's faithful schoolmaster: by exposing sin and silencing every excuse, it strips away the illusion of self-righteousness and drives the sinner to the only Savior who can rescue him (Gal 3:24; Rom 3:20). The law cannot save, but it can, mercifully, make us desperate for the One who can. For the one already in Christ, the law is no longer a ladder to climb for salvation or to earn God's love; that love is already ours, freely, in his Son. Yet the moral heart of the law — which is love, love for God and neighbor (Rom 13:10; Matt 22:37–40) — remains the very shape of the redeemed life. (Its old shadows, the ceremonies and sacrifices, have done their work and found their home in Christ; its abiding moral substance stands.) What was once an external code demanding from without, the Spirit now writes on the heart from within (Jer 31:33), enabling us to walk in it — not as cowering slaves earning a wage, but as beloved children, free at last to love (Rom 8:3–4). This is the glad paradox: freed from the law as a way to be saved, freed for the law as the way of love, and carried along in it now by the power of the Spirit.

It is worth noting, with respect, how this passage looks through dispensational eyes, since many faithful believers (perhaps your own fellowship) read it that way. Dispensational theology stresses a sharp distinction between Israel and the church and between the successive eras, or dispensations, of God's dealings. On this reading the Law of Moses was given to national Israel as a single, unified code, and at the cross that whole code came to an end for the believer; the Christian now lives not under the Law of Moses at all but under "the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2; 1 Cor 9:21), the commands of the New Testament. Many dispensationalists are therefore wary of the Reformed threefold division of the law (moral, ceremonial, civil) and of calling the Mosaic moral law the believer's rule; they prefer to say we follow Christ's commands, led by the Spirit. Classic dispensationalists also tended to read the Sermon on the Mount as primarily kingdom law — ethics belonging to the coming earthly kingdom — with only secondary application to the church now, though many today (the progressive dispensationalists) apply it directly to Christian living.

The difference from the covenantal reading offered above is real, yet narrower than it first appears. Both sides gladly confess that we are saved by grace through faith and not by law-keeping, that the believer is not under the Mosaic law as a covenant of condemnation, that Christ fulfilled the law, and that the law still convicts the sinner and drives him to Christ. The chief divergence lies in the framework: where the Reformed see one covenant of grace running through both Testaments and the moral law abiding as the believer's guide (the third use), the dispensationalist sees a sharper break — the Mosaic code ended, and the believer now guided by the law of Christ. In practice both walk the same road of Spirit-empowered love; they chart it differently. (See the note at 4:17 on the kingdom for the larger picture behind this difference.)

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Feel first the shock of these words. In that world the scribes and Pharisees were the gold standard of holiness; no one was reckoned more devout. So when Jesus says you must out-righteous the most righteous men alive or you "will never enter the kingdom of heaven," it lands like a thunderclap. The ordinary listener thinks: if they fall short, what hope is there for me? The Pharisee bristles: who is this to say my righteousness is not enough? Jesus means to unsettle them both — to close off every road of self-confidence before he opens the only door that works.

"Relaxes" on the surface warns any teacher who loosens God's commands and trains others to do the same. But there is a sharp irony here, and Jesus surely has the Pharisees in view: the men who looked strictest were in truth the great relaxers. They buried the law under a mountain of extra rules, yet hollowed out its real weight — and at points their traditions actually cancelled God's commands. Jesus would later expose exactly this: by their rule of "Corban" they let a man neglect his own aged parents and so "made void the word of God" by their tradition (Mark 7:9–13). To keep the letter while killing the heart, and to prize human tradition over God's clear word, is the worst relaxing of all.

How should we hear it today? Old Joe may worry: if not one command may be relaxed, must I still keep the Sabbath, the food laws, the feasts? Read it with verses 17–18 in hand. Jesus upholds the law's full authority — but he fulfills it, and its ceremonial, shadow parts (sacrifices, clean and unclean foods, holy days, the Sabbath as a sign) reach their goal in him. They were "a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ" (Col 2:16–17). So we honor those laws not by repeating the shadows but by trusting the One they always pointed to; to rest in Christ is not to relax the law but to keep it at its deepest. The moral substance abides in full force — and a rhythm of rest and worship remains God's good gift — while the verses just ahead show Jesus pressing that moral law deeper than the Pharisees ever dreamed. Freed from the ceremonial burden, we are bound more sweetly to love.

Notice, too, that the one commended both "does them and teaches them." Teaching is not enough; the kingdom prizes doing. This is the note James will sound: "be doers of the word, and not hearers only" (Jas 1:22); a faith that produces nothing is dead (Jas 2:17). But hear it through the gospel: this is about the trajectory of a life, not the perfection of it. The "great in the kingdom" are not the flawless but the sincere — those whose hearts mean to obey, who keep turning back after every stumble, and whose doing springs from grace received, not merit earned.

What, then, was wrong with the Pharisees' righteousness, and what must exceed it? Their flaw was not too much obedience but hypocrisy: they did their good works for their own honor rather than for God — a costume worn for the applause of men, as chapter 6 will lay bare (alms, prayer, and fasting done "to be seen"). A righteousness that surpasses theirs must therefore be of a wholly different kind, and it comes in two layers. First and foundationally, it is a righteousness that is not our own at all: the perfect righteousness of Christ, credited to us through faith (Phil 3:9). That alone truly exceeds the Pharisees and opens the kingdom, for it is flawless — and it is a gift. Then, flowing out of that gift, comes a real if imperfect righteousness of the heart: the Spirit giving a new heart and moving us to walk in God's ways (Ezek 36:26–27). Theirs was wide, shallow, and for show; this is deep, genuine, and for God.

So let the verse land as Jesus intends. He sets the bar impossibly high — surpass the holiest people you know — not to crush you, but to drive you off your own righteousness and into his. Received by faith, his perfect righteousness becomes yours; and the same grace that clothes you sends the Spirit to make you, slowly and truly, into the kind of person these words describe. The mountain you could never climb turns out to be, in Christ, first a gift and then a joy. You are not weighed, found wanting, and sent away; you are clothed, accepted, and changed from the inside out. Obey, then — not to win a love you lack, but because that love is already, freely, yours.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment." But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, "You fool!" will be liable to the hell of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first antithesis penetrates murder to its root: anger. The law prohibited the act; Jesus prohibits the inner state from which the act grows. He is not adding a new law alongside the old but revealing what the old law always implied about the seriousness of human life and the dignity of persons made in God's image. Every insult is an assault on someone who bears the divine image. The escalating liability — judgment, council, hell — tracks the escalation of contempt: from anger (the emotion) to insult (the word) to "you fool" (the verdict that dismisses a person as worthless). To preach the full force of this image, a congregation needs to know what each level of liability actually was. "Judgment" referred to the local town court — a council of twenty-three elders in each village, the normal venue for property disputes and lesser offences. "The council" was the Sanhedrin, the Great Council in Jerusalem: seventy-one members, the supreme religious and judicial authority of all Israel, convened only for the gravest capital cases. "Hell of fire" is Gehenna — the Greek form of ge-hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom, a ravine running along the south side of Jerusalem. Its history was notorious: it was the site where King Manasseh had sacrificed children to the Ammonite god Molech (2 Kings 23:10), an act so abominable that King Josiah defiled the valley afterwards to prevent any future use. By the time of Jesus, the Valley of Hinnom had become Jerusalem's garbage dump — a place where refuse smoldered continuously, where the bodies of executed criminals were disposed of, and where the fires never quite went out. That perpetually burning ravine outside the city wall had given first-century Jews their primary image for the place of eternal judgment. The escalation is therefore not merely rhetorical but architectural: from the village court to the supreme national tribunal to the judgment seat of God himself — three levels of accountability corresponding to three levels of contemptuous speech. Jesus treats contemptuous speech as a moral catastrophe, not a social failing. The tongue that dismisses a person as worthless attacks someone who bears the image of God.

But is all anger sin? No — there is such a thing as holy anger. God himself is "angry with the wicked every day" (Ps 7:11); Jesus looked around "with anger" at hard hearts (Mark 3:5) and drove the money-changers from his Father's house. So Scripture can say, "Be angry and do not sin" (Eph 4:26). When Old Joe hears that a child has been abused or the innocent crushed and something in him burns, that fire can be right — it is love for the good recoiling at evil, a faint echo of God's own heart. Yet holy anger is rarer than we like to think, and it bears clear marks: it is stirred by God's concerns, not our wounded pride; it stays under control rather than flaring into contempt or revenge; it is slow, for "the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:19–20); and it spends itself in doing good and seeking justice, never in writing a person off as worthless. Hold most of our anger up to that test and we find it is really about us — our rights, our comfort, our honor — which is precisely the anger Jesus warns against.

So what should you do the next time anger rises? First, be slow — do not speak or strike in the heat; "a soft answer turns away wrath" (Prov 15:1). Second, look underneath it: ask what was really threatened, and you will usually find a bruised pride or a cherished idol rather than the glory of God — name it honestly to him. Third, take the anger to God before you take it to the person; pour it out to him and leave room for his justice, for "vengeance is mine, says the Lord" (Rom 12:19). Fourth, remember the gospel: you are the servant forgiven an unpayable debt (Matt 18:21–35), and the cross both shows that your own sin deserved wrath and that Christ has borne it — and that memory melts contempt into mercy. Then move toward the person: forgive, bless, and where you can, be reconciled — which is exactly where the next verses lead. And when the anger is the holy kind, let it drive you to your knees and into action for the wronged, never into bitterness. When you fail — and you will — do not despair; confess it, receive fresh forgiveness, and let the Spirit go on retraining your heart. He is not finished with you yet.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The practical implication of the first antithesis is stunning: reconciliation with a brother takes priority even over temple sacrifice. Not "after worship, attend to relationships" but "before worship, attend to relationships." God is not honored by worship offered by an unreconciled heart. The sequence is precise: remember, leave, go, reconcile, return. The gift waits at the altar while you attend to the broken relationship — because the God to whom the gift is offered cares more about the brother than the offering. This principle runs through all of Scripture: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" (Hos. 6:6; Matt. 9:13). Vertical worship and horizontal relationship cannot be separated.

Notice carefully whose fault is in view: "your brother has something against you." This is not the case where someone has wronged you (that is Matthew 18:15); here you are the one in the wrong, and your brother is rightly aggrieved — and yet the burden to act still falls on you. Put the two passages side by side and the net is complete: if someone sins against you, you must go to him (18:15); if you have sinned against someone, you must go to him (here). Neither the wronged nor the wrongdoer is left an excuse to sit still. Love takes the first step in both directions.

What, then, does "be reconciled" actually look like? Suppose Old Joe has wounded his brother — a cutting word, a broken promise, a wrong quietly covered up. He is to go, and to go humbly. He names the specific sin plainly: "I was wrong to speak to you the way I did." He does not dress it up, excuse it, or smuggle in blame — no "I'm sorry if you were offended," no "but you started it." He owns it, shows real sorrow, and asks the costly little question pride hates: "Will you forgive me?" Where damage can be repaired or repaid, he repairs it. And the brother, for his part, is called to forgive as God in Christ forgave him (Eph 4:32) — to say, and to mean, "I forgive you," and then to keep that word: not to rake it up again, not to hold it over Joe's head, not to nurse it in his own heart or rehearse it to others. Forgiveness is a promise to bury the matter, as God buries our sins and remembers them no more (Jer 31:34).

But what if the brother will not be reconciled — what if Joe goes, confesses honestly, and is met with a cold shoulder? Is Joe now trapped, unable to worship with a clear heart? No. Paul gives the freeing limit: "If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all" (Rom 12:18). So far as it depends on you. Joe is answerable for his own part — honest confession and a genuine reaching out; he is not answerable for the other man's response, which he cannot control. Having truly sought peace, he may come and worship with a clear conscience, leaving his brother in God's hands and standing ready to be reconciled the moment the door opens. Another's unforgiveness can grieve you, but it cannot hold your worship hostage.

verseByVerse.quote: Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
verseByVerse.commentary: The court parable extends the teaching about reconciliation into practical urgency: settle debts before they reach judgment. The application is both horizontal (literal legal prudence) and eschatological (settle your account with God while there is time). The "last penny" (the smallest Roman coin) conveys the completeness of the debt that must be paid if reconciliation is refused and judgment comes. Jesus consistently frames the urgency of repentance in terms of limited time before a judgment that cannot be appealed. The window for reconciliation — with brothers, with God — is now. It will not always be open. The wise person settles debts while settlement is still possible.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall not commit adultery." But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second antithesis goes to the root of adultery: the intentional look of desire. Jesus does not criminalize involuntary attraction but the cultivated, intentional gaze — the look that uses another person as an object for self-gratification. The heart is the seat of adultery before the body is. This teaching demolishes every defense that stops at "I haven't done anything wrong" — the interior life is the domain of God's law as much as the external act. It also shows what adultery really is: the violation of covenant love, which begins not with the body but with the refusal of the heart to honor the exclusive claim of marriage. Faithfulness in marriage is a matter of the eyes and the heart, not only the bedroom.

Put some real-life color on this, for the line truly matters. It is no sin to notice that someone is beautiful — God made beauty, and the eye that registers it is working as he designed. Nor is the first, involuntary glance a sin, any more than the first arrival of a tempting thought is. Being tempted is not the same as sinning; our Lord himself "was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin" (Heb 4:15). What Jesus condemns is the second look that becomes a lingering, the desire deliberately fed, the imagination invited to stay and feast. Luther put it homely: you cannot stop a bird from flying over your head, but you can stop it building a nest in your hair. The bird is the temptation; the nest is the sin.

So consider Old Joe, whose eyes keep getting drawn where they should not linger, who looks away — and then walks off weighed down with guilt. Hear this clearly: the looking away is not his failure, it is his obedience — a small daily victory, and heaven is not frowning at it. Much of the burden he feels is false guilt, the accuser heaping condemnation on a man who actually fought and won, and "there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1). Where he truly did let the gaze linger and feed, the remedy is not to wallow but to confess it at once and receive the cleansing already promised (1 Jn 1:9), then walk on forgiven. And for the fight itself Scripture hands him tools: make Job's covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1); bounce the glance away quickly and flee rather than negotiate (2 Tim 2:22); and do not merely suppress the thought but replace it — turn the heart to Christ, give God thanks, even breathe a prayer for that person as a soul he will meet at the judgment, not an object to be used. Deepest of all, the cure for a wandering eye is a captured heart: as Christ becomes our greater treasure and joy, purity grows less from gritted teeth and more from love. The aim is not a man who never feels temptation, but a man increasingly satisfied in his Savior — and that man can lift his head.

verseByVerse.quote: If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hyperbole is violent precisely because the stakes are real. Jesus is not teaching self-mutilation — a blind man can still lust, a handless man can still sin. He is teaching the radical, decisive, immediate action required when sin has a foothold. "If your right eye" — the favored, dominant eye — "causes you to sin": even your best faculty, your sharpest tool, must be sacrificed if it is the instrument of your fall. Nothing is too precious to surrender in the war against sin. The repeated reference to hell (Gehenna, the valley of refuse outside Jerusalem associated with judgment) underscores that the war is not about self-improvement but about eternal life. Sin is not inconvenient; it is lethal.

What might such "cutting off" look like in Old Joe's ordinary week? Start with the picture Jesus is using: a surgeon amputating a gangrenous limb. No one enjoys losing a hand — but better to lose the hand than let the poison take the whole body. That is the logic: deal with sin as ruthlessly as a doctor deals with spreading death. Now make it concrete. First, if the phone in his pocket has become the doorway to lust through late-night scrolling, the "eye" must go — install a filter, hand the phone to his wife at night, even trade the smartphone for a plain one. The device is good; if it is the bridge to sin, the bridge comes down. Second, if a certain friendship, or an old flame, keeps dragging him into gossip, drink, or compromise, he may have to step back from it — even a dear relationship, if it is the hook that keeps catching him. Third, if the road home runs past the bar, or the bottle sits waiting in the cupboard, he changes the road and empties the cupboard; he stops feeding the very thing he is trying to starve. Notice that in each case what is surrendered is something good or precious (the right eye, the right hand) — Jesus is not asking us to give up obvious evils only, but to part with anything, however valued, that has become the instrument of our fall. Radical? Yes. But a man does not haggle with gangrene.

verseByVerse.quote: It was also said, "Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce." But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third antithesis addresses divorce. The certificate of Deuteronomy 24:1 was a concession to hardness of heart, not God's design (Matt. 19:8). Jesus restores the original intention: marriage is a covenant, and its dissolution is not a legal technicality but a moral rupture. The exception for sexual immorality acknowledges that the covenant can be broken by the other party; but apart from that, remarriage constitutes adultery — the ongoing violation of a covenant that God intended to be permanent. Jesus is not creating a hierarchy of sins but exposing the gravity of what society had trivialized. Marriage is not a contract to be terminated; it is a covenant image of God's own faithfulness to his people.

Let us walk through this slowly, because Jesus packs a great deal into a few words. In his day divorce had become casual and one-sided: a man could hand his wife a certificate and send her off, sometimes for the flimsiest reason (one famous rabbi allowed it even for a spoiled meal). It left women shamed and destitute, for a divorced woman usually had to remarry simply to survive. When Jesus says such a man "makes her commit adultery," he means this: because the divorce was not on valid grounds, in God's sight she is still bound to her first husband — so when she remarries (as she almost must), that new union counts as adultery, and the guilt traces back to the husband who wrongly cast her out. And "whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery" follows for the same reason: if her divorce was illegitimate, she is still another man's wife in God's eyes, and to marry her is to take what was not free to be taken.

Does this, then, forbid every divorced person from ever remarrying? Not quite — and the hinge is that small phrase, "except on the ground of sexual immorality." By making an exception, Jesus signals that there is a ground on which a marriage is genuinely broken, where divorce is permitted and a later remarriage is not adultery. So the sweeping "no remarriage" one might hear at first is really aimed at remarriage after an unjust, groundless divorce. Where there is true biblical ground, the picture changes.

Here we step onto contested ground, where faithful, Christ-loving brothers land in different places — so hold your convictions firmly but your charity wider. The historic Reformed position (as in the Westminster Confession) recognizes two grounds on which divorce is permitted and the innocent party is free to remarry: first, sexual immorality, the exception Jesus names here and in 19:9; and second, the willful, irreparable desertion Paul addresses — "if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so... the brother or sister is not enslaved" (1 Cor 7:15). Others read the exception more narrowly and conclude that no remarriage is permitted while the former spouse lives. Both camps are seeking to honor the same Lord and the same texts; this is a place for humility, not contempt.

That frame answers your two questions. If a marriage is broken by adultery, the innocent spouse — the one sinned against — is, on the mainstream Reformed reading, free to remarry; the covenant has been shattered by the other's unfaithfulness, and the exception clause exists precisely for such a case (a minority would still counsel against it, and they should be respected). And what of violence and heavy abuse? Scripture does not name it in so many words here, yet two things must be said plainly. First, and without any hedging: an abused spouse must get to safety — God never calls anyone to remain in danger, and the church must protect, never pressure. Second, many faithful pastors rightly judge that brutal, unrepentant abuse is itself a profound breaking of the marriage covenant, a true desertion of every vow to love and cherish, and so falls under the principle of 1 Corinthians 7. On that reading divorce is indeed permitted; some brothers would frame it more cautiously as separation, but none should ever bind a victim to ongoing harm. The God who hates the treachery of unjust divorce (Mal 2:16) does not delight in the slow destruction of one of his children.

Through it all, keep two truths together. Marriage is holy, a living picture of Christ's unbreakable covenant with his church (Eph 5:31–32), and divorce is always a tragedy, never a triviality. Yet for the reader who carries a broken marriage or a remarriage in his past, these words are not a sentence of permanent condemnation. There is full forgiveness at the cross for every sin, this one included, and grace to walk faithfully from today forward. Jesus guards marriage so fiercely because he is himself the Husband who will never divorce his bride — and that faithfulness is at once our standard and, when we have failed it, our refuge.

verseByVerse.quote: Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn." But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. Let what you say be simply "Yes" or "No"; anything more than this comes from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This fourth antithesis addresses oaths. The law permitted them and required that they be kept; the trouble was the whole system of evasion that had grown up around them. People swore by lesser things — heaven, earth, Jerusalem, their own head — treating such oaths as less binding than one sworn by God's name, a tidy loophole for the careful liar. Jesus cuts straight through it: every oath finally invokes God, for everything is his. Heaven is his throne, earth his footstool, Jerusalem his city, and you cannot so much as turn one hair white or black — your very head is his, not yours. There is no oath that does not call on God, and so no oath you can quietly break.

But the real target lies deeper than oath-formulas. The very need for oaths exposes how unreliable ordinary speech has become; an honest person reinforcing his word with a vow is half-admitting that his plain word is not trusted. So Jesus calls for a people whose word simply stands: "Let what you say be simply Yes or No." This is not a ban on every solemn vow in a lawful setting — Paul himself calls God as his witness (2 Cor 1:23), and God swears by his own name — but a call to such everyday truthfulness that reinforcement becomes pointless. Anything piled on top "comes from evil," a symptom of the fall's fracturing of human speech. In the kingdom a Christian's bare word should be as good as another man's sworn oath.

Does this mean Old Joe must blurt out everything he knows? No. To be truthful is not the same as to be transparent about all things at all times. Scripture nowhere commands us to tell everyone everything; it forbids us to deceive. There is room for holy discretion — for keeping a confidence, for guarding what is not ours to share, for the wise silence Jesus himself kept before his accusers (26:63; 27:14), for simply declining a question that is not rightly asked. The line is clear: you may keep silent, but you may not lie; you need not say all, but what you do say must be true. Love will sometimes hold its tongue, but it will never speak a falsehood.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth." But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus turns to retaliation. "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" (the lex talionis) was never a license for revenge; it was a courtroom rule limiting punishment to fit the crime — a mercy, really, restraining the runaway blood-feuds of a violent world. Jesus now carries his disciples beyond even that restraint, from measured justice to refused vengeance.

The fifth antithesis on non-retaliation has been the most discussed and most misapplied. "Do not resist evil" does not mean passive acquiescence to all injustice; it means refusing the spiral of personal vengeance. The slap on the right cheek in the ancient context was typically a backhanded blow — an insult, not an assault. Turning the other cheek is not offering to be beaten twice; it is refusing to be drawn into the cycle of honor-shame retaliation. Similarly, surrendering the cloak with the tunic (all one had) is not masochism but a willingness to absorb personal loss rather than fuel a legal war. Jesus is teaching a transformed relationship to personal rights: hold them loosely, suffer loss without bitterness, refuse the calculus of revenge.

Bring it home to today. The "slap on the cheek" is rarely a literal blow for Old Joe; it is the insult, the affront to his pride — the colleague who belittles him in the meeting, the driver who leans on the horn and gestures, the cutting reply waiting to be typed under someone's post. The flesh wants the last word, the comeback, the even score; to turn the other cheek is to let the insult fall without firing back, refusing to feed the quarrel. The "tunic and cloak" is the personal grievance over money or property — the neighbor whose careless mowing wrecks your hedge, the handyman who overcharges, the relative who never repays the loan — and here it means being willing to swallow a loss rather than wage a bitter war to defend every last right. It reaches even into the home: when a spouse snaps or a teenager throws a barbed word, the kingdom way is to answer with calm instead of returning fire and letting the cycle spin on.

This is not a doormat's passivity, nor does it cancel the protection of the weak or the place of lawful justice; it is the deliberate surrender of personal vengeance. And Old Joe can let go of his rights like this only because they are safe in better hands. He follows the One who, "when he was reviled, did not revile in return... but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly" (1 Pet 2:23) — the Christ who absorbed the ultimate wrong, our sin, and answered it with a cross. A man who knows his honor and his future are secure in such a Savior can afford to lose an argument, swallow an insult, and even bless the one who wronged him.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The compelled second mile refers to the Roman practice of impressment — a soldier could compel a civilian to carry his pack one mile. Going a second mile is the voluntary act that transforms the resentful conscript into the willing servant. It is one of Scripture's most potent images of grace operating in ordinary, coerced situations. The command to give to beggars and not refuse borrowers extends the principle to economic life: the disciple holds his resources with an open hand, shaped by the generosity of the God who gives to all. None of this abolishes prudence or property rights; it reorients the heart's default posture from self-protection to self-giving.

Picture it today. The second mile is the willing extra: the worker who does more than the bare minimum and serves "heartily, as for the Lord" (Col 3:23); the man who, asked for one favor, cheerfully gives a little more; the believer who keeps serving a demanding boss or an awkward neighbor with grace instead of grumbling. This is the good sense in the common phrase "go the extra mile." But mark the limits, for love is not the same as having no boundaries. The extra mile is a free gift of love, not bondage to another's every demand. It does not mean endless overtime that swallows your evenings and starves your family — for caring for your household is itself a command of God (1 Tim 5:8), and a man who neglects his wife and children to chase his employer's approval (or his own ambition) has not gone the extra mile; he has merely changed which duty he is failing. Jesus himself withdrew to rest and pray, and said no when love required it. The point is a generous, willing heart — held by a wisdom that weighs the other things God has also given you to do.

The same heart, and the same wisdom, govern giving. "Give to the one who begs" forbids the tight fist and the grasping spirit that says, "what is mine is mine." The disciple's default is open-handed, ready to part with his money for someone in need. Yet generosity is meant to be wise, not naive, for love seeks a person's real good. Where the state already provides for basic needs, or where organized begging-rings exploit both the giver and the poor souls they put on the street, simply handing over cash may not help and can even feed harm — an addiction, or a criminal handler. There love still gives, but gives shrewdly: a meal rather than money, support to a shelter or mercy ministry that truly lifts people, time and the gospel alongside the gift. Two ditches line this road. One is the hard heart that hides its stinginess behind "they'd only waste it"; the other is a thoughtless giving that funds the very thing destroying a man. Walk between them — and when in doubt, lean to the side of open-handed mercy, for it is better now and then to be taken advantage of than to nurse a miserly heart.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy." But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This sixth and final antithesis is the most radical of all. "Hate your enemy" was never in the law of Moses; it was a popular gloss that fenced the word "neighbor" so as to shut enemies out. Jesus tears the fence down: love has no exception clause. To love an enemy is not merely to tolerate him or refrain from harming him; it is active goodwill that seeks his welfare even while he seeks your ruin — and its sharpest form is prayer, for to pray for a persecutor is to stand before God on his behalf and to begin to want for him what God wants. This is humanly impossible, which is precisely the point: only the grace of the kingdom can produce it.

Why love like this? Because it is the family likeness of God himself, who "makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust" — his kindness falls even on those who curse him. To love only those who love you back is mere reciprocity; it costs nothing and proves nothing, for even tax collectors and pagans manage that. The kingdom calls for a love that reaches past tribe, family, and affinity to the very people outside the circle. And we have known this love ourselves: "while we were still enemies" God loved us and gave his Son (Rom 5:8). We are simply to pass on the love that first reached us.

That is why Jesus can say, "You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." The word (teleios) means whole, complete, undivided as much as flawless: the Father's "perfection" here is the wholeness of a love that knows no exceptions. His children are called to that same undivided love — not as a crushing legal bar, but as the shape of the life the Spirit is steadily growing in those who belong to him.

What might this look like for Old Joe? It is praying, by name and for his good, for the colleague who undermined him or the relative who has turned cold. It is the neighbor everyone gossips about finding his walk shovelled and no note left. It is choosing words that bless rather than bite about the man who wronged you, and quietly doing him a kindness when the chance comes. It is refusing to gloat when an enemy stumbles. None of it waits for the other person to deserve it — that is exactly the point.

But hear clearly what this does not mean. To love an enemy is not to pretend that evil is good, nor to leave the wicked unopposed. You may love a man and still report his crime, still shield the weak from him, still let just consequences fall — for God himself, all kindness, is also the righteous Judge. Nor does it mean staying in harm's way: loving an abuser does not require remaining his target, and praying for a violent man is fully compatible with getting yourself and others to safety. Enemy-love seeks the offender's true good and refuses personal revenge; it does not abolish justice, wisdom, or self-protection. Love and a clear-eyed stand against evil are not enemies.

5.theology:
The Law and the Gospel: The Threefold Use of the Law. Reformed theology has distinguished three uses of the law: the civil use (restraining evil in society), the pedagogical use (revealing sin and driving us to Christ), and the normative use (guiding the life of the believer). Matthew 5 exercises the second use with particular intensity: Jesus presses the law so deeply inward that no one can claim compliance, and in doing so drives every hearer to the mercy of the one who fulfilled what we cannot.

But Matthew 5 also exercises the third use: the Beatitudes, the salt and light images, and the love of enemies are not legal demands for the unregenerate but the description of the life the Spirit produces in those who are already citizens of the kingdom. The Sermon on the Mount is simultaneously gospel (this is what the kingdom looks like) and law (this is what you cannot achieve without the Spirit). Held together, they produce the only life worth living: dependent, transformed, and directed toward the glory of the Father.
5.examples:
Then: The Beatitudes describe the whole history of faithful Israel: Abel the righteous who was persecuted, Abraham the meek who sojourned in a land not his own, Hannah who mourned and was comforted, David the poor in spirit who wrote “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 51:17). The Beatitudes are not new values; they are the values of the faithful covenant people, now fully embodied in the King who pronounces them and perfectly exemplified in his own life.

Now: The world’s beatitudes are the inverse of Jesus’: blessed are the confident, the successful, the powerful, the popular, the comfortable. The Sermon on the Mount is a collision with that value system at every point. The Christian who takes these beatitudes seriously will find themselves increasingly out of step with the surrounding culture — and increasingly at home in the kingdom. The persecution promised in verses 10–12 is not a possible outcome but a promised one: the world does not celebrate the values of the kingdom because the world is not the kingdom. But the kingdom is coming — and the persecuted will inherit it.

6.title: The Hidden Life of the Kingdom
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. <sup>2</sup>Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>3</sup>But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, <sup>4</sup>so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>5</sup>And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>6</sup>But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>7</sup>And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. <sup>8</sup>Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. <sup>9</sup>Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. <sup>10</sup>Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. <sup>11</sup>Give us this day our daily bread, <sup>12</sup>and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. <sup>13</sup>And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. <sup>19</sup>Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, <sup>20</sup>but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. <sup>21</sup>For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. <sup>24</sup>No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money. <sup>25</sup>Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? <sup>26</sup>Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? <sup>33</sup>But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. <sup>34</sup>Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is a sustained meditation on hiddenness. Give in secret. Pray in secret. Fast without showing it. The recurring phrase is “your Father who sees in secret will reward you” — and it upends the entire economy of religious performance. If God sees in secret, then the audience that matters most cannot be seen. The religious life that performs for human approval has traded the eternal reward for the temporary one, and the exchange is catastrophic.

At the centre of the chapter stands the Lord’s Prayer — six petitions that together describe the whole of what the kingdom life looks like in communion with the Father. First, God’s glory: hallowed be your name. Then God’s reign: your kingdom come. Then dependence: daily bread. Then forgiveness: both received and given. Then protection: from temptation, from evil. The prayer moves from adoration to petition, from God’s agenda to human need, from the cosmic to the daily. It is the complete grammar of prayer in twenty-five words.

The chapter ends with an antidote to anxiety that is also a diagnosis of its cause. Anxiety is the fruit of serving the wrong master (v. 24). When God and money compete for ultimate allegiance, anxiety is the symptom of the conflict. The cure is not financial security but reorientation of treasure: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who clothes the lilies and feeds the birds will add what you need. This is not a prosperity promise; it is a priority promise. When the kingdom is first, everything else finds its proper place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Piety Before the Father: Giving, Prayer, and Fasting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses three practices central to Jewish piety — almsgiving, prayer, and fasting — and in each case distinguishes the performance of these acts for human recognition from the genuine practice of them before God. The hypocrites have their reward: human applause, now and fully paid. Those who give, pray, and fast before the Father alone receive what the Father alone can give. The section includes the Lord's Prayer as the model of kingdom-oriented prayer: God-centered in its priorities, dependent in its petitions, and honest about the human need for forgiveness.
verseByVerse.theology: The three acts — giving, prayer, fasting — are not optional extras but the basic disciplines of covenant life: relationship with the neighbor (giving), relationship with God (prayer), and relationship with the self (fasting). Jesus does not question whether his disciples will do these things; he assumes they will ("when you give," "when you pray," "when you fast"). The question is motive and audience. Hypocrisy is not performing religious acts — it is performing them for the wrong audience. The hypocrite plays to the crowd; the disciple plays to the Father. The Father's reward — his presence, his approval, his delight — is infinitely superior to human applause.
verseByVerse.examples: The Lord's Prayer contains the whole theology of the kingdom in miniature. It begins with the Father's character and glory (hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done) before turning to human need (daily bread, forgiveness, protection). The order is the order of Christian living: God first, then us. The disciple who prays this prayer daily is being trained in a way of seeing the world: God's kingdom is the primary reality; my needs are real but secondary; forgiveness received must be forgiveness extended.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is the banner over everything that follows. Jesus is about to give three examples of devotion — giving, prayer, and fasting — and this single warning governs all three: beware of doing your righteousness to be seen. Notice that it is not the deeds he forbids but the audience you perform them for. Only a chapter earlier he said, "Let your light shine before others, that they may... give glory to your Father" (5:16); here he says, do not parade your righteousness to be glorified yourself. The same act can spring from opposite hearts: the question is whether you are living before the eyes of the crowd or the eyes of your Father.

This struck close to home, for showy piety was the very air the religious elite breathed. Among the most admired teachers of the day, devotion had become a kind of public theater — alms given with fanfare, long prayers offered where the most people would notice, fasting worn on the face for all to see. In a culture built on honor and shame, religion was a recognized road to status, and Jesus' hearers would have known exactly the sort of person he meant.

And what does he mean by "no reward from your Father"? Simply this: if you do your righteousness to win human applause, then human applause is the whole of your pay — and that is all you will ever get. You chose your paymaster. The one who performs for the crowd is settled up by the crowd; nothing further is owed him from heaven — not because the Father is stingy, but because the deed was never really done for him. This "reward" is not the earning of salvation, which is God's free gift; it is the Father's fatherly delight and recompense over what his children do out of love for him. To trade that boundless, eternal reward for a few moments of being noticed is the worst bargain a soul can make.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hypocrites' trumpet-sounding before their charitable gifts is almost certainly hyperbole — a vivid image of the person whose generosity requires an audience. "They have received their reward" translates a commercial term (apechousin): paid in full, the account settled, nothing more coming. Human praise is real but small, present but passing; the Father's reward is eternal and overflowing — but it goes to those who were not chasing the lesser thing.

But notice what should drive our giving in the first place: not reward at all, but mercy. The very phrase "give to the needy" means literally to do an act of mercy — help reaching down to the poor because their need stirs our compassion. We give because we have seen a brother in want and love will not look away (1 Jn 3:17), and because we are imitating a God who is rich in mercy and gave to us when we could never repay (Eph 2:4). So the secrecy Jesus commands is not coldness; it is love so taken up with the person in need that it forgets itself. Giving to be seen keeps one eye on the mirror; giving for mercy's sake has both eyes on the neighbor and on God.

The instruction that the left hand not know what the right is doing is not a command to be deceptive but to be unselfconscious — to give without the inner register of self-congratulation that counts and remembers and expects recognition. Genuine generosity is not only hidden from others; it is, ideally, hidden from ourselves. We give, and we move on. The Father "who sees in secret" is the most attentive and the most just of all possible audiences: nothing done for him is missed, nothing is undervalued, nothing is forgotten. The reward is not named precisely because its content exceeds specification — it is the gift of God himself, which is everything.

Picture it simply. Old Joe hears of a young family at church who have fallen behind on their rent. He could write the check after the service, mention it to a few friends, and feel the warm glow of being known as a generous man — and that glow would be the whole of his pay. Or he can slip the money to the pastor in an unmarked envelope, "for the Hendersons, and please don't say who," then walk away and very nearly forget he did it. No one claps. But the Father saw — the Father who misses nothing, undervalues nothing, forgets nothing — and that quiet envelope, given for love and not for show, is laid up with him forever. Which giver would you rather be?

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Standing prayer was normal Jewish practice — the posture of prayer. Jesus is not condemning the posture but the location chosen for maximum visibility: the synagogue and street corner, where the most people would notice. The alternative is not a different posture but a different room — the private room with the door shut, where the only audience is the Father. The room (tameion) was typically an inner storeroom, the most private space in a house. The point is not that only private prayer counts but that the motive of all prayer must be communion with the Father, not the cultivation of a reputation for piety. God responds to the cry of the heart, not the performance for the crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Gentile error is not length but magic — the assumption that words multiply and repetition compels divine attention. Pagan prayer often treated the gods as powers to be manipulated through the right formula repeated often enough. Jesus forbids this not because brevity is always better but because prayer is not a technique for bending God's will but a conversation with a Father who already knows. The staggering statement — "your Father knows what you need before you ask him" — does not make prayer superfluous; it makes prayer a relationship rather than a transaction. We pray not to inform God but to align our desires with his, to open our lives to what he already knows we need.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray then like this: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer opens not with our needs but with God himself — his name, his kingdom, his will — before it ever reaches our bread. Jesus teaches us to begin with the relationship and with God's glory; the very ordering retrains the heart, for we are made for God's agenda, not merely his assistance.

And feel first the wonder of the address: "Our Father." The eternal God, who needs nothing, who flung the galaxies into being and dwells in unapproachable light, invites us to call him Father. In the Old Testament hardly anyone dared address God so personally; yet Jesus hands his ragged disciples the family word. We can do this only because the Son has made us sons and daughters and the Spirit cries within us, "Abba! Father!" (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6). This is no distant force and no stern tyrant, but the Father of the prodigal who runs down the road to meet his returning child. And it is "our" Father — we never pray alone, but as part of a great family. That a sinner like you may look up and say "Father," and be heard, and be loved, is a marvel that should never grow stale.

"Hallowed be your name." The word "hallowed" simply means treated as holy, honored, held precious. A name in the Bible stands for the whole person, so God's name is God himself as he has made himself known. This petition therefore asks: may you, Lord, be revered and loved and taken seriously — in a world that uses your name as a curse or forgets it altogether, in your church, and (here it turns personal) first of all in my own heart, on my own lips, in my own life. It is a prayer that God would stop being treated as common — and it begins with me ceasing to treat him so. Before I ask God for anything, I ask that he be honored as the treasure he is.

"Your kingdom come." Is the kingdom here already, or still to come? Both — and the prayer holds the two together. God's saving reign has truly arrived in Jesus (see the note at 4:17) and presses forward now wherever the gospel takes root and hearts bow to the King; yet its full and visible glory still waits for Christ's return. So to pray "your kingdom come" is to ask two things at once: extend your reign today — in me, in the lost being saved, in your church — and hasten the day you come again to make all things new. We pray it standing in the overlap of the ages, longing for more of what has already begun.

"Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven." In heaven God's will is done perfectly, gladly, without delay or grumbling; the angels delight to obey, and nothing there resists him. This petition asks that earth become like that — that God's good and perfect will be embraced and obeyed here as joyfully and fully as it is above. And, as ever, it starts at home: it is the prayer of a surrendered heart that says with Jesus in the garden, "not my will, but yours, be done" (Lk 22:42). It is at once submission (let your will, not mine, rule me), mission (let your will sweep over this rebellious world), and hope (let the day come when heaven and earth are one and every knee gladly bows).

verseByVerse.quote: Give us this day our daily bread,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Give us this day our daily bread." After God's name, kingdom, and will, the prayer turns to our needs — and the very first is the humblest: bread, and only for today. "This day," not this year; like the manna that fell one morning at a time (Ex 16), it trains us in daily dependence rather than self-sufficient hoarding.

And do not think this petition is only for the poor. The man with a full bank account needs it just as much — perhaps more — for wealth tempts us to forget that every loaf comes from the Father's open hand. Money in the bank cannot make your heart beat, hold off illness, or secure tomorrow; rich and poor alike live, each day, on mercy. So Scripture prays, "give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you" (Prov 30:8–9). To ask for daily bread when the cupboard is stocked is to confess, gladly, that it is all gift.

And "bread" stands for more than food. The old teachers were right that under this one word we may bring to God everything we need for body and life: health and work, shelter and provision, strength for the day's tasks — yes, and wisdom for the meeting, patience with the children, courage for the hard conversation. Whatever today actually requires of you, you may ask your Father for it here, one day at a time. He welcomes the small, ordinary, practical requests of his children.

verseByVerse.quote: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." Here a real fear can rise up: am I earning God's forgiveness by forgiving others? Must I perform mercy in order to purchase pardon? No — and it is vital to see why. The forgiveness God grants is bought entirely by the blood of Christ and received by faith alone, never earned by anything we do (Eph 1:7). This petition is not a price tag on pardon.

What, then, does the "as" mean? It is a correspondence, not a payment. We come asking mercy as people who are themselves showing mercy — for the forgiven heart forgives. Jesus made this unforgettable in the parable of the servant forgiven a debt he could never repay, who then seized a fellow servant by the throat over a trifle (Matt 18:21–35). His refusal to forgive proved he had never really grasped the mercy shown to him. So an unforgiving, grudge-nursing heart is no small fault; it is evidence that God's grace has not truly landed.

It helps, too, to hold two things apart. Our standing before God as forgiven children — our justification — is settled once for all by faith and cannot be lost. But our daily fellowship with the Father, like a child's warmth with a parent, is chilled when we cling to bitterness; so we keep coming, keep confessing, keep being cleansed. That is why the order always runs from grace outward: "forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (Eph 4:32). We forgive because we have been forgiven, not in order to be. So if forgiving someone feels impossibly hard, do not grit your teeth and try to earn heaven by it — go back and look again at the mountain of debt God cancelled for you at the cross. A heart melted by mercy received becomes, almost without trying, a heart that gives mercy away.

verseByVerse.quote: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Lead us not into temptation" does not imply that God tempts his people (James 1:13) but asks that he not allow us to be brought into trials beyond our strength (1 Cor 10:13). The prayer owns our fragility before temptation and casts the whole burden of protection on the Father. "Deliver us from evil" — the Greek can mean "the evil one" (Satan) or "evil" as a force; both are true. So the prayer ends just where it began: in dependence on the Father, not in self-confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verses 14–15 turn the forgiveness-petition into a direct, sobering statement: those who forgive receive forgiveness; those who refuse to forgive find the same barrier raised before them. This is the one petition Jesus singles out to underline, the one that carries its own condition.

Yet the severity here is not a withdrawal of grace but a revelation of what genuine grace-reception looks like. The one who has truly grasped the enormity of his own forgiveness cannot keep withholding it from others — as the parable of the unforgiving servant will dramatize (18:21–35). An unforgiving heart is no small spiritual weakness; it is evidence that the grace of the gospel has not yet sunk in. (See verse 12 for why this is correspondence, not payment: we forgive because we have been forgiven, never in order to be.)

verseByVerse.quote: And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The turn to fasting follows the same logic as giving and prayer. The hypocrites fast dramatically, inviting sympathy and admiration for their spiritual rigor; they disfigure their faces so the fast will be noticed — and that applause is their whole reward. The gloomy, advertised face is the announcement of piety, which is precisely what real fasting must never be.

The instruction to anoint the head and wash the face is the instruction to appear normal — to conceal the fast from public view. Fasting was typically visible; Jesus reverses the signal: dress as if you are not fasting, so the fast stays between you and God alone. The pattern is now familiar — the secret act, the seeing Father, the certain reward. The three disciplines together shape the whole person: generosity toward others, communion with God, discipline of self — each practiced habitually, privately, and before the Father whose reward outweighs all human recognition.

Should Old Joe be fasting, then, if he never has? Start with what Jesus actually says: "when you fast," not "if" — just as with giving and praying, he simply assumes his disciples will do it. He fasted himself (4:2), and when asked why his disciples did not, he answered that the wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, "but the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast" (9:14–15) — that is, in this present age, ours. And the early church did: they fasted and prayed before sending out missionaries (Acts 13:2–3) and appointing elders (Acts 14:23). Yet notice what is missing — nowhere is fasting laid down as a law with required days (that was the Pharisees' way, twice a week and on show). So fasting is a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: no one should bind your conscience to it or let you feel condemned for neglecting it, and yet neither should you simply shrug off what your Lord plainly assumed his people would do.

Why fast, and for what? Fasting is voluntarily setting aside food (or some other comfort) for a season in order to seek God. It intensifies prayer, especially at weighty moments and decisions (Acts 13:2–3; Ezra 8:21–23); it humbles us in repentance and grief over sin (Joel 2:12); and above all it turns the body's hunger into a cry of the heart — "man shall not live by bread alone" (4:4) — a way of saying, "Lord, I want you more than I want food." It is not a hunger strike to twist God's arm, not a diet for self-improvement, and not a badge of piety to flaunt; it adds nothing to a standing already complete in Christ. We fast not to be loved but because we are loved, hungering for more of him. And there is a tender thread in it: we fast because the Bridegroom is away for now, longing until he comes and the fast gives way to the wedding feast (9:15).

How, in practice? Start small and simple — skip a meal or a day, drink water, and let each pang of hunger send you to prayer; fasting without seeking God is merely dieting. Pair it with Scripture and prayer, for the whole point is to feed on God. Keep it hidden, exactly as these verses urge — between you and your Father, no gloomy face, no announcement. And use wisdom with your health: if illness, pregnancy, or a fragile history makes food-fasting unwise, you may set aside other comforts instead — screens, sweets, leisure — for God looks at the heart, not the empty stomach. Do it as worship, free of legalism and free of guilt: not a box to tick, but a way to say, with your whole body, "you are better to me than bread."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–34 — Treasure, Vision, and Trust: Seeking the Kingdom First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 6 addresses anxiety about material provision through three related teachings. Disciples are commanded not to store up earthly treasure (perishable, vulnerable) but heavenly treasure (imperishable, secure). The eye as the lamp of the body: a healthy eye (generous spirit) fills the whole person with light; a diseased eye (stinginess) fills it with darkness. You cannot serve both God and money. Then the great anxiety passage: do not be anxious about food or clothing, because the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies knows your needs. Seek first the kingdom and his righteousness, and everything else will be added.
verseByVerse.theology: The teaching on anxiety is not a command to be carefree but to be properly ordered: anxiety is the symptom of inverted priorities — seeking the lesser things first and trusting God to manage them, rather than seeking God first and trusting him to manage everything else. The birds and lilies do not "seek" anything in the human sense; they simply exist in dependence on the Creator who provides. The disciple is not to live without thought for the future but without anxious preoccupation with it — trusting the Father's knowledge and provision while attending to the kingdom. Anxiety is fundamentally a theological problem: it reflects a practical unbelief in the Father's care.
verseByVerse.examples: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness" is the organizing principle of the entire Sermon on the Mount. Everything else — the beatitudes, the antitheses, the disciplines of chapter 6 — flows from this reorientation of desire. The person who is genuinely seeking God's kingdom first finds that anxiety about secondary things diminishes, not because circumstances change, but because the center of gravity of the heart has shifted. Worry is the heart occupied with what it fears it won't have; trust is the heart occupied with the One who has everything and gives freely.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sets two treasuries side by side, and the contrast is not now-versus-later but secure-versus-doomed. Earthly treasure has three enemies — moth, rust, and thief — and every earthly possession is already drifting toward one of them. Treasure in heaven (mercy shown, obedience offered, lives invested in for God) lies beyond the reach of all three. He is not banning savings or property; he is forbidding the heart that makes accumulation its great project. The question he presses is simply: what are you building, and will it last?

Then he exposes how the heart actually works: "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." We assume the heart leads and our money follows; Jesus says it runs the other way — put your money somewhere and your heart moves in after it. Do you want to love God's kingdom more? Invest in it, and watch your affections follow. The eye drives the same point home: a "healthy" eye (the word means single, clear, generous) floods the whole person with light, while a "bad" eye (grudging, stingy) leaves everything dark — and the darkness that imagines itself light ("how great is the darkness!") is the worst kind of all, for the miser who calls his grip mere prudence cannot even see his own night.

Finally the knife: "No one can serve two masters... you cannot serve God and money." A slave in that world belonged wholly to one owner; divided loyalty was no loyalty at all. God and money (Mammon — wealth set up as a rival lord) issue opposite commands: one says hold loosely and give, the other says grip tight and keep; one says trust me, and so does the other. You cannot obey both with the same heart. Money is a good servant and a deadly master, and Jesus forces the question of which it has become to you.

So what should Old Joe actually do? Hold his money with an open hand. Let him earn honestly, and save and provide wisely — that is good stewardship, not greed — but give generously and gladly, steadily sending treasure on ahead to heaven through care for the poor, the work of the church, and the spread of the gospel; let his giving lead his heart God-ward. Let him run the simple diagnostics: Where do my daydreams drift? What would rob my peace if I lost it? What could I not bear to part with? And let him hold the whole of it loosely, as a steward and not an owner, trusting his Father for tomorrow rather than his bank balance.

And what does this not mean? It is not a call to poverty, nor a sin to own a home, hold a pension, or enjoy God's good gifts with thanksgiving — for God "richly provides us with everything to enjoy" (1 Tim 6:17). Saving for your family is not the same as hoarding; planning is not the same as trusting in riches. The issue is never the figure in your account but the master of your heart: a poor man can worship money as surely as a rich man, and a rich man can hold his wealth open-handed for God. Jesus is not against money in your wallet; he is against money on the throne. Dethrone it, and you are free.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That "therefore" ties this straight to money: anxiety is simply Mammon-service in another dress — the heart gripped by what it dreads losing. So Jesus floods the fear with reasons. From the greater to the lesser: if God gave you life and a body, will he not give the food and clothes to sustain them? From creation: the birds neither sow nor store, yet your Father feeds them; the wildflowers neither toil nor spin, yet they outshine Solomon in his robes — and you are worth far more than sparrows, and longer-lived than grass that is here today and burned tomorrow. From sheer futility: not one anxious hour ever added a single hour to anyone's life. Worry is the illusion of control — it drains today without mending tomorrow.

Jesus names the disease gently: not unbelief but "little faith" — faith that truly knows God yet has not learned to rest in him. The pagans make food, drink, and clothing the great chase of their lives; the believer's difference is not that he has no needs but that he has a Father who knows them — love, wisdom, and limitless power meeting in the One who feeds the birds. So the cure is not to stop needing but to re-aim the heart: "seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added." Make God's reign your organizing priority, and the necessities fall into place behind it. And take it a day at a time: today's troubles are enough for today; do not haul tomorrow's into it.

Picture it. The sparrow on the windowsill never lies awake doing sums, yet it is fed — and you are worth a thousand sparrows. The weed in the ditch is dressed finer than a king for a single day before the mower comes; will your Father forget to clothe his own child? Worry, someone said, is like a rocking chair: plenty of motion, and it gets you nowhere. But hear what this does not mean: it is no ban on work or planning. The birds are busy all day gathering the food God provides; diligence and sensible saving are not the enemy — gnawing dread that crowds out trust is. So work hard, plan wisely, and then hand the result to your Father; when the fear rises, turn it into prayer (Phil 4:6); and each morning seek his kingdom first, and trust the rest to follow.

And what is it, day to day, to "seek first" the kingdom? Not to bolt a religious slot onto a self-centered life, but to re-center the whole of life on Christ as King. It means giving God the first of your time, not the leftovers — meeting him in his Word and in prayer before the rush swallows the day; pursuing his righteousness, actually growing in holiness and obedience; and letting his concerns — the lost, the church, the poor, the spread of the gospel — shape how you spend your money, your hours, your strength. At every fork the question quietly shifts from "which path gives me the most comfort?" to "which most serves my King?" Put him at the center, and he himself promises to carry the rest.

6.theology:
Prayer and the Fatherhood of God. The Lord’s Prayer is the fullest Trinitarian statement about prayer in the New Testament. We pray to the Father, in the name of the Son (the one who taught us to pray this way and who intercedes for us, Rom. 8:34), in the power of the Spirit (who helps us in our weakness and intercedes with groaning too deep for words, Rom. 8:26). Reformed theology has always understood prayer as Trinitarian from beginning to end: the Father hears, the Son mediates, the Spirit enables.

The address “Our Father” is the fruit of adoption — the doctrine that those who trust in Christ are received into the family of God with all the rights and privileges of sons (Gal. 4:5–6). We do not pray as strangers petitioning a distant deity; we pray as children talking to a Father who knows us, loves us, and has already given us his Son. The confidence of Christian prayer rests entirely on the prior act of God in adoption, not on the fervency or frequency of the one praying.
6.examples:
Then: The contrast between secret devotion and public performance runs through the Old Testament. Hannah prayed so quietly that Eli thought she was drunk (1 Sam. 1:13) — and God heard. Daniel opened his window toward Jerusalem and prayed three times a day without announcement, in full view of a hostile empire (Dan. 6:10). The great saints of Israel prayed to an audience of One — and their prayers are the ones that shaped history. The hypocrites who prayed on street corners are forgotten; their reward was fully paid and fully spent.

Now: The anxiety Jesus addresses in verses 25–34 is the defining emotional experience of our age. Financial anxiety, career anxiety, health anxiety, relationship anxiety — the modern world has more to worry about (in terms of information access about possible threats) than any previous generation.
