Jesus’ answer is not information management but kingdom orientation: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who holds all things will hold yours. This is not naive — it is the most realistic posture available to a creature who is not God. You are not in control of tomorrow; the Father is. Trust the Father.

7.title: The Narrow Gate
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Judge not, that you be not judged. <sup>2</sup>For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. <sup>3</sup>Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>4</sup>Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ when there is the log in your own eye? <sup>5</sup>You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. <sup>6</sup>Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. <sup>7</sup>Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. <sup>8</sup>For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>9</sup>Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? <sup>10</sup>Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? <sup>11</sup>If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! <sup>12</sup>So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets. <sup>13</sup>Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. <sup>14</sup>For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few. <sup>15</sup>Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. <sup>16</sup>You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? <sup>17</sup>So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. <sup>21</sup>Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. <sup>24</sup>Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. <sup>25</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. <sup>26</sup>And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. <sup>27</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it. <sup>28</sup>And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, <sup>29</sup>for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 concludes the Sermon on the Mount with a series of choices, each framed as a binary: the wide gate or the narrow, the false prophet or the true, the one who hears and does or the one who hears and does not. The Sermon that began with Beatitudes ends with warnings. The kingdom is real and its entrance is narrow; the alternatives are easy and lead to destruction. This is not the comfortable conclusion of a TED talk; it is the solemn close of the greatest sermon ever preached.

The famous “Judge not” (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Bible. Jesus is not prohibiting all moral discernment — he commands it in verse 6 (discern who receives what is holy) and verses 15–16 (recognise false prophets by their fruit). He is prohibiting hypocritical judgment: condemning in others what you excuse in yourself. The log-and-speck image is both humorous and devastating — the person with a beam in their eye offering to perform eye surgery. Self-examination must precede fraternal correction.

The parable of the two builders is the Sermon’s climax and its challenge. Both builders hear the words of Jesus; both face the same storm. The difference is foundation: rock or sand. And the foundation is not intellectual agreement with Jesus’ teaching but doing it — the obedience that grows from genuine faith. The crowds are astonished at the end because Jesus teaches with authority, not as the scribes. He does not say “thus says the LORD”; he says “I say to you.” He is the rock on which the house is built.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Judgment, Prayer, and the Two Ways: Concluding the Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sermon on the Mount concludes with four warnings and a call. The warning against judging hypocritically (vv. 1–6), the invitation to persistent prayer (vv. 7–12), and the double warning about the narrow gate and false prophets (vv. 13–23) all converge on the final parable of the two builders (vv. 24–27). The Sermon does not end gently: it ends with a stark choice between two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and the crowds are astonished not by the gentleness of what they heard but by the authority of the one who said it.
verseByVerse.theology: The command not to judge (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Sermon and one of the most misunderstood in the Bible. Jesus does not prohibit discernment (he commands it in v. 6 and vv. 15–20); he prohibits the hypocritical judgment that ignores one's own sin while scrutinizing another's. The warning about false prophets extends the theme: discernment is required, but it must begin with self-examination. The Sermon ends where it must — with the question of foundation. Hearing Jesus's words and not doing them is not neutrality; it is the choice of sand. The storm will decide what you built on.
verseByVerse.examples: The final verse — "he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes" — is Matthew's first and defining portrait of Jesus as teacher. The scribes taught by citing authorities: "Rabbi X says..." Jesus taught by assertion: "I say to you." This is either the most arrogant teaching in human history or the teaching of the one to whom all authority belongs. Matthew does not leave the reader in the middle. The crowd was astonished. The question is what they did with the astonishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge not, that you be not judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, "Let me take the speck out of your eye," when there is the log in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Judge not" has become secular culture's favorite verse — the one command everyone still keeps. But Jesus means something precise. He is not banning moral evaluation or the naming of wrong (he does both all through the Sermon); he is banning the hypocritical tribunal of the self-righteous, who build careful cases against others while suppressing the evidence against themselves. And the warning has teeth: "with the measure you use it will be measured to you." The harsh judge is the one most exposed to harsh judgment — from God, who sees every page of the file.

The picture that follows is deliberately absurd: a man with a plank jutting from his own eye, leaning in to perform delicate surgery on the speck in his brother's. The speck is real — the brother does have a fault — but the log makes the would-be surgeon both blind and dangerous. Notice, though, that Jesus does not say "leave the speck alone." He says, "first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly" to help. Self-examination is not an excuse never to correct; it is the qualification for correcting rightly — humbly, as one patient helping another, not as a spotless judge.

And this is where verse 6 belongs — you are right to wonder about it, but it is no stray fragment. Having warned against being too severe a judge, Jesus now warns against being no judge at all. "Dogs" and "pigs" picture those who have shown settled, aggressive contempt for holy things; to keep pressing pearls upon them is only to watch the treasure trampled and to invite their attack (cf. 10:14). So the two sayings are a matched pair, the two ditches on either side of the road: verses 1–5 say, do not be censorious; verse 6 says, do not be naive. Real discernment walks between them — humble about ourselves, yet wise about where we spend what is holy.

For Old Joe, then: deal honestly, and first, with your own sin before you reach for a brother's; when you must correct, do it gently, as a fellow sinner and not a saint sitting in judgment; and stay wise — keep holding out Christ, but do not mistake love for the refusal ever to discern, nor go on forcing holy things upon those who only want to trample and turn. Neither a harsh heart nor a gullible one, but a clear and humble eye.

verseByVerse.quote: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ask... seek... knock" are present-tense imperatives: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. Prayer here is the posture of radical dependence — an admission that what we most need lies beyond our power to produce. That fits everything before it: the Sermon has described a life impossible by human effort, and now Jesus shows where the strength for it comes from. The demands drive us to our knees, and the door is one that opens.

Why pray with such confidence? Because of who we are asking. No decent father, handed a request for bread, slips his child a stone; asked for a fish, he does not palm off a snake. And if flawed, sinful parents still know how to give good gifts, "how much more" will the perfect Father give good things to his children. Our boldness rests not on our worthiness, nor on our persistence as a technique, but on his settled goodness.

So what may Old Joe bring? Anything that befits a child of this Father and his kingdom: daily provision, wisdom for a hard decision, the salvation of a wayward son, courage to obey the very commands of this Sermon, and — the best gift of all — the Holy Spirit himself (Luke 11:13, where Matthew's "good things" becomes "the Holy Spirit"). And he is to keep coming even when the door seems shut, like a child who knows his father is home.

But hear clearly what this does not mean. It is no blank check, no heavenly vending machine, no promise that whatever we crave will be handed over if only we believe hard enough or ask often enough. The promise is "good things" — and a good Father gives what is good, not always what is wanted. Sometimes the loving answer is "no," or "wait," or "I have something better"; the very picture assumes a child may reach for a serpent thinking it a fish, and a good father will not give it. So a prayer answered differently is not the Father failing but the Father fathering. We ask boldly and persistently — yet always, at heart, "according to his will" (1 Jn 5:14), trusting that he is wiser and kinder than our requests.

One honest puzzle remains: if a believer already receives the Holy Spirit the moment he trusts Christ (Eph 1:13; Rom 8:9), why would Jesus tell us to ask for him? Two things. First, in its own setting the promise looked ahead to Pentecost; the disciples were soon told to wait and pray for the promised Spirit, and they did (Lk 24:49; Acts 1:14; 2:1–4). Second, and for us now: we do not keep asking to receive the Spirit as though we lacked him — we have him already, and for good. We ask, rather, for more of his work — to be filled afresh again and again (Eph 5:18; and Acts 4:31, where already Spirit-filled believers are filled once more for boldness), for his power, his comfort, his help to put sin to death and bear fruit. It is not begging for a Guest we do not have, but asking the Guest who lives within to fill the whole house. And Luke can call him the supreme "good thing" the Father gives, because in giving us the Spirit, God gives us nothing less than himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary: "So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them." This is the famous Golden Rule, and notice its shape: it is positive, not merely negative. The world's wisdom says, "Do not do to others what you would hate done to you" — refrain from harm. Jesus asks more: actively do for others the good you would want for yourself. Picture what you would long for if you stood in their shoes — then go and be that for them. He calls it the summary of "the Law and the Prophets," because love for neighbor, in its most generous and active form, is the very heart of God's law. And it flows straight from what precedes: children who have received good gifts from their Father (vv. 7–11) become, in turn, givers of good gifts to others.

verseByVerse.quote: Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sermon on the Mount ends with a series of stark antitheses, and this is the first: two gates, two ways, two destinations, two crowds. The wide gate and easy way are not characterized as explicitly wicked — the point is their accessibility, their lack of demand. The narrow gate and hard way are characterized by difficulty — the word means "compressed," "constricted," like a passage one must squeeze through. The many and the few are not presented with pleasure; Jesus is not delighted that the many choose destruction. But he refuses to soften the reality. The kingdom is not for everyone in the sense that everyone enters it equally; it is entered through a narrow passage that requires the abandonment of self-reliance and the acceptance of Jesus on his terms.

Many are confused about which is which, because our culture prizes being "broad-minded" and suspects anything "narrow." Jesus reverses the valuation. The broad gate looks free, open, and welcoming — room for everyone and everything — yet it ends in destruction; the narrow gate looks cramped and costly, yet it opens onto life. The key is to see what the narrow gate actually is: it is Christ himself. "I am the door," he says (Jn 10:9); "I am the way... no one comes to the Father except through me" (Jn 14:6). It is narrow because there is only one way to God, and because you must come stripped — you cannot carry your self-righteousness, your sins, or your idols through it; you enter low and empty-handed, alone, trusting him. The "hard way" beyond the gate is the road of discipleship this whole Sermon has described, costly and against the grain of the world — and it is found by few because few are willing to come on those terms.

But guard against four misreadings. First, "hard" does not mean we earn life by effort: the gate is a Person, not a performance; we enter by grace through faith, and the road is hard not because we buy heaven by struggle but because following Christ in a fallen world costs us. Second, "narrow" is not the sour, judgmental narrowness of the Pharisees that Jesus condemned; it describes the singular way of salvation, not a cramped or unkind spirit. Third, the broad road is not crowded only with the obviously wicked — it is thronged with respectable, moral, religious people too, even some who cry "Lord, Lord" (vv. 21–23); you can be very devout and still be drifting the easy way, which is exactly what makes this warning so searching. Fourth, "few" is no excuse for either despair or smugness: the gate stands open and the invitation goes to all — "enter" is a command anyone may obey — and those who do enter only by grace, with nothing to boast of.

So hear the verse as Jesus meant it: not a gloomy verdict to depress you, but a loving, urgent summons. Two roads lie before every person, and there is no third. The easy way asks nothing now and costs everything at the end; the narrow way costs you yourself now and gives you life forever. And here is the wonder — the narrow gate is never locked: the One who is the door flung his arms wide on a cross so that whoever will may come. Enter.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Thus you will recognize them by their fruits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Beware of false prophets." They come in sheep's clothing — not as obvious enemies but as members of the flock, harmless-looking and wise-sounding; the danger is precisely that they do not look like wolves. And note that this is an internal threat: those who arise within the community and lead it astray. How are they known? By their fruits — not by their rhetoric, charisma, spiritual claims, or apparent success, but by the observable evidence of character and teaching over time.

Jesus drives it home with a law of nature: grapes do not grow on thornbushes, nor figs on thistles; a healthy tree bears good fruit and a diseased tree bad, and neither can do otherwise. The tree determines the fruit, as the heart determines the life. This is Reformation truth before the Reformation — no amount of external religious performance can squeeze good fruit from a corrupt root; it will always, in the end, show its true nature. Genuine fruit grows only from a heart made healthy by the grace of God. False teachers may mimic the kingdom's language and produce impressive-looking fruit for a season, but it will not survive the test of time, nor of the One who sees the roots as well as the branches.

And the fruitless tree meets the same end John the Baptist warned of: it "is cut down and thrown into the fire" (cf. 3:10) — a reminder of the eschatological edge running through the whole Sermon, that the character and fruit being formed now carry eternal weight. So the passage closes where it began, on the practical note: "you will recognize them by their fruits." Recognition is possible, and required. The church is not to be naive about those who claim to speak for God; it is to look, patiently, for the fruit that only a true work of God can produce.

What, concretely, does good and bad fruit look like? Look in three places. First, the teaching: good fruit is teaching faithful to Scripture, which exalts Christ and his cross and calls people to repentance and grace; bad fruit twists the Bible, soft-pedals sin, peddles a gospel of self, money, or works, and quietly draws disciples after the teacher rather than the Lord (cf. Acts 20:30). Second, the character: good fruit is the fruit of the Spirit — "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control" (Gal 5:22–23), shown in humility, honesty, sexual purity, integrity with money, and kept promises; bad fruit is the works of the flesh — pride, greed, immorality, manipulation, deceit, a quick temper, and a trail of wounded people and broken trust (Gal 5:19–21). Third, the effect on others: good fruit leaves people loving Christ more, growing in holiness, leaning harder on God; bad fruit leaves them puffed up, or crushed, or fleeced, with the leader exalted and God's name dragged down.

Two cautions keep this from going wrong. Do not mistake mere success for good fruit — crowds, eloquence, charisma, and visible "results" can all be counterfeited; it is character and faithfulness that cannot. And give it time: a single failure does not make a diseased tree, for even true believers still sin and stumble. What you are watching for is the settled pattern and direction of a life as it ripens — or rots — over the long haul.

verseByVerse.quote: Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. On that day many will say to me, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?" And then will I declare to them, "I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most startling warning in the whole Sermon: people who called Jesus "Lord, Lord," who prophesied, cast out demons, and did mighty works in his name — shut out of the kingdom. These are not pagans or casual churchgoers but people with a robust claim to spiritual experience and ministry success. Yet the test, Jesus says, is "the will of my Father" — not charismatic power, not visible results, not even an orthodox profession, but the obedience that flows from a real relationship with him. The gifts and the performance can all be present where the relationship is absent.

And his verdict is the most chilling sentence in the Gospel: "I never knew you" — not "I knew you once," not "I knew you slightly," but never. The ministry was real, the experiences were real, the words were sincere — yet to know Christ and be known by him, the mutual embrace of true saving faith, was missing the whole time. So the question this presses on us is not how impressive our spiritual resume is, but whether we actually know, and are known by, the Lord we serve (cf. 2 Tim 2:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sermon ends with its final image: two builders. The wise man "hears these words of mine and does them"; the foolish man hears and does not. Both heard the very same Sermon — and that is Matthew's point: hearing is not enough. The Sermon must become the foundation of a life, not merely the content of a memory.

Both houses face the same storm; the Sermon does not promise shelter from suffering. The rain, floods, and winds beat on the wise builder and the foolish alike — the difference lies entirely in the foundation, not the weather. Obedience to Christ's words does not insulate us from trial; it determines what survives it. The foolish builder is no idler: he too has heard, chosen a site, and built. The sand of easy religion, self-sufficient morality, or nominal Christianity can hold up a comfortable house — until the storm comes. And the storm always comes. Only what is built on Christ's own words, lived out in obedience, will stand.

"And great was the fall of it" — Matthew lets the words stand without softening. The collapse of the life built on sand is catastrophic, and Jesus does not soften it. The Sermon closes not with a consolation but with a verdict: both builders heard every word, and only one house is left standing.

So let us be crystal clear about the two foundations, because the whole difference is one word: doing. Both men heard; only one did. To build on sand is to hear Jesus and not obey him — to sit under good preaching and nod along, to know your Bible and even enjoy discussing it, to attend church, to have been baptized, to be a decent and respectable person — while the words never actually change how you live on Monday morning. It is admiring Jesus' teaching without submitting to it; a religion that costs little and alters nothing. Many such houses look perfectly fine in fair weather.

To build on the rock is to hear Jesus and do what he says — resting your whole life on Christ himself, and therefore actually obeying him: forgiving the one who wronged you, turning from the sin you have been quietly petting, telling the truth when a lie would be easier, loving the awkward neighbor, putting the kingdom first with your calendar and your wallet. The rock is Christ and his word; to build on it means your security, your identity, and your hope all rest on him, and that trust works its way out into a changed, obedient life. And mark this, so it never collapses into mere effort: the doing does not earn the house — it shows the foundation is real. A faith that truly rests on Christ will always, in time, get up and obey him. That, and nothing flimsier, is what stands when the storm comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sermon ends and the narrative pans to the crowd: they were astonished (exeplessonto — struck out of their wits, overwhelmed). The Sermon on the Mount produces astonishment in all who truly hear it; no one who seriously reckons with its demands — poverty of spirit, purity of heart, love of enemies, single-hearted seeking of the kingdom — can come away unchanged. The only options are to be astonished into obedience or to walk away back to the wide gate.

The scribes taught by citation: "Rabbi so-and-so says..." Their authority was borrowed, derived, and validated by appeal to tradition. Jesus taught by assertion: "But I say to you." His authority was inherent, native, and required no external validation. This is either breathtaking arrogance or the self-presentation of the one to whom "all authority in heaven and on earth has been given" (Matt. 28:18). Matthew's Gospel will force this choice again and again. The crowd's astonishment is the right first response; the question is what comes next. Will the astonishment become allegiance? Will the hearing become obedience? The Sermon has been preached. The builder must now choose the site.

7.theology:
Hearing and Doing: Faith and Works in Reformed Theology. Matthew 7:24–27 has sometimes been read as teaching salvation by works: do the words of Jesus and be saved. Reformed theology reads it more carefully. The doing is not the foundation; the rock is. The foundation is Christ himself, received by faith. The doing is the evidence and expression of genuine faith — what James calls the faith that works (Jas. 2:17).

Calvin wrote that we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. The wise builder who hears and does is the person who has been genuinely changed by the words of Jesus — not merely intellectually persuaded but existentially transformed. The doing of the Sermon on the Mount is not the cause of salvation but its fruit; not the foundation but the superstructure. And the foundation, as Paul will make clear (1 Cor. 3:11), is Jesus Christ himself — the one whose words these are.
7.examples:
Then: The two builders have their Old Testament counterparts in the wise and foolish in Proverbs: the one who builds their house on wisdom (Prov. 9:1) and the one who builds on folly (Prov. 9:13–18). Israel’s history is the extended parable of a nation that heard God’s word at Sinai and alternately built on it (David, Hezekiah, Josiah) and ignored it (the cycle of judges, the divided monarchy, the exile). The storm that came on the sandbuilders in Israel’s history was Babylon — and Jeremiah watched the great fall of it (Jer. 7:1–15, which echoes this passage).

Now: The Sermon on the Mount ends with the most personal challenge of the entire Gospel so far: what are you building on? The storm is coming — the storms of suffering, of loss, of death — and the question that will matter then is being answered now by what you build with your ordinary days. The person who reads the Sermon and is intellectually impressed but does nothing with it is the sand builder. The person who allows its demands to drive them to the Christ who fulfils them, and who in the Spirit begins to do what the Sermon commands — that person is building on rock. The flood will reveal the foundation. Build now while the weather is good.

8.title: The King’s Authority Over All
8.text: <sup>1</sup>When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. <sup>2</sup>And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>3</sup>And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>5</sup>When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, <sup>6</sup>“Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly.” <sup>7</sup>And he said to him, “I will come and heal him.” <sup>8</sup>But the centurion replied, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. <sup>9</sup>For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>10</sup>When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, “Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. <sup>11</sup>I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, <sup>12</sup>while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” <sup>13</sup>And to the centurion Jesus said, “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” And the servant was healed at that very moment. <sup>14</sup>And when Jesus entered Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. <sup>15</sup>He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him. <sup>16</sup>That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.” <sup>23</sup>And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. <sup>24</sup>And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. <sup>25</sup>And they went and woke him, saying, “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.” <sup>26</sup>And he said to them, “Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?” Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. <sup>27</sup>And the men marveled, saying, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?”
8.overview:
Matthew 8 is a gallery of authority. Coming down from the mountain where he gave the law of the kingdom, the King now demonstrates the power of the kingdom. In rapid succession Jesus heals a leper with a touch, a Gentile servant with a word, a feverish woman with a hand, and a raging sea with a rebuke. The crowds ask the right question: “What sort of man is this?” Matthew intends the reader to answer: the Son of God, in whom all authority in heaven and on earth is vested.

The chapter also sounds the notes of grace toward outsiders. A leper — ritually unclean, excluded from community — is touched rather than avoided. A Roman centurion — a Gentile, an occupier — displays faith that shames Israel. Jesus announces that many from east and west will recline at the messianic banquet while presumptuous insiders face exclusion. The kingdom breaks every boundary of ethnic privilege. The centurion’s faith is the model: he grasps that Jesus’ authority is absolute, that his word accomplishes what he speaks. This is saving faith — resting wholly on the word of the King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Messiah Heals: Authority over Leprosy, Paralysis, and Fever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew groups ten miracles in chapters 8-9, presenting Jesus as the one Isaiah promised: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases" (v. 17, citing Isa. 53:4). The leper, the centurion's servant, and Peter's mother-in-law are the first three — representing the ritually unclean, the Gentile, and the woman. Jesus heals all with equal authority and without discrimination.
verseByVerse.theology: Each healing is an enacted parable of salvation: Jesus touches what is untouchable (the leper), heals at a distance by his word alone (the centurion's servant), and raises up those laid low by sickness. The healing of disease and the forgiveness of sins are not unrelated — both are expressions of the same redemptive authority. Isaiah 53:4 locates these healings within the atonement: Jesus bore our diseases not merely by healing them but ultimately by carrying them on the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The centurion's faith astonishes Jesus and becomes the template for Gentile inclusion: "not even in Israel have I found such faith." Faith is not a Jewish property or a product of religious background; it is the trust that recognizes authority and rests in it. The centurion understood command-and-response because he lived under authority. His insight: if Jesus commands, it is done.

verseByVerse.quote: When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first miracle after the Sermon on the Mount is the healing of a leper — the man most excluded from Israelite society, prohibited by law from approaching others and required to warn them away by crying "Unclean!" His prayer is a model of faith: it affirms Jesus's power without presuming on his will ("if you will"). He does not demand; he trusts. The kneeling is an act of worship before a word is spoken. This is faith that knows its place: not bargaining with God but casting itself entirely on his sovereign mercy. The form of the prayer is one the church has prayed ever since: Lord, you can — we believe in your power; if you will — we submit to your wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, "I will; be clean." And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus could have healed with a word — he heals the centurion's servant without touching him. Here he touches the leper. The touch is the point: the law said the one who touched a leper became unclean. Jesus reverses the flow of contamination — his holiness is so powerful that it does not contract the leper's uncleanness; it expels it. "I will; be clean" is among the most sovereign utterances in the Gospels: no formula, no process, no prayer — simply the will of the Creator-King restoring what disease had destroyed. The instruction to show himself to the priest honors the Mosaic law (Jesus came not to abolish but to fulfill, 5:17). Under Leviticus 13–14 a "leper" was not merely sick but ceremonially unclean: only a priest could declare him clean and readmit him to the worship and life of Israel, and the healed man had to bring the offerings Moses prescribed. So Jesus sends him through that God-given procedure — the proper, public way an outcast was restored to the people of God. And it served a second purpose: when a priest had to examine a cleansed leper (a thing all but unheard of, seen only with Miriam and Naaman in the whole Old Testament), it stood as living proof before the religious leaders that One had come wielding power that belongs to God alone.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, "Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly."
verseByVerse.commentary: A Roman centurion commanded one hundred soldiers in the occupying army — the face of Gentile imperial power in Galilee. Yet he comes to Jesus in appeal, not command. The word translated "appealing" (parakalon) carries the sense of urgent request, even entreaty. His concern is for a servant — a person of low status — whose suffering moves him enough to seek healing from a Jewish teacher. The centurion's social position makes his coming remarkable; his moral concern for a servant makes it striking. Those with power often notice only their own needs. This man uses his power on behalf of the powerless. His character prepares us for his faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I will come and heal him." But the centurion replied, "Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed."
verseByVerse.commentary: "I am not worthy to have you come under my roof" — the centurion's self-assessment stands in contrast to his social position. He is the powerful one; Jesus is the itinerant Jewish teacher. Yet he recognizes a holiness in Jesus that makes even his Gentile home a potentially inappropriate space. More than humility, this is theological perception: he sees in Jesus an authority so absolute that physical presence is unnecessary. "Only say the word" — three words in Greek — is the most economical expression of faith in the Gospels. It understands that Jesus's word is as efficacious as his presence, that distance is no obstacle to omnipotent command. This is why the church prays to the ascended Lord: distance is irrelevant to his power.

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, "Go," and he goes, and to another, "Come," and he comes, and to my servant, "Do this," and he does it." When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, "Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith."
verseByVerse.commentary: The centurion's logic is an argument from analogy: because he is under authority, his commands carry the weight of the authority above him. When he says "Go," Roman imperial power stands behind the word. He sees that Jesus operates under divine authority — that when Jesus speaks, the power of the Creator stands behind the word. This is the theological core of faith: not confidence in the one praying but confidence in the authority of the one addressed. Jesus marvels — the only time Matthew uses this word of Jesus responding to a human. The faith of a Gentile soldier exceeded anything in Israel. Faith is not a national or religious achievement; it is perception of who Jesus is, available to anyone who truly sees.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. And to the centurion Jesus said, "Go; let it be done for you as you have believed." And the servant was healed at that very moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion's faith becomes the occasion for a startling eschatological declaration: Gentiles from every direction will share the messianic banquet with Israel's patriarchs, while the "sons of the kingdom" — those who assumed membership by birth — will be excluded. The reclining at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is the language of intimate fellowship at the feast that Isaiah promised (Isa. 25:6-8). The "outer darkness" with weeping and gnashing of teeth is Matthew's recurring image for final exclusion (cf. 22:13; 25:30). The kingdom was never a biological inheritance; it was always by faith. The centurion knew this instinctively; Israel's leaders did not.

"Let it be done for you as you have believed" — faith is the channel through which the healing flows, but it is not the source of it. The centurion's faith did not heal his servant; Jesus's word did. But faith positioned the centurion to receive what only Jesus could give. "At that very moment" — distance collapses before omnipotent word.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus entered Peter's house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then enters Peter's house: the miracles are not separated by theological reflection but flow one into the next. The healer of lepers and the healer of paralysis now finds a simple fever in a family member's household. There is no threshold of severity below which Jesus is unconcerned. He heals the grand miracle and the ordinary illness with equal attention.

Peter's mother-in-law rises from fever and immediately serves — a detail Matthew notes without commentary. The restored life expresses itself in service: this is the New Testament pattern of grace. She does not recover slowly; she is immediately well enough to minister.

verseByVerse.quote: That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick, This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evening scene is one of Matthew's most evocative: the whole town gathered at the door (Mark 1:33), bringing their sick and demonized. Jesus heals "all who were sick" — not the most deserving, not the most faithful, not the most urgent. All. The breadth of his healing ministry anticipates the breadth of the gospel: "whoever comes to me I will never cast out" (John 6:37).

Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4 — the fourth Servant Song — and applies it to Jesus's healing ministry. This is a remarkable interpretive move: Isaiah's "took our illnesses and bore our diseases" is applied not (yet) to the cross but to the healings in Galilee. The healings are not separate from the atonement; they are its advance expression. Jesus was bearing the weight of human brokenness throughout his ministry, not only at Calvary. The cross is the ultimate and once-for-all bearing of sin and its consequences; the healings are enacted promises that the one who would bear all things was already present and already at work. Every healing was a Calvary-shadow, every restoration a resurrection-foretaste.

Does God still heal like this today? Two things must be held together. First, yes — God is sovereign and good, he still hears prayer, and we are plainly told to pray for the sick (Jas 5:14–15). He has never stopped healing in answer to the cries of his people. But second, we must read these Gospel healings in their place. They came in a cluster, and clusters of miracles in Scripture gather around the great moments of fresh revelation — Moses and the exodus, Elijah and Elisha, and now Christ and his apostles — not evenly across every age. Their purpose was largely to authenticate: to mark Jesus out as the Messiah and his apostles as his accredited messengers (Heb 2:3–4; 2 Cor 12:12). They were signs of a unique hour, not a promise of constant, on-demand healing for the church.

And the healings are the kingdom's down-payment, not its full payout. Isaiah's "he bore our diseases" is purchased at the cross, yet the complete and final healing — no more sickness, no more death — belongs to the resurrection and the new creation. We live in the "already and not yet." That is why, even in the apostolic age, healing was never automatic: Paul's thorn was left in place (2 Cor 12:7–9), he left Trophimus sick (2 Tim 4:20), prescribed wine for Timothy's stomach (1 Tim 5:23), and Epaphroditus nearly died (Phil 2:27). So pray boldly for healing, and trust God to answer as he wills — but beware the cruel teaching that healing is guaranteed if only your faith is strong enough. It was not promised even to apostles, and it heaps guilt on the suffering for their own pain. Sometimes grace is given to carry us through the sickness rather than to remove it (2 Cor 12:9) — and every believer will be perfectly and finally healed at the resurrection, if not before. (Godly Christians differ on whether the miraculous gift itself continues; all agree God still heals in answer to prayer.)

A word, too, on those "oppressed by demons," since the topic puzzles many: barely present in the Old Testament, suddenly everywhere in the Gospels, then quietly receding. The dark powers are real throughout Scripture, but the spotlight shifts. In the Old Testament they lurk mostly in the background — behind idolatry, which Scripture calls sacrificing to demons (Deut 32:17; Ps 106:37), in the occasional evil spirit (Saul, 1 Sam 16), in Satan the accuser (Job 1; Zech 3) — yet open, individual possession and exorcism are almost absent. Then in the Gospels it erupts, because the King has come. The arrival of God's kingdom in Jesus forces the kingdom of darkness into the open; light invades the dark, and the demons manifest, scream, and are routed with a word. This is kingdom warfare: "if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (12:28); the strong man is being bound and his house plundered (12:29). The eruption is less new activity than the enemy's panic before the invading King.

And why does it fade in the rest of the New Testament? Not because the demonic vanished, but because the decisive battle was won: at the cross Christ "disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them" (Col 2:15). The letters still take the unseen war with deadly seriousness — but they reframe it: less the spectacular seizing of individuals, more the believer's daily, sober resistance to "the spiritual forces of evil," clothed in the whole armor of God (Eph 6:12), resisting the devil so that he flees (Jas 4:7; 1 Pet 5:8–9), giving him no foothold (Eph 4:27). The defeated enemy still prowls, but now he meets a people covered in Christ's victory. (The word "oppressed" covers a range, from outward affliction to inward possession; and note that one indwelt by the Spirit of God is not owned by such powers — the Christian fights from within Christ's triumph, never under the enemy's ownership.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–34 — The Cost of Following and the Lord of Storm and Demons
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 8 moves from healing to the cost of discipleship and the authority of Jesus over creation and the demonic. Two would-be followers learn that Jesus offers no earthly security (no place to lay his head, no leave for burial rites). Then Jesus stills a storm with a rebuke and casts demons into pigs, and the Gadarenes ask him to leave. The sequence shows that following Jesus is neither comfortable nor universally welcomed.
verseByVerse.theology: The stilling of the storm is the Christological center of the chapter: "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?" The disciples' question is Matthew's question to the reader. Only the Creator can command his creation. The storm-still and the Gadarene exorcism together display authority over the two great threats of the ancient world — chaos (the sea) and the demonic (the Legion). Both submit instantly. The appropriate response is not comfort but worship — and the disciples begin to learn it.
verseByVerse.examples: The Gadarenes' request that Jesus leave their region is one of the saddest verses in the Gospels. They preferred their pigs to their Deliverer. The economy of the region mattered more than the liberation of two men in chains. This is not ancient history; every age chooses its pigs. The question Jesus poses to every community: what do you value more than the healing he brings?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. And a scribe came up and said to him, "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary: A scribe — an educated religious professional — offers unreserved following: "wherever you go." The enthusiasm is admirable, the commitment apparently total. But Jesus tests it before accepting it. The offer of discipleship made to Jesus is always tested, because Jesus knows the human heart and knows what the cost of following actually is. He does not receive every profession of loyalty at face value; he presses on it to see what it will bear. The scribe's willingness is not questioned — it is examined. The following verses reveal what "wherever you go" actually means, and whether the scribe was prepared for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." Another of the disciples said to him, "Lord, let me first go and bury my father." And Jesus said to him, "Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head" — itinerant homelessness was the condition of Jesus's ministry. He is warning the scribe: I offer no earthly security, no home, no fixed address. Following me means sharing this. The second would-be follower offers a request that sounds entirely reasonable: let me bury my father. In Jewish culture, burial of a parent was among the most sacred obligations. Yet Jesus's reply will be shockingly absolute. The juxtaposition of the two cases — one offering too much (naive enthusiasm) and one offering conditional terms — together reveal the radical nature of the kingdom's claim on its disciples.

"Leave the dead to bury their own dead" is one of Jesus's most demanding sayings. The "dead" who bury are the spiritually dead — those who have not yet responded to the call of the kingdom. The point is not that family obligations are unimportant but that the call of Jesus overrides even the most sacred cultural and familial duty when it conflicts with it. The kingdom cannot wait for the next convenient window. This is the costliness of discipleship that the scribe's enthusiasm had not reckoned with.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. And they went and woke him, saying, "Save us, Lord; we are perishing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples who do follow get into the boat — and immediately encounter the test of the storm. Following Jesus leads straight into difficulty; he never promised otherwise.

Jesus asleep in the storm is one of the Gospel's most humanly tender and theologically rich images. He sleeps the deep sleep of a man exhausted by ministry — genuine human tiredness. Meanwhile the boat is being swamped. The disciples' cry — "Save us, Lord; we are perishing" — is the cry of the church in every storm. Three words in Greek (Kyrie, soson, apollymetha) that the church has prayed across twenty centuries in every form of crisis. The prayer is panicked, but it is prayer — they run to Jesus, not away from him. Fear is not the opposite of faith; indifference is. These frightened men knew where to turn.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?" Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. And the men marveled, saying, "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus rebukes the disciples before rebuking the storm — the order is deliberate. Their fear is the primary problem; the storm is secondary. "O you of little faith" — oligopistoi, the same word used in 6:30. They believe, but their faith is too small for the crisis. Then he rises and speaks to the storm as to a subordinate — and it obeys. The sea that swallows nations (Ps. 107:23-30) instantly stills at one word. The disciples' question — "What sort of man is this?" — is the right question, the question Matthew's whole Gospel is answering. Only the Creator commands creation. The Psalms give God's people the answer they could not yet fully see: "He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed" (Ps. 107:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. And behold, they cried out, "What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Gadarene exorcism is the storm's counterpart: authority over chaos at sea, now authority over chaos on land. Two men possessed by demons so violent that no one dared approach them — living in tombs, outside civilization, beyond human help. The demons recognize Jesus immediately and perfectly: "Son of God." The demonic world has no christological confusion. They know who he is and what his coming means for them. "Before the time?" — they know there is an appointed day of final judgment, and they are not sure this is it. Their theology is accurate; their allegiance is catastrophically wrong. Knowing the truth about Jesus while not submitting to him is the condition of the damned.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. And the demons begged him, saying, "If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs."
verseByVerse.commentary: The demons do not dispute Jesus's authority to cast them out — they beg only for the destination. Even their request must be submitted to him; they cannot act without his permission. The pigs are unclean animals in Jewish law — an appropriate destination for unclean spirits. There is dark irony in the request: the demons prefer anything to the abyss, even the bodies of animals. Jesus permits it. The permission is not explained — Matthew does not supply a theological rationale. The sovereign permits what the sovereign permits, and the outcome (the demons's evident capacity for destruction, the pigs' death) is part of the revelation of what these beings do when given freedom. The demonic destroys whatever it inhabits.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go." So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, including what had happened to the demon-possessed men.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Go" — one word in Greek. The same sovereign economy of speech that stilled the storm casts out the Legion. The rush of two thousand pigs (Mark 5:13) into the sea dramatizes what would have happened to the men if the demons had remained. The herdsmen's report carries the news to the city — and the city's response will be to ask Jesus to leave. The miracle that liberates two men destroys an economic asset. The community calculates its loss, not its gain. Two sons of Adam restored to their right minds are valued less than a herd of pigs. This is not only ancient callousness; it is the universal human tendency to resist the disruptive grace that costs us something.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They begged him to leave their region" — the same word used by the demons in verse 31 (parekaloun). The city begs as the demons begged; their request is essentially the same. They want Jesus gone. Two men set free, a demonic stronghold broken, an entire community freed from the terror of those tombs — and the response is to ask the healer to go away. The economy of the region, represented by the drowned pigs, matters more than the liberation of two neighbors. Jesus grants their request: he will not stay where he is not wanted. This is the most terrible expression of God's sovereignty — that he honors human rejection by departing. The Gadarenes got what they asked for.

Do not rush past how sobering this is. We are fond of a Jesus who relentlessly pursues every sinner and never, ever lets go — and the seeking Shepherd of Luke 15 is gloriously real. But here is the other side of the truth, the side we prefer to forget: when a people settle their hearts against him and say "depart," he can and does take them at their word. This is the judgment Paul names in Romans 1, where three times "God gave them up" — handed them over to the very sins they preferred (Rom 1:24, 26, 28). The most fearful answer God ever gives to a prayer is to grant the request "leave me alone." The Gadarenes asked him to go, and he went.

Scripture sounds this warning more than once. "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever" (Gen 6:3). Of stubborn Israel: "I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels" (Ps 81:12). Of idol-wedded Ephraim: "leave him alone" (Hos 4:17). Over Jerusalem Jesus himself wept, "How often would I have gathered your children... and you would not! See, your house is left to you desolate" (23:37–38) — he grieves to leave, but he leaves. Yet hear the mercy folded inside the warning: today he has not left. The door still stands open, and he still knocks (Rev 3:20). So this story is no counsel of despair but a summons to urgency: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts" (Heb 3:15); "seek the LORD while he may be found, call upon him while he is near" (Isa 55:6). The terror is real — and so, right now, is the open door.

8.theology: The authority of Christ. Chapter 8 is a sustained meditation on the authority of the Son of God. He has authority over disease (leper, fever), over distance (servant healed at a word), over demons (v. 16), and over creation (storm). Reformed theology insists that this authority is not delegated but inherent: Jesus is not a prophet with God’s power on loan but the eternal Son in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Col 2:9). His healing word and his saving word are the same — both accomplish what they declare. The centurion’s faith grasps this: faith is resting on the word of One who has absolute authority to perform what he promises.
8.examples:
Then: A Roman officer, trained in chains of command, recognized the absolute authority of Jesus. His faith put to shame those who had grown up with the Scriptures but had domesticated their expectations of the Messiah.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that regards faith as a psychological coping mechanism. The centurion’s faith is the opposite: it is epistemically grounded in the nature of the One trusted. We trust Christ not because belief makes us feel better but because he is the Lord of heaven and earth whose word does not return void. When we pray, we address the One who stilled the Sea of Galilee.

9.title: The King’s Authority to Forgive
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. <sup>2</sup>And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” <sup>3</sup>And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.” <sup>4</sup>But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts? <sup>5</sup>For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>6</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” —he then said to the paralytic— “Rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>7</sup>And he rose and went home. <sup>8</sup>When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men. <sup>9</sup>As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>10</sup>And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. <sup>11</sup>And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>12</sup>But when he heard it, he said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>13</sup>Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’ For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>35</sup>And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. <sup>36</sup>When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. <sup>37</sup>Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; <sup>38</sup>therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
9.overview:
Chapter 9 begins with the most audacious claim in Jesus’ ministry: “Your sins are forgiven.” The scribes immediately see the implication — only God can forgive sins — and charge blasphemy. Jesus responds by healing the paralytic as evidence that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The miracle is the sign; forgiveness is the substance. This is Matthew’s thesis: Jesus has come not primarily to heal bodies but to heal souls, not primarily to liberate from Roman occupation but to liberate from the bondage of sin and guilt.

The call of Matthew himself is a microcosm of the gospel. A tax collector — a collaborator with Rome, a social and religious outcast — is called with a two-word summons. He rises and follows. The banquet that follows is a picture of the kingdom: Jesus eating with the unworthy, the Pharisees scandalized, Jesus quoting Hosea 6:6 (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice”). The chapter closes with Jesus surveying the harassed crowds with compassion and calling for labourers. The mission of the King now extends through his people.

Read straight through, the chapter reveals a second pattern woven beneath the miracles: in story after story faith stands beside unbelief, and the two are sifted apart. The paralytic comes carried by friends whose faith Jesus sees (v. 2) — while the scribes silently cry blasphemy. Matthew rises at a word — while the Pharisees mutter at the table. The ruler kneels and the unclean woman reaches, both in bold faith — while the hired mourners laugh him to scorn. The blind men confess “Yes, Lord” — while the watching Pharisees, at the chapter’s climax, sneer that he casts out demons “by the prince of demons” (v. 34). The same Jesus, the same works — and they divide every heart that meets them: some come empty-handed and receive everything, while others, certain they need nothing, receive nothing and only harden. This is the dividing line the whole Gospel will trace, and it is why the chapter closes not in triumph but in compassion for the harassed and helpless crowds (vv. 36–38) — the harvest is plentiful, and this faith must be carried to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Forgiveness, Fellowship, and Fasting: Who Has Authority?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus returns to Capernaum and heals a paralyzed man by first forgiving his sins — triggering the first direct conflict with the scribes. He then calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with sinners, outraging the Pharisees. When John's disciples ask why Jesus's disciples don't fast, Jesus answers with three images: the bridegroom, the unshrunk cloth, and the new wine. The old forms cannot contain the new reality that has arrived.
verseByVerse.theology: The paralytic episode is the theological pivot: Jesus claims authority to forgive sins, which belongs to God alone. The scribes are theologically right that only God forgives sins; they are catastrophically wrong in their conclusion that Jesus is therefore blaspheming. The miracle of healing is offered as proof of the greater miracle of forgiveness — the visible confirms the invisible. Matthew's call and the meal with sinners then demonstrate what forgiveness looks like in practice: the Physician comes for the sick, not the healthy.
verseByVerse.examples: The three images of newness — bridegroom, cloth, wineskins — announce that Jesus is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfillment and transformation. The joy of the bridegroom's presence cannot be contained in old mourning forms. The new covenant is not a patch on the old but its completion. The Pharisees' question about fasting reveals that they are still thinking in terms of the old forms; Jesus is announcing that the age of the bridegroom has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Their faith" — not only the paralytic's but his friends', whose effort carried him to Jesus. Faith is not always individual; the community of faith can carry those whose own faith is weak or absent. Jesus sees the faith of the group and responds to the paralytic. "Take heart, my son" — words of tender paternal address before any act of healing. Then the unexpected: before addressing the paralysis, Jesus addresses the deeper problem. "Your sins are forgiven" would have stunned the room. The man came for his legs; Jesus goes straight to his soul. The physical need is real and will be addressed; the spiritual need is deeper, and Jesus addresses it first.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, "This man is blaspheming." But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, "Why do you think evil in your hearts?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The scribes' reasoning is correct as far as it goes: only God can forgive sins (Isa. 43:25; Mark 2:7). Therefore a man who claims to forgive sins is either God or a blasphemer. They choose blasphemer — not because the evidence compels it, but because their hearts are already closed to the alternative. Jesus knows their thoughts — another claim to divine knowledge. He does not deny that forgiveness belongs to God; he implicitly claims to be the God who forgives. The question "why do you think evil in your hearts?" presses at the motivation behind their theological conclusion: is this a genuine inquiry after truth, or is the conclusion already settled?

verseByVerse.quote: "For which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" — he then said to the paralytic — "Rise, pick up your bed and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary: The argument is elegant: saying "your sins are forgiven" is unverifiable — no one can check it. Saying "rise and walk" is immediately testable. Jesus will provide the verifiable miracle as evidence for the unverifiable claim. If he can do the greater (command a paralyzed body to move), he can do the lesser (forgive sins) — because both require the same divine authority. "The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" is the first time Matthew uses "Son of Man" as a self-designation in connection with authority. The title from Daniel 7:13-14 — the one given dominion over all — is here claiming that dominion extends to the forgiveness of sins. The healing is not a distraction from the theology; it is the proof of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and went home. When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men.
verseByVerse.commentary: The paralytic rises, takes his mat, and goes home — the three actions commanded, performed in order, completed without explanation. The crowd's response combines fear and glorification: they are frightened by what they have witnessed (the appropriate response to a theophany) and they give glory to God. "Who had given such authority to men" — they perceive correctly that the authority comes from God but frame it as God having granted authority to a human representative. This is partially correct: Jesus is the Son of Man through whom God acts. The full truth — that the one acting is himself God the Son — will take the whole Gospel to disclose. But the crowd's instinct to glorify God is the right beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him. And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary: Matthew the tax collector is called with the same two-word command as the fishermen: "Follow me." Tax collectors were despised as collaborators with Rome and known for dishonest exaction — they were excluded from synagogue life and considered beyond the pale of respectable Jewish society. Matthew does not hesitate. He rises from his tax booth — abandoning a lucrative position — and follows. The immediate consequence is a meal: Matthew hosts Jesus, and the guest list is the crowd that Jesus has come to save. Reclining at table in the ancient world was an act of fellowship and equality — to eat with someone was to accept them. Jesus accepts sinners at table. This is the shape of the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" But when he heard it, he said, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." Go and learn what this means: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees' question is addressed to the disciples, not to Jesus — a social strategy for undermining a teacher through his followers. Jesus answers anyway, with the physician analogy. The logic is irrefutable: a doctor goes to the sick, not the healthy. If Jesus is the physician of souls, the appropriate address for his ministry is the population that knows it is sick — tax collectors, sinners, the morally compromised. The Pharisees' implicit self-identification as "healthy" is the most dangerous misdiagnosis in the chapter. The sick person who knows they are sick can receive the physician; the "healthy" person who has never acknowledged their need cannot. Self-righteousness is the one condition that excludes the cure.

"Go and learn" — a rabbinic formula, addressed here to the rabbis as if they were students who had missed the lesson. The Hosea 6:6 quotation ("I desire mercy, and not sacrifice") does not abolish sacrifice; it establishes the priority. Ritual observance without the heart of mercy is not religion but its counterfeit. "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners" — the irony is biting: there are no righteous ones, only those who know they are sinners and those who don't.

verseByVerse.quote: And then the disciples of John came to him, saying, "Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made." Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's disciples ask sincerely, not with hostility: they and the Pharisees fasted often, yet Jesus' disciples did not. Why? A word on their practice helps. The law of Moses commanded only one fast a year — the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to "afflict" itself (Lev 16:29–31). Every other fast was added by tradition: after the exile, four annual fasts mourned the fall of Jerusalem (Zech 8:19), and by Jesus' day the devout fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays (cf. Lk 18:12). So the "frequent fasting" they mention was custom, not command. Behind it lay real longing: fasting expressed grief over sin, repentance, and yearning for God to send his deliverance and his Messiah. At its best it was the posture of a people still waiting.

And that is just why Jesus' disciples were not fasting: the waiting was over. "Can the wedding guests mourn while the bridegroom is with them?" Jesus is the long-promised Bridegroom (cf. Isa 62:5; Jn 3:29), and his presence turns the hour into a wedding feast. Fasting belongs to absence and mourning; feasting belongs to the joy of his being here. But mark the shadow that falls across the sentence: "the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away" — the first veiled hint in Matthew of the cross. After he is gone, his people will fast again, as the early church did (Acts 13:2–3), now longing for his return.

The two little parables drive the same point home: do not stitch the new onto the old. A patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment tears away and makes the rip worse; new, still-fermenting wine bursts old, brittle skins, and both are lost. Jesus is the new wine, the kingdom arrived; the "old" is the whole framework of mourning, waiting, and ritual that belonged to the age before the King appeared — the fasting-as-mourning included. You cannot cram the joy of the wedding into the forms of the funeral. This is no attack on the Old Testament, which is old wine now come to full maturity in him; it is a warning against forcing kingdom-life into a religious system too rigid to hold it. The new covenant calls for new wineskins — a life and worship freshly shaped by Christ, not merely patched onto what came before.

So should Christians fast? Jesus plainly assumes we will ("then they will fast"; and "when you fast," 6:16), and the early church did, at prayer and at weighty decisions (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Yet — tellingly — the epistles lay down no command, no required days, no rule. Fasting is therefore a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: a way to humble ourselves, sharpen prayer, and hunger for God, never a badge to earn his favor. (The how and why are unfolded more fully at 6:16–18.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–38 — The Harvest Is Plentiful: Four More Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew compresses four more miracles into a rapid sequence: a ruler's dead daughter raised, a hemorrhaging woman healed on the way, two blind men given sight, a mute demoniac freed. The chapter ends with a summary of Jesus's teaching and healing throughout all the cities and villages, and the saying about the plentiful harvest and the few laborers. The pace is breathless — Matthew is showing the sheer scope of Jesus's ministry, the range of human need he addresses, and the consistency of his compassion.
verseByVerse.theology: The two miracles of verses 18-26 are intertwined: the ruler's daughter dies while Jesus is on the way to heal her, and the hemorrhaging woman receives healing by touching his garment. Both cases involve women (a girl and a woman), both involve twelve years (the woman's illness, the girl's age in Mark's account), and both require faith that presses past social convention. Jesus stops for the bleeding woman even while the child lies dying — he does not hurry past need in order to reach crisis. Both receive exactly what they need.
verseByVerse.examples: The harvest saying (vv. 37-38) is the theological conclusion of the two miracle chapters: the need is vast, the laborers few, and the solution is prayer — not human strategy, not program development, but asking the Lord of the harvest to send workers. The church has often responded to the harvest by increasing activity; Jesus commands increasing prayer. The two are not incompatible, but prayer is the first and foundational response.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, "My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live." And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, for she said to herself, "If I only touch his garment, I will be made well." Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, "Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well." And instantly the woman was made well. And when Jesus came to the ruler's house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, he said, "Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. And the report of this went through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A synagogue ruler — a man of religious rank and standing — comes and kneels before Jesus. His faith outruns anything he has yet seen: not merely "heal my sick child" but "my daughter has just died... come and lay your hand on her, and she will live." Jesus rises at once and follows, without a question or a condition. This is how he answers a sincere cry: immediately, going where he is needed.

On the way the story is interrupted — as Matthew means it to be. A woman who had bled for twelve years comes up behind him. Under the law (Lev 15:25–27) such a discharge made her perpetually unclean: barred from synagogue and temple, unable to embrace a friend or receive a greeting without defiling them, cut off for twelve years from the ordinary touch of human belonging. To press through the crowd is to defile everyone she brushes — an act of sheer desperation. She does not announce herself; she reaches: "If I only touch his garment, I will be made well." And what she touches is the tasseled fringe (Num 15:38–40) that symbolized the very law which had shut her out — reaching past the law that condemned her to the One who fulfills it.

Jesus turns: "Take heart, daughter" — the same tender word he gave the paralytic (9:2). He sees the person, not just the affliction. "Your faith has made you well" — not that faith itself healed her, but that it joined her to the One who did. Twelve years end in an instant.

Then he reaches the ruler's house, already loud with flute-players and wailing mourners — the machinery of death. "The girl is not dead but sleeping," he says (the word he will use of Lazarus, Jn 11:11); to the Lord of life, death is a sleep he can break. They laugh — the laugh of those who know a corpse when they see one. He puts them out, takes the girl by the hand (as he had touched the leper), and she rises — egeiro, the word for resurrection itself.
