verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith."
verseByVerse.commentary: "If you have faith and do not doubt" — the condition for mountain-moving prayer is not the absence of all uncertainty but the undivided commitment of trust that does not look away from Jesus to the obstacle. The mountain thrown into the sea is the same hyperbole as the mustard-seed faith of 17:20 — something humanly impossible accomplished through faith in the God for whom all things are possible. "Whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith" — not a blank check for any request, but the promise that prayer rooted in genuine trust in God's character and submitted to God's will receives what it asks. The tree withered; the disciples are invited into the same authority — not over fig trees, but over the seemingly immovable obstacles of kingdom work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Authority Questioned: Three Parables of Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chief priests and elders challenge Jesus's authority: by what authority do you do these things? Jesus answers with a counter-question about John's baptism that they refuse to answer, then tells three parables of judgment: the two sons (the one who refused then obeyed vs. the one who agreed but didn't), the wicked tenants who killed the vineyard owner's son, and the implied parable of the rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118. The parables systematically indict the religious leadership of Israel for rejecting God's messengers and the Son himself.
verseByVerse.theology: The authority question and Jesus's counter-question about John expose the leaders' bad faith: they do not want to know the source of Jesus's authority; they want to discredit him publicly. Their refusal to answer John's question (whether from heaven or from men) reveals that they are governed by crowd opinion rather than truth-seeking. Jesus therefore refuses to answer them directly — but he answers indirectly and devastatingly through the three parables. The wicked tenants is the most explicit: they will kill the son, and the vineyard will be given to others who will produce its fruits.
verseByVerse.examples: The rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118:22 — the same psalm shouted at the triumphal entry — completes the argument. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; what the religious establishment rejects, God establishes as the foundation of his kingdom. The chief priests and Pharisees understood that he was speaking about them — and they wanted to arrest him but feared the crowds. The rejection is comprehensive; the judgment is announced; the crowds are the only restraint preventing its immediate human execution.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, "By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?" Jesus answered them, "I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary: The authority question is the central question of chapters 21-23: who gave Jesus the right to enter as he did, cleanse as he did, teach as he does? The challenge is from the Sanhedrin's official leadership — chief priests and elders — the highest religious court in Israel. Jesus responds with a counter-question: not evasion but Socratic logic. He will answer their question, but first they must answer his. The counter-question is designed to expose the ground on which they actually stand — not truth-seeking but reputation-management. If they answer honestly, they will convict themselves; if they refuse, they will expose their bad faith. Either way, the pretense of genuine inquiry is dissolved.

verseByVerse.quote: The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" And they discussed it among themselves, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say to us, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But if we say, 'From man,' we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold John to be a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary: The leaders' deliberation is entirely pragmatic: what answer will minimize damage to our position? "From heaven" commits them to believing John, which commits them to accepting what John pointed to. "From man" offends the crowd that regards John as a prophet. Truth is nowhere in the calculation. They are not asking what the right answer is; they are asking what the safe answer is. This is the defining characteristic of political religion: questions of authority are decided not by evidence and conscience but by crowd management. The leaders who should be guiding Israel's conscience are instead consulting its pulse. Their refusal to answer is the answer that Jesus needs.

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And he said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work in the vineyard today.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: "We do not know" — the most intellectually dishonest words in the Gospel, from the people most obligated to know. The men who have devoted their lives to determining what is true and what is false in matters of religion, who hold positions of religious authority precisely because they are supposed to know such things, claim not to know. The claim is false — they know; they simply cannot afford to say. Jesus honors the form of their answer by declining to answer his own question, then immediately obliterates their rhetorical position with the parable of the two sons. The parable needs no introduction; it is its own answer to the authority question.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he answered, 'I will not,' but afterward he changed his mind and went. And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, 'I go, sir,' but did not go."
verseByVerse.commentary: The two sons represent two responses to the Father's call. The first refuses outright — insolent, disrespectful — then repents and goes. The second says the right words — "I go, sir" (kyrie — Lord!) — with apparent respect, and does not go. The contrast is between profession and performance, between religious compliance and genuine obedience. The second son's "I go, sir" is the language of the Pharisees who say "Lord, Lord" (7:21) — the right words without the transformed will that produces action. The first son's repentance and going — however rough the initial response — is genuine obedience. God values the repentance that actually changes direction over the profession that leaves everything unchanged.

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the two did the will of his father?" They said, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him."
verseByVerse.commentary: "The tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you" — the most direct verdict in the controversy: the most visibly sinful people, who repented at John's preaching, are ahead of the most visibly religious, who did not. The first son is the tax collector and prostitute: they said no to God through their lives, but John's preaching changed their direction. The second son is the chief priest and elder: they said yes through their religious profession but have not moved. "Even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds" — they watched the repentance of tax collectors and prostitutes, saw the evidence of genuine transformation, and remained unmoved. Hardened hearts do not soften in the presence of more evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants and went into a far country. When the season for fruit came, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary: The vineyard parable draws directly on Isaiah 5:1-7, where the vineyard is Israel and the owner is God. The detailed preparation — fence, winepress, tower — establishes the care invested before the lease. The owner's departure and the sending of servants for fruit is the pattern of prophetic history: God entrusts Israel to its leaders (the tenants), and repeatedly sends messengers (the prophets) to call for the fruit of righteousness. The fruitlessness of Isaiah's vineyard (5:2) and the violence of the tenants in this parable are the same story intensified: Israel did not merely fail to produce fruit; its leaders actively resisted those who came asking for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them."
verseByVerse.commentary: The servants who are beaten, killed, and stoned are the prophets: Abel (first martyr), Zechariah son of Jehoiada (stoned in the temple court, 2 Chron. 24:20-21), and the prophets throughout the history of Israel who were rejected and killed. "Again he sent other servants, more than the first" — the owner's patience is extraordinary, almost incomprehensible. He keeps sending despite the violence against his messengers. This is the patience of God across the centuries of Israel's history: prophet after prophet sent to a people that consistently rejected them. The history of prophecy is the history of rejected messengers, which is the history of divine patience stretched to its outer limit.

verseByVerse.quote: "Finally he sent his son to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: "Finally he sent his son" — the eschatological "finally" of God's ultimate act of self-giving. After all the prophets, the Son. "They will respect my son" — the owner's hope, not his certainty. He sends his son in the hope that the son will command a different response than the servants. Instead, the tenants recognize the son precisely as the one whose death will benefit them: "the heir — if we kill him, the inheritance is ours." The logic of murder for gain: silence the rightful heir and seize what is his. This is the exact logic of the leaders who are plotting Jesus's death: get rid of him before he displaces us. The parable is transparent; the leaders will recognize themselves (v. 45).

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?"
verseByVerse.commentary: "Threw him out of the vineyard and killed him" — Jesus is killed outside Jerusalem ("outside the gate," Heb. 13:12), thrown out of the city as the son is thrown out of the vineyard. The sequence — throw out, then kill — reverses the logical order of murder and disposal, which suggests deliberate prophetic shaping: crucifixion outside the city walls is the fulfillment. "When therefore the owner comes" — the eschatological question: what happens when the patient owner returns to judge? Jesus asks the leaders to pronounce their own verdict, exactly as Nathan made David pronounce the verdict on himself (2 Sam. 12:5-6). The trap is perfect: their answer is their own condemnation.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons." Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the Scriptures: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The leaders speak their own judgment: the wretched tenants will be miserably destroyed, the vineyard given to others who produce fruit. They have convicted themselves with their own words. Psalm 118:22-23 — the same psalm from the triumphal entry — becomes the capstone argument: the rejected stone (Jesus, rejected by the builders who are the religious leaders) has become the cornerstone. This is not a human strategy; it is "the Lord's doing" — the divine reversal that makes human rejection into divine establishment. "It is marvelous in our eyes": the word means "beyond ordinary sight," a marvel that exceeds normal comprehension. The resurrection will be exactly this: the builders' rejected stone becoming the church's foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him."
verseByVerse.commentary: "The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits" — the most explicit announcement of Israel's leadership's judgment in Matthew. The "people" (ethnos) is the new community of the church, constituted not by ethnic Israel but by those who produce kingdom fruit — Jew and Gentile who receive the Son. The stone becomes a weapon: those who stumble over it are broken (a reference to Isa. 8:14-15, the stumbling stone); those on whom it falls are crushed (Dan. 2:34-35, 44-45, the stone that becomes a mountain). The stone of judgment is the same stone of salvation — the same Christ who is the cornerstone for believers is the crushing stone for those who reject him.

verseByVerse.quote: When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary: "They perceived that he was speaking about them" — they understand the parable perfectly. There is no ambiguity, no need for explanation. The self-knowledge this produces is not repentance but intensified murderous intent: "they were seeking to arrest him." The knowledge of their own guilt does not open the door to conversion; it accelerates their determination to eliminate the one who named them. Only the crowd restrains them — the same crowd management that prevented them from answering the John question (v. 26). The leaders of Israel are governed entirely by fear of the crowd and desire for power. The crowd holds them back; within days, the crowd will be turned against Jesus, and the restraint will be removed.

21.theology: Christ as the true Temple. The temple cleansing in Matthew 21 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the replacement and fulfilment of the temple. The temple was the place where God dwelt with his people, where sacrifice was made, where prayer ascended. Jesus embodies all three functions: he is Emmanuel — God dwelling with his people; he is the Lamb whose self-offering ends the sacrificial system; he is the mediator through whom prayer reaches the Father (John 14:13–14). John’s Gospel makes this explicit (“the temple he had spoken of was his body”, John 2:21). The destruction of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 was the confirmation that the type had given way to the antitype.
21.examples:
Then: The crowds welcomed Jesus with genuine excitement and completely wrong expectations. They wanted a Maccabean king who would drive out Rome; they got a crucified Servant who would drive out death. The Palm Sunday crowd’s theology is a warning: it is possible to praise Jesus enthusiastically while fundamentally misunderstanding who he is and what he has come to do.

Now: The fig tree is the perennial warning against fruitless religion — maintaining the form of Christian practice without the substance of faith, repentance, love, and transformed life. The church with its worship services, theological conferences, and evangelical brands may be full of leaves. The question Jesus asks of every institution and every individual is the same: where is the fruit?

22.title: The Great Banquet and the Hard Questions
22.text: <sup>2</sup>The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son, <sup>3</sup>and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. <sup>9</sup>Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find. <sup>10</sup>And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests. <sup>14</sup>For many are called, but few are chosen. <sup>21</sup>They said, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” <sup>29</sup>But Jesus answered them, “You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. <sup>30</sup>For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>31</sup>And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” <sup>37</sup>And he said to him, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. <sup>38</sup>This is the great and first commandment. <sup>39</sup>And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. <sup>40</sup>On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.” <sup>42</sup>“What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “The son of David.” <sup>44</sup>He said to them, “Then how is it that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord?’
22.overview:
Chapter 22 is a day of public controversy in Jerusalem. The religious establishment sends wave after wave of opponents — Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees — each with a question designed to trap Jesus. He answers all of them and turns the final question back on his attackers, leaving them silenced. Matthew arranges the chapter as a trial in which the judge is the one in the dock: every party that challenges Jesus is exposed by his answers, and the final question — “Whose son is the Christ?” — reveals that the Messiah is not merely David’s descendant but David’s Lord.

The chapter opens with the parable of the wedding banquet, which recapitulates the entire history of Israel’s rejection of God’s invitations and the extension of grace to the Gentile roads and byways. “Many are called, but few are chosen” is not a statement about the inefficacy of the gospel but about the mystery of election: the call goes out wide; the choice of God secures who will respond. The banquet hall will be full — but with those God has chosen, not those who presumed on their invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Parable of the Wedding Banquet and the Question about Taxes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus responds to the religious establishment's rejection with the parable of the wedding banquet, showing that Israel's leaders have spurned the King's invitation and the Gentiles will fill the hall. The Pharisees and Herodians then try to trap him on the question of taxes, only to be confounded by his sovereign wisdom.
verseByVerse.theology: God's saving invitation is gracious, urgent, and dangerous to refuse. The parable teaches that election overturns human expectation — the unworthy are brought in — yet grace does not abolish accountability: the man without a wedding garment is cast out. Jesus' reply to the tax question establishes the two-kingdoms principle: civil and divine obligations each exist, and neither cancels the other.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin notes the wedding garment as imputed righteousness — those who come must be clothed in Christ, not merely physically present. Keller observes that the parable's shock is that the first guests were religious insiders; the gospel always upends social and religious hierarchy.

verseByVerse.quote: And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The kingdom of heaven is not a vague spiritual state but a royal administration with a King and a Son — and the image Jesus uses to describe it is a wedding feast. In the ancient Near East, a royal wedding was not a private ceremony but a public celebration that could last for days: the king slaughtered his finest cattle, opened his finest stores of wine, and treated the feast as a public display of his wealth and generosity. The Isaiah 25:6 background gives the image its full theological weight: 'The LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined.' God's eschatological purposes, Isaiah promised, culminate not in solemnity but in celebration — a feast prepared by the LORD himself, for all peoples. That promise finds its fulfilment in the Son's wedding. Jesus speaks again in parables because the leaders who rejected his earlier direct teaching have hardened hearts that see but do not perceive; the parable simultaneously discloses truth to those with ears to hear and conceals it from those who have refused to hear. Carson observes that the parable functions as both invitation and indictment — the same feast is celebration for the guests who come and condemnation for those who refused.

verseByVerse.quote: and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Again he sent other servants, saying, "Tell those who are invited, See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast."
verseByVerse.commentary: The repeated sending of servants mirrors God's patient repetition of prophetic invitation to Israel. The dinner is fully prepared — salvation is accomplished, not pending. The language echoes Proverbs 9:1–5. Israel's leaders refused not from ignorance but from contempt. Lloyd-Jones notes that one of the most devastating indictments in Scripture is that those most expected to welcome the King's Son were the very ones who refused him.

verseByVerse.quote: But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The refusals are graduated: some are merely indifferent (absorbed in commerce and property), others are actively violent. Both responses characterize Israel's history with the prophets. Indifference is not neutral — it is contempt dressed in busyness. The killing of servants is not metaphorical flourish but literal prediction: Jesus himself will be killed, and his apostles after him. Sproul notes that persecution of God's messengers reveals the depth of human hatred for God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city.
verseByVerse.commentary: Most commentators see this as a direct reference to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus elsewhere predicts explicitly (Matt. 24; Luke 19:41–44). Divine patience has limits; grace spurned becomes judgment unleashed. The God of the New Testament is no less holy than the God of the Old. Calvin writes that God's wrath against those who abuse his mercy is not vindictiveness but the necessary righteousness of the King whose son they have despised.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to his servants, "The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find."
verseByVerse.commentary: Unworthiness disqualifies the invited; grace then reaches the roads and hedgerows. The first guests had covenant status, religious pedigree, and generations of promise behind them — and they refused. The new guests have none of this: they are strangers gathered at random from the main roads, people who had no reason to expect a royal invitation and had never been inside the king's hall. This is the Gentile mission in parabolic form — the gospel going out to those with no religious standing, no ancestral claim, nothing to leverage. Yet the invitation they receive is as genuine as the one the first guests scorned: these people are truly invited, truly welcomed, truly guests at the King's table. Begg observes that the feast never empties — the King is determined that his hall will be full, and his sovereignty over the guest list ensures it will be. The parable overturns every religious calculation about who deserves to be at the feast; the deserving refused, and the undeserving fill the hall. This is grace in its most structural form.

verseByVerse.quote: And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Both bad and good" — grace does not wait for improved moral credentials. The servants' instruction is comprehensive and non-selective: gather all whom you find. There is no pre-screening for suitability, no pause to assess whether the person on the road deserves an invitation to a royal banquet. The gospel offer is genuinely indiscriminate. The fullness of the hall is the Father's sovereign determination that the Son shall not lack a bride; the comprehensive gathering of everyone found on the roads is the means by which that determination is accomplished. This verse is the missionary heartbeat of the parable: go, gather, fill. Keller notes that the early church fulfilled this literally and visibly — Jews and Gentiles, slave and free, the morally respectable and the morally compromised, all seated at the same table, to the profound astonishment of the surrounding Greco-Roman world, where such social mingling was unthinkable. What the servants were commanded to do across the roads, the church is commissioned to do across the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. And he said to him, "Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?" And he was speechless.
verseByVerse.commentary: The parable takes a sharp turn: grace is not universalism. Presence at the feast without the wedding garment — in context, the righteousness of Christ imputed by faith — means judgment. The man is speechless because there is no defense. Calvin's insight is powerful: the garment is provided by the king (cf. Isa. 61:10; Rev. 19:8), so to lack it is to have refused it. Mere external association with Christianity does not constitute saving faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the attendants, "Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." For many are called, but few are chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary: The outer darkness — exclusion from joy and light — is the consequence of appearing at the feast without the wedding garment. The garment in its original cultural context was almost certainly provided by the host for those who needed one; to arrive without it was not poverty but refusal. Calvin reads the wedding garment as the righteousness of Christ imputed to the believer: the King provides the clothing required for the feast, and to lack it is to have declined what was freely offered, not to have failed to manufacture what was required. The man's speechlessness is the silence of someone with no defense, because there is none — you cannot explain why you refused the host's own gift. The binding and the outer darkness are the consequence not of dramatic wickedness but of the single refusal of the King's provision. The final verse distills the parable's entire theology: "many are called" (the general gospel offer goes out genuinely and widely to all), "but few are chosen" (effectual calling belongs to the elect whom God draws to the feast). This is not fatalism but the Reformed doctrine of grace: the outward call goes to all without distinction; the inward call secures the response of those God has chosen. Sproul writes that this distinction simultaneously grounds evangelism (preach to all without exception) and assurance (God secures his own).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, "Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances."
verseByVerse.commentary: The flattery is designed to disarm. By acknowledging Jesus' integrity, they hope to force him into a politically dangerous answer on taxes. The alliance of Pharisees and Herodians — normally rivals — shows that hostility to Christ unites opponents. Their false praise ironically testifies to the truth: Jesus is not swayed by human opinion, which is precisely why their trap will fail. Carson notes that in trying to compromise him, they bear unintentional witness to his character.

verseByVerse.quote: "Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The dilemma is a pincer: say yes, and lose the crowds who resent Roman taxation; say no, and be liable to arrest for sedition. The question assumes Jesus must choose between loyalty to God and loyalty to Rome. But Jesus refuses their framing. The question "is it lawful" invokes Torah, but Jesus will answer from creation and covenant rather than from political calculation. Stott observes that Jesus always transcends the false choices posed by his enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, "Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus names their sin directly: malice, hypocrisy. He is not deceived by their performance of respect. The denarius — the Roman coin bearing Caesar's image — becomes his teaching aid. In asking them to produce it, he reveals they already participate in the Roman economic system. Sproul notes that their willingness to carry Roman currency undercuts their claim to be struggling with the principled question; it was political theater, not genuine conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
verseByVerse.commentary: The image and inscription establish ownership. Caesar's coin bears Caesar's image — return it to him. But humanity bears God's image (Gen. 1:26–27) — render yourselves to God. The two-kingdoms principle is established: civil government has legitimate authority in its sphere; God's authority is ultimate and total. This verse has shaped centuries of Reformed political theology. Calvin, Luther, and later Kuyper all wrestle with how these two obligations relate. The genius of Jesus' answer is that it neither divinizes Caesar nor anarchizes the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary: Marvel without repentance is the most tragic response to Jesus. The Pharisees and Herodians are silenced and amazed — they cannot fault his answer — yet they walk away unchanged. Intellectual acknowledgment of Jesus' wisdom without submission to his lordship describes much of modern religious life. Ferguson notes that the enemies of Jesus frequently marvel at him in Matthew, yet marvel becomes its own form of rejection when it stops short of worship and obedience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Resurrection, the Great Commandment, and David's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three more debates with Jewish leaders culminate in Jesus silencing all questioners and turning the tables with his own unanswerable question. The Sadducees' denial of resurrection is refuted from the Torah itself. The double love command is affirmed as the heart of the Law. And Jesus' question about David's Son exposes the inadequacy of a merely human Messianic expectation.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus demonstrates mastery of the entire Hebrew canon — Torah (resurrection from Exodus), Prophets (implicit), and Psalms (Psalm 110 on David's Lord). The sequence shows that he is not merely a teacher among teachers but the one to whom all Scripture points and before whom all human wisdom fails. The double love command — love God, love neighbor — cannot be obeyed apart from him who is both fully God and our perfect neighbor.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin writes that Jesus' use of Exodus 3:6 to prove resurrection is a masterclass in reading the whole Scripture as the living word of a living God. MacArthur notes that when Jesus asks whose son the Christ is, he is not creating a puzzle but compelling his hearers to reckon with his own divine identity.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses said, 'If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Sadducees accepted only the five books of Moses and denied bodily resurrection, angels, and spirits. Their question is designed to make resurrection look absurd by piling up an extreme hypothetical. The premise is Deuteronomy 25:5-6, the law of levirate marriage — so called from the Latin levir, meaning "husband's brother." The law was straightforward: if a married man died without a son, his surviving brother was obligated to marry the widow. The firstborn son of that union would then carry the dead brother's name and inherit his property, preserving the family line and keeping land within the extended family. The purpose was practical and humane: it protected widows from destitution (a widow with no son had no legal protector or means of support in ancient Israel), maintained the continuity of the household, and kept the family inheritance intact. The institution is illustrated in the book of Ruth, where Boaz acts as a kinsman-redeemer for the widow Naomi and her daughter-in-law Ruth. A man who refused his obligation could be publicly shamed — the woman was to pull off his sandal and spit in his face before the elders (Deut. 25:9-10). The Sadducees construct a hypothetical so extreme it borders on comedy: seven brothers, one woman, seven consecutive levirate marriages, all without a son. Their punch line — "in the resurrection, whose wife will she be?" — is designed to make resurrection seem logically impossible or socially absurd. Carson notes they assume that resurrection life must be identical to earthly life, a category error Jesus will expose. Like many sophisticated objections to Christianity, theirs is built on a false premise about the nature of the life to come.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. So too the second and third, down to the seventh."
verseByVerse.commentary: The escalation to seven brothers underscores the intended absurdity: if resurrection is real, the scenario becomes social chaos. The Sadducees' argument is clever but presupposes resurrection life is simply a continuation of earthly arrangements. Their error is common to all who try to domesticate eternity within the categories of time. Sproul observes that the question "whose wife will she be?" reveals how earth-bound their thinking is — they cannot conceive of a transformed existence that transcends the structures of this age.

verseByVerse.quote: "After them all, the woman died. In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her."
verseByVerse.commentary: The question sounds devastating to the doctrine of resurrection, but its force depends entirely on the assumption that resurrection life replicates earthly life. Jesus will show this assumption is the error, not the doctrine. The Sadducees' real problem is not a logical puzzle but a failure of imagination shaped by unbelief. As Paul will later write, "What you sow is not the body that is to be" (1 Cor. 15:37). The resurrection body is real, physical, and glorious — but transformed beyond earthly patterns.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered them, "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus diagnoses two failures: ignorance of Scripture and ignorance of God's power. Marriage is a this-age institution given for procreation and companionship; in the resurrection, the fullness it pointed to — union with God — will be present without need of the shadow. "Like angels" does not mean bodiless or ethereal but refers to their non-marrying state. Carson notes this is not a demotion of marriage but an elevation of what resurrection life will be. The power of God is not constrained by the arrangements of this passing world.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus refutes the Sadducees from their own accepted Scripture — Exodus 3:6, spoken to Moses centuries after the patriarchs had died. God speaks of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as alive — meaning they are alive to God now and will be fully alive in the resurrection. This is resurrection proved from the Torah itself, on Sadducean ground. Calvin finds this argument conclusive: if God is in covenant with persons, he cannot be God of corpses. The covenant relationship implies ongoing existence and ultimate bodily renewal.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowds consistently respond with astonishment to Jesus' teaching (cf. 7:28; 13:54). But astonishment is not yet faith. The Sadducees are silenced; the crowd is amazed; yet neither group kneels in worship. This pattern warns the reader: intellectual marvel at Jesus — even recognizing his teaching as authoritative — falls short of the discipleship he demands. Begg notes that the goal of hearing Jesus is not wonder but transformation, not applause but allegiance.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees see Jesus' refutation of the Sadducees not as an opportunity to learn but as a moment to press their own attack. The lawyer's question is described as a "test" — not sincere inquiry but adversarial probing. The religious establishment is united in its determination to destroy Jesus even as they are divided among themselves. MacArthur notes that the question about the greatest commandment was a genuine rabbinic debate, but here it is weaponized as a trap rather than pursued as wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments in the Torah and debated their relative weight and priority. The question about the "great commandment" was real and disputed. The lawyer hopes either that Jesus will slight some commandments by elevating others, or that he will give an answer that alienates part of his audience. But Jesus' answer will be so comprehensive — and so rooted in the Shema itself — that no objection is possible. The question, meant to trap, becomes an occasion for Jesus to reveal the entire law's inner logic.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:5 — the Shema, the heart of Jewish daily prayer. The command is total: heart, soul, mind — every faculty of the person wholly directed to God. This is the first commandment because all other obedience flows from this center. Calvin writes that love for God is not an emotion added to religious duty but the animating principle without which no commandment is truly kept. The Reformers understood this as simultaneously exposing human inability (we do not love God this way) and defining the shape of the new life given in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary: The second command — from Leviticus 19:18 — is "like" the first in structure and dignity. Love for God that does not overflow into love for neighbor is self-deception (1 John 4:20). Together these two commands are not a reduction of the Law but its summary: every commandment hangs on these two pegs. Keller notes that "as yourself" is not a command to self-love but a standard — the natural concern we have for our own wellbeing should characterize our concern for others. The Law is fundamentally relational, not ritual.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, saying, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "The son of David."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus now takes the offensive. His question about the Messiah's identity is not an intellectual curiosity but a Christological confrontation. "Son of David" was the standard messianic answer — correct as far as it goes, but radically incomplete. Jesus will show that it does not go far enough. The Pharisees answer confidently, unaware they are about to be exposed. Carson observes that their answer reflects genuine Scripture knowledge but a failure to see that the Scriptures point to one greater than David's dynasty — one who is David's Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus cites Psalm 110:1 — the most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. David, writing by the Spirit, calls the Messiah "my Lord" — a form of address no Jewish father would use of his own descendant. The Psalm describes this Lord enthroned at God's right hand, exercising divine authority over all enemies. The implication is inescapable: the Messiah must be more than David's biological heir. He must share the divine identity. Sproul writes that Jesus is using Psalm 110 to unveil his own pre-existence and divine Sonship from the Psalter itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then David calls him his Lord, how is he his son?" And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary: The question has no answer within a purely human Messianic framework. The Messiah must be both son of David (human descent, legal heir) and David's Lord (divine in nature, eternal in existence) — which is exactly who Jesus is. His enemies are silenced, not converted. The irony is that the one who answers every question is himself the Answer. After this, the controversy dialogues end; what follows in chapters 23–25 is Jesus' own discourse. Ferguson notes that silence before Christ is either the silence of worship or the silence of condemned unbelief.

22.theology: Election and the free offer of the gospel. The parable of the wedding banquet and the phrase “many are called, but few are chosen” bring together two truths that Reformed theology has always insisted must be held together. The general call of the gospel goes out to all people without exception — “Go therefore to the main roads and invite as many as you find.” This is the free and genuine offer of the gospel, and it must be preached without restriction. At the same time, the effectual call of God draws the chosen to the feast. Both are real; both are necessary. The preacher does not know who the elect are; he simply opens the banquet doors as wide as the gospel goes and trusts God with the result.
22.examples:
Then: The religious leaders tried to trap Jesus with politics (tribute coin), doctrine (resurrection), law (greatest commandment). He answered all three with Scripture, clarity, and a question they could not answer. The one they thought to judge was the judge.

Now: The same four questions are still asked of Christians today — political, doctrinal, ethical, and Christological. The answers Jesus gives are still sufficient. Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s; God claims your whole self made in his image. The resurrection is secured by the living God who keeps covenant. Love God with everything; love your neighbour as yourself. And the Christ is both Son of David and Lord of David — the God-man who saves.

23.title: Woe to You, Scribes and Pharisees
23.text: <sup>2</sup>The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat, <sup>3</sup>so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice. <sup>4</sup>They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. <sup>11</sup>The greatest among you shall be your servant. <sup>12</sup>Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. <sup>13</sup>But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. <sup>23</sup>Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. <sup>27</sup>Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. <sup>37</sup>O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>38</sup>See, your house is left to you desolate. <sup>39</sup>For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’
23.overview:
Chapter 23 is the fifth and final discourse of Matthew — and the most sorrowful. It begins with a warning to the crowds and disciples about the Pharisees (vv. 1–12), then delivers seven woes against the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 13–36), and closes with a lament over Jerusalem (vv. 37–39) that is one of the most heartbreaking passages in all of Scripture. The woes are not vindictive; they are diagnostic. Jesus names the disease precisely so that it can be seen for what it is: a religion of external performance concealing internal corruption, a leadership that burdens rather than shepherds, a tradition that has become a wall keeping people out of the kingdom.

The lament over Jerusalem (“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem”) reveals the heart behind the woes. Jesus does not pronounce judgment with cold severity; he pronounces it with the grief of a hen who would have gathered her chicks but could not because they would not come. The image is maternal, tender, aching. The holy Judge is also the loving Shepherd who weeps over the city he must judge. Both are true: God is not willing that any should perish, and God judges unrepentant hardness of heart. The cross, which is days away, is where both truths converge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Seven Woes: The Hypocrisy of Scribes and Pharisees (Part One)
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus turns from silencing his opponents to pronouncing solemn judgment upon them. The woes are not rage but grief-laden indictments from the Judge who is also the Savior. The religious leaders have taken the seat of authority but have abandoned the heart of the law. Their outward performance masks inward decay.
verseByVerse.theology: The seven woes reveal the anatomy of religious hypocrisy: performance divorced from reality, burden-laying without mercy, expansion of symbols without expansion of love. Jesus here teaches his disciples by negative example — the kingdom community is to be characterized by servant-hearted humility, not status-seeking religion. The woes are simultaneously warning and invitation: turn before the judgment falls.
verseByVerse.examples: Lloyd-Jones writes that the Pharisees are the most terrifying example in Scripture of religion without regeneration — people who knew the Bible, observed religious duties, and were zealous for God, yet were children of hell. Calvin notes that the woes are spoken publicly because public sin requires public reproof.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat,"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus addresses both the crowds and his disciples — this is public, comprehensive teaching. He begins not with condemnation but with acknowledgment: the scribes and Pharisees hold legitimate teaching authority as interpreters of Moses. "Moses' seat" was the formal chair of the synagogue teacher. Jesus does not dismiss institutional authority, but he distinguishes between the office and the character of those occupying it. Carson notes this is a crucial principle for church life: authority structures matter, but character and integrity determine whether they serve their purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice."
verseByVerse.commentary: The gap between proclamation and practice is the essence of hypocrisy. Jesus commands submission to correct teaching even when the teacher's life is inconsistent — truth is not invalidated by the messenger's failure. But he exposes the fatal credibility gap: those who preach repentance without practicing it, who demand righteousness they themselves do not embody. Begg notes this verse has been called the most uncomfortable verse for all preachers — we stand under the same indictment whenever our pulpit and our life diverge.

verseByVerse.quote: "They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger."
verseByVerse.commentary: The rabbinical tradition had multiplied regulations — oral law piled atop written law — creating a crushing system of obligation. The leaders designed the system but insulated themselves from its demands through legal technicalities and status exemptions. This is the opposite of Jesus' yoke, which is easy and light (11:28–30). The contrast is between religion as burden and grace as rest. Keller notes that performance-based religion always crushes the conscience while rewarding the proud — those with the most status find ways to exempt themselves from the demands they impose on others.

verseByVerse.quote: "They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues"
verseByVerse.commentary: Phylacteries were small leather boxes containing Scripture portions, worn on forehead and arm in obedience to Deuteronomy 6:8. Fringes were the tassels commanded in Numbers 15:38–40. Both were legitimate practices — but enlarging them for visibility transforms a devotional practice into a performance. The love of honored seating completes the picture: all of religion has been conscripted into the service of social advancement. Calvin writes that when religious practice becomes an instrument of reputation rather than a response to grace, it is no longer worship — it is idolatry of the self.

verseByVerse.quote: "and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers."
verseByVerse.commentary: Public honorifics feed the status-hunger that drives hypocritical religion. Jesus forbids his disciples from seeking such titles — not as a mechanical rule against the word "rabbi" but as a prohibition of the status-seeking the title represents. "You are all brothers" levels the community: every disciple stands equally as learner before the one Teacher. MacArthur notes that the health of a church community is measured partly by whether its members seek to serve or to be served, to give honor or to receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary: The prohibition on "father" and "instructor" extends the same principle: no human being should occupy the place of ultimate spiritual authority that belongs to God alone. This does not forbid calling one's parent "father" or acknowledging a mentor's role, but it prohibits the spiritual inflation of human authority into a surrogate for divine fatherhood. The Reformation recovered this principle against medieval ecclesiastical structures that made the Pope a spiritual father in an absolute sense. All human teaching is derivative; only Christ is the instructor of the soul.

verseByVerse.quote: "The greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted."
verseByVerse.commentary: The kingdom inverts the world's hierarchy. Status is gained through service, not self-promotion. This is not merely an ethical principle but a reflection of the gospel itself: the Son of God humbled himself to a servant's death (Phil. 2:5–8) and was exalted to the highest name. The divine order — humility before exaltation — governs both Christ's own story and the pattern for all who follow him. Sproul writes that the preacher who seeks the humblest place will be raised; the one who seeks the highest will find it taken. The eschatological reversal is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: "But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first woe is the most damning: they block the very entrance to the kingdom. By distorting Scripture, adding traditions that obscure grace, and leading the people away from the Messiah, they have become gatekeepers who lock the door from the outside. They themselves have not entered — for entering requires humility, repentance, and trust in the coming one — and they impede others. Carson notes this is the ultimate irony: those most responsible for guiding Israel to the Messiah have become the primary obstacle. Religious leaders bear an enormous accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves."
verseByVerse.commentary: Verse 14 — concerning devouring widows' houses — is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew (it appears in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47) and is bracketed or footnoted in the ESV. Verse 15 pronounces woe on missionary zeal divorced from truth: Jewish proselytism was real and vigorous, but bringing converts into a system of hypocritical works-religion produces not kingdom citizens but people doubly hardened against grace. Keller observes that religious systems can produce zealous converts to the system itself — people passionate for their tradition's forms — who are further from God than before they converted.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, blind guides, who say, 'If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.' You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The third woe targets the scribal tradition of oath-taking, which had developed elaborate hierarchies of binding and non-binding oaths. The tradition effectively allowed people to swear deceptively — invoking temple while meaning only gold, thus preserving a technical loophole. Jesus dismantles this by asking which is greater: the thing or the sacred context that gives it significance. Their system exalts the material symbol over the divine reality. This is idolatry in liturgical form — treating the vessel as more important than the one who fills it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you say, 'If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.' You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The logic of the previous woe is repeated with a different example — altar versus gift upon it — to show the pattern is systemic. The scribes have inverted the proper order: they exalt visible, tangible things (gold, gifts) over the invisible realities (God's presence, consecration) that make those things holy. This is the inner logic of all idolatry. Sproul notes that the blind leading the blind is doubly tragic — the leaders cannot see their own error, so they compound it in their followers. Self-deceived teachers are more dangerous than openly corrupt ones.

verseByVerse.quote: "So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus restores the proper logic: every oath by a sacred object implicitly invokes God, because God is the sanctifying reality behind every holy thing. You cannot separate the altar from the One for whom it was built, or the temple from the One who inhabits it. Therefore oath-manipulation — trying to invoke the symbol without binding obligation to the God of the symbol — is dishonest at its root. This anticipates Jesus' earlier teaching (5:33–37): let your yes be yes. All words spoken before God carry weight, whether one says so explicitly or not.

verseByVerse.quote: "And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it."
verseByVerse.commentary: The climax of the oath-teaching: heaven itself is God's throne, so swearing by heaven is swearing by God. No sphere of existence is neutral or secular in an ultimate sense — all creation is God's domain, and all speech is uttered in his presence. The scribal tradition of oath-manipulation collapses entirely under this logic: there is nowhere to swear that is not already consecrated by God's sovereignty. Calvin writes that this teaches a total accountability — we are never off the record, never in a context where our words are merely human. Every word is spoken coram Deo.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–39 — Seven Woes Concluded and the Lament over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final four woes deepen the indictment from external performance to internal corruption: meticulous tithing while neglecting justice, external cleanliness concealing inner greed, whitewashed tombs — beautiful outside, dead inside. The chapter ends not in triumph but in grief: Jesus' lament over Jerusalem is one of the most tender and anguished moments in the Gospels.
verseByVerse.theology: The movement from woe to lament is theologically significant: judgment and grief coexist in God's heart. Jesus pronounces woe on the leaders while weeping over the city. This is not contradiction but the complexity of divine love — God is both just and compassionate, both holy in his anger and grieved in his heart. The lament over Jerusalem reveals that the judgment he pronounces is not what he desires but what justice requires when love is spurned.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson notes that the image of the hen gathering her chicks is one of the most powerful pictures of Christ's longing for sinners — and the devastation is that Jerusalem would not. Keller points out that the woes are diagnostic: they identify the spiritual diseases that kill — self-deception, pride, external performance — precisely so we may seek the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees tithed garden herbs to the tenth — meticulous attention to minor obligations — while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness, the moral weight of the law (cf. Mic. 6:8). Jesus does not dismiss the tithe: "these you ought to have done." But precision about small things cannot compensate for the absence of large ones. The gnat and camel image is vivid: the camel was the largest unclean animal, the gnat the smallest. They strain at gnats — nitpicking minor regulations — while gulping camels whole — violating the law's heart. This describes all religion that has lost its moral center.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean."
verseByVerse.commentary: The sixth woe uses a domestic image: a cup scoured on the outside but filthy inside is useless and deceptive. External religious performance cannot substitute for inner transformation. "Greed and self-indulgence" are the actual contents of the Pharisees' hearts — desire for wealth and pleasure dressed in pious clothing. The remedy is not better external performance but inner cleansing — which only God can provide (Ezek. 36:26). Keller writes that this woe is the most relevant to respectable religious people: we are extraordinarily skilled at managing external appearances while cultivating unclean desires within.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness. So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary: The whitewashed tomb is perhaps Jesus' most devastating metaphor for religious hypocrisy. Tombs were whitewashed before Passover so pilgrims would not accidentally contract ceremonial uncleanness by touching them — making them beautiful on the outside while concealing death and corruption within. The Pharisees are exactly this: morally attractive by social appearance, spiritually dead within. "Hypocrisy and lawlessness" — not just performance but actual violation of God's law beneath the performance. Sproul notes that this describes the natural heart of every person apart from regeneration; the Pharisees are not uniquely wicked but uniquely exposed.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, saying, 'If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The final woe is the most ironic: they honor dead prophets while plotting to kill the living one. Their monument-building is a form of self-congratulation — "we would not have done what our fathers did" — which is itself the arrogant self-righteousness that drove the persecution of the prophets in the first place. Jesus is about to be crucified by men who are decorating the tombs of those crucified by their ancestors. Carson notes this is the clearest example in the Gospels of the self-deception at the heart of unbelief: we consistently imagine ourselves exempt from the very sins we condemn in others.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Fill up the measure" is a solemn juridical statement: the accumulated guilt of generations will now reach its fullness in the murder of the Son. Jesus is not commanding them to sin but announcing what they will do — and that in doing it they will complete the pattern that makes judgment inevitable. The patience of God is not infinite in the sense of indefinitely absorbing rejection; there is a fullness of iniquity after which judgment falls (cf. Gen. 15:16). This verse shows Jesus approaching the cross not as a victim but as one who sees and names what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: "You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town,"
verseByVerse.commentary: "Serpents" and "brood of vipers" — language John the Baptist also used (3:7) — identifies the leaders with the ancient adversary, the deceiver of Eden. Hell (Gehenna, the valley of Hinnom) is not hyperbole but judicial reality. Even now Jesus sends messengers — apostles, teachers — knowing they will be killed, because God's way of dealing with sin is to send grace into the midst of it. The future persecutions described here are fulfilled in Acts and the apostolic letters. MacArthur notes that this verse shows the cross is not the end of God's mission but the beginning of a new, worldwide sending.

verseByVerse.quote: "so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation."
verseByVerse.commentary: From Abel (the first murder in Scripture, Gen. 4) to Zechariah (2 Chron. 24:20–22, the last murder recorded in the Hebrew canon) — the entire span of innocent blood reaches its culmination in the rejection of the Son. "This generation" bears the fullness of covenantal accountability because this generation has the greatest light and rejects it most fully. The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 is the historical judgment Jesus sees approaching. Yet this does not mean every individual is damned — thousands in Jerusalem responded to the apostolic preaching. The judgment is covenantal and national, not mechanically individual.

verseByVerse.quote: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! See, your house is left to you desolate."
verseByVerse.commentary: The woes break open into lamentation. "How often would I have gathered" — the heart of Christ is exposed: longing, repeated, patient, refused. The image of the hen covering her chicks with her wings is tender and maternal, drawn from Old Testament imagery of God's protective care (Ps. 91:4; Deut. 32:11). And yet: "you were not willing." Human will refuses divine love. This is not Calvinism versus Arminianism in tension but the simultaneous truth: God genuinely desires, humans genuinely refuse, and God's sovereignty encompasses both. Ferguson writes that this verse should shatter any caricature of a cold, indifferent deity — the Son of God weeps over the city that will kill him.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: This is Jesus' farewell to the temple and to Jerusalem as it is. "You will not see me" — his presence, his teaching, his offer of mercy — will be withdrawn. The future seeing, with the acclamation of Psalm 118:26, points to the parousia when every eye will see him (Rev. 1:7) and — for the redeemed — to the conversion of Israel Paul anticipates in Romans 11:25–26. The chapter ends on both judgment and hope: the city will be desolate, but the King will return. Desolation is not the final word; the final word is the blessed coming of the Lord in glory.

23.theology: The danger of religious hypocrisy. Matthew 23 is the most sustained treatment of hypocritical religion in the New Testament. The Reformers used it relentlessly against the medieval Catholic establishment; every subsequent generation has needed to hear it applied to itself. The structural sin of the Pharisees — outward conformity concealing inward corruption, burden-laying without burden-sharing, precision in minor matters and blindness to major ones — is the perennial disease of organized religion. The only cure is genuine regeneration: the new heart of Ezekiel 36 that produces obedience from the inside rather than performance for the outside. The woes are also a mirror: every reader must ask which whitewashed tomb they are decorating.
23.examples:
Then: The Pharisees were the most theologically serious people in first-century Judaism. They memorized Scripture, tithed fastidiously, prayed publicly, and honoured the tradition of the fathers. And Jesus pronounced seven woes over them. Theological seriousness and religious diligence are not equivalent to knowing God.

Now: Every church tradition has its own version of the Pharisaic trap: the evangelical who is doctrinally precise but personally unkind; the liturgical churchgoer who loves the service but not the neighbour; the activist who fights for justice but has no interior life. The woes are not for the obviously wicked but for the outwardly religious. That is why they are so searching. The question is not “Am I religious?” but “Does my religion proceed from a heart that loves God and loves my neighbour?”

24.title: The End of the Age
24.text: <sup>2</sup>But he answered them, “You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>4</sup>And Jesus answered them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>6</sup>And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>14</sup>And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come. <sup>27</sup>For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>30</sup>Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. <sup>36</sup>But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only. <sup>42</sup>Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming. <sup>44</sup>Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.”
24.overview:
The Olivet Discourse (chapters 24–25) is Jesus’ extended teaching on the end of the age, delivered on the Mount of Olives overlooking the temple. It is the most complex and debated passage in Matthew, weaving together two horizons: the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 and the final coming of the Son of Man at the end of history. Jesus deliberately leaves the two horizons blurred, because the near event (Jerusalem’s fall) is the type and foretaste of the far event (the final judgment).

The chapter resists every system that charts the future with calendar precision. “No one knows the day or the hour” (v. 36) is not a temporary limitation but a theological statement: the appropriate posture before the end is not calculation but watchfulness, not a schedule but readiness. The gospel of the kingdom must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 14) — the mission is the church’s present calling. The Son of Man will come as lightning, suddenly and unmistakably. Until then: stay awake.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — Signs of the End and the Great Tribulation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Olivet Discourse is Jesus' most extended prophetic teaching, delivered on the Mount of Olives in response to the disciples' question about the destruction of the temple and the signs of his coming. Jesus warns against false messiahs, describes wars and catastrophes as birth pains, predicts terrible tribulation, and commands vigilance against deception.
verseByVerse.theology: The Olivet Discourse holds together near fulfillment (destruction of Jerusalem, AD 70) and far fulfillment (the parousia) in a manner characteristic of OT prophetic double horizons. The two events are theologically linked: the judgment on Jerusalem is a type of the final judgment; the salvation of the elect in both is grounded in God's sovereign care. Central themes are perseverance under persecution, refusal of false messiahs, and the certainty of Christ's ultimate triumph.
verseByVerse.examples: Carson's commentary on Matthew is indispensable on ch24: he argues for a dual fulfillment — vv.4-35 addressing primarily AD 70 with typological extension to the end, and vv.36-51 addressing the parousia explicitly. Sproul's 'The Last Days According to Jesus' takes a largely preterist view. Both agree the chapter demands watchful, faithful living in every generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus left the temple and was going away, when his disciples came to point out to him the buildings of the temple. But he answered them, "You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary: The departure from the temple is ominous — the same movement as the glory of the LORD departing from the temple in Ezekiel 10–11. The disciples point admiringly to Herod's magnificent reconstruction; Jesus pronounces its doom. Not one stone on another — fulfilled with terrible precision in AD 70 when Titus's armies burned the temple and soldiers pried apart the stones to retrieve the melted gold. The physical destruction Jesus predicts is simultaneously a theological statement: the temple's function has been fulfilled and superseded in himself. Carson notes the disciples' admiration and Jesus' judgment represent two different ways of seeing the same stones.

verseByVerse.quote: As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and the end of the age?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples conflate two questions — the destruction of the temple and the end of the age — perhaps assuming they are simultaneous events. The Mount of Olives is the prophetic location of the Lord's return in Zechariah 14:4. Their question is sincere but theologically compressed: they cannot yet imagine a gap of centuries between the temple's fall and the parousia. Jesus' answer in what follows addresses both questions, often without clearly marking the transitions, reflecting the prophetic pattern of near and far horizons telescoped together.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first and repeated warning is against deception. Jesus does not begin with cosmic catastrophe but with the vulnerability of his disciples to false messiahs. False christs have appeared throughout church history — and the warning implies they will multiply near the end. "In my name" — they will not deny Jesus but claim his title for themselves, which makes them more dangerous. Begg notes that the primary threat to the church in every era is not external persecution but internal doctrinal corruption — wolves who speak Christ's name while denying his lordship.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places."
verseByVerse.commentary: "See that you are not alarmed" — the command to remain unshaken in the face of catastrophe is itself a theological statement: Christians are to interpret geopolitical upheaval through the lens of God's sovereignty, not succumb to panic. Wars, famines, and earthquakes are not signs that God has lost control but "birth pains" — the painful but purposeful preliminary labor before the new creation arrives. Every generation has experienced these realities; this universality is part of Jesus' point. MacArthur notes the disciples must learn to live between the first and second comings without either despair or complacency.

verseByVerse.quote: "All these are but the beginning of the birth pains. Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations for my name's sake."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Birth pains" — the metaphor is crucial. Pain does not mean hopelessness; it signals that something is being born. The persecution Jesus predicts for his disciples is not incidental to the age but constitutive of it: following the crucified Messiah means sharing in the pattern of his rejection. "For my name's sake" — the identity of the one they follow is the reason for the hatred. The world's rejection of the church is ultimately the world's rejection of Christ himself. This has been the experience of martyrs in every century and on every continent.

verseByVerse.quote: "And then many will fall away and betray one another and hate one another. And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray."
verseByVerse.commentary: The internal dangers of the church under pressure begin with apostasy and betrayal — those who appeared to belong fall away and turn on their former companions. Persecution does not merely thin the visible church; it provokes active hostility from those who were never truly rooted. False prophets compound the damage from within, exploiting the disorientation of crisis to lead others further astray. Carson notes that the most devastating losses in a suffering church are not those taken by martyrdom but those driven away by false teaching that promises easier alternatives than the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: "And because lawlessness will increase, the love of many will grow cold."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Love growing cold" is perhaps the saddest phrase in the discourse: not open rejection of Christ but the slow cooling of fervor, the attrition of faithful perseverance. Lawlessness — the rejection of God's moral order — is both the cause and the context in which love cools. When the law's authority is dismissed, love, which the law commands, is also abandoned.
