According to the Mishnah's tractate Sanhedrin, capital trials had to be held during daylight hours, not at night; the verdict of death could not be delivered on the same day as the hearing (a night was required between examination and verdict, to allow for mercy); the Sanhedrin was to meet in the Hall of Hewn Stones within the temple precincts, not in the high priest's private residence; and capital cases could not be tried on the eve of a Sabbath or festival. This trial violates every one of these requirements — held at night, in Caiaphas's house, on the eve of Passover, with the verdict reached before dawn. Yet it proceeds to its predetermined conclusion. The high priest's charge of blasphemy reveals what is really at stake: Jesus' claim to divine identity. His answer — 'You have said so... you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds' — combines Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13, the two most exalted messianic texts in the Hebrew canon. He is claiming to be both the enthroned Lord and the cosmic judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson on Peter's denial: the fall is catastrophic but not final — Jesus had already prayed for him (Luke 22:32) and promised to go before him to Galilee (Matt. 26:32). Peter's bitter weeping is the beginning of repentance, and repentance is the path back. Begg notes that the parallel between Jesus' trial and Peter's denial is Matthew's most powerful literary juxtaposition: inside, Jesus confesses truth at the cost of his life; outside, Peter denies truth to save his life.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man; seize him."
verseByVerse.commentary: "One of the twelve" — Matthew's repeated designation of Judas by his apostolic status heightens the betrayal's horror. The crowd armed with swords and clubs is disproportionate to the arrest of a single teacher, suggesting fear of popular resistance. The kiss — a greeting of affection and respect — becomes the instrument of betrayal: the most intimate gesture of love is weaponized as the signal of death. This is what Satan does with good things: inverts them, corrupts them, makes love serve murder. Keller notes that the kiss in Gethsemane is the most concentrated image of the nature of sin — it uses the form of love while emptying it of all love's content.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came up to Jesus at once and said, "Greetings, Rabbi!" And he kissed him. Jesus said to him, "Friend, do what you came to do." Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Friend" — Jesus addresses Judas as hetaire, a term of address rather than intimate friendship, carrying a note of reproach in Matthew's usage (cf. 20:13; 22:12). Even now Jesus does not curse Judas but speaks with sorrowful directness: do what you came to do. He is neither surprised nor out of control. He is arrested willingly. The laying of hands on Jesus — the one who had laid hands on the sick to heal them — is a profound reversal: the Healer is seized, the one who gave life is taken to death. Carson notes that Jesus' composure in arrest stands in complete contrast to the armed crowd's anxiety, demonstrating who is actually in control of the moment.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Then Jesus said to him, "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter (named in John 18:10) acts with sincere if misguided courage. His sword represents the human instinct to defend Christ by force — an instinct that misunderstands both the nature of the kingdom and the nature of this particular hour. Jesus heals the ear (Luke 22:51) and commands the sword sheathed. The principle — "all who take the sword will perish by the sword" — is not absolute pacifism but a repudiation of violence as the church's means of advancing or defending the gospel. The kingdom does not come by the sword of steel but by the word of the cross. MacArthur notes that this is the last healing miracle before the resurrection, and it is performed on an enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?"
verseByVerse.commentary: A Roman legion was approximately six thousand soldiers; twelve legions of angels would be an overwhelming force. The point is not a boast but a demonstration: Jesus is not arrested because he lacks power but because he chooses not to exercise it. The constraint is Scripture — it must be so. The cross is not forced upon Jesus by superior strength but embraced by him in fulfillment of the Father's eternal plan. This verse is the theological backbone of the Passion narrative: every moment of apparent helplessness is in fact an expression of the most sovereign freedom — the freedom of love that refuses rescue in order to accomplish redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled." Then all the disciples left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' rebuke exposes the hypocrisy of the arrest: they did not seize him in the temple because they feared the crowd; the nocturnal ambush is cowardice dressed as law enforcement. His appeal to the public nature of his teaching — nothing hidden, nothing seditious — stands as a rebuke to the secrecy of the whole conspiracy. "All this has taken place that the Scriptures might be fulfilled" — then the disciples flee, fulfilling the prediction of verse 31. Their flight is both failure and prophecy. The disciples' abandonment is painful but not fatal: the one they leave behind is going to accomplish what no armed disciple could help him accomplish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the outcome.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Following at a distance" — Peter's position is literally and spiritually accurate. He has not completely abandoned Jesus; he is brave enough to enter the courtyard. But the distance is real. Inside, Jesus faces the high priest; outside, Peter faces a servant girl. The two scenes will be Matthew's parallel accounts of two very different responses under pressure. "To see the outcome" suggests Peter's uncertainty — he does not know what will happen, has not understood the predictions of resurrection, and enters the courtyard as a spectator of a drama he does not yet comprehend. His following-at-a-distance is better than flight but still far short of standing with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward
verseByVerse.commentary: The council begins with its conclusion (death) and works backward to find a charge — the definition of a show trial. "The whole council" — the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish judicial body — is assembled for a predetermined verdict. The procession of false witnesses who cannot agree is both legally fatal (two witnesses must agree, Deut. 19:15) and ironically revealing: Jesus is so innocent that even those trying to condemn him cannot find consistent false testimony. Carson notes that the very impossibility of finding valid charges against Jesus is Matthew's implicit argument for his sinlessness — the court of his enemies cannot convict him.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "This man said, 'I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The distortion of Jesus' actual statement (John 2:19 — "Destroy this temple" spoken of his body) into a threat to demolish the physical temple is a half-truth that becomes a lie. The irony is profound: in three days, after the true temple of his body is destroyed and rebuilt in resurrection, the old temple's function will be permanently superseded. What the witnesses misrepresent as a threat is actually a prophecy of the resurrection, which is the very thing that will make the Jerusalem temple obsolete. God's purposes are so comprehensive that even the lies of his enemies serve his truth.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up and said, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, "I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' silence before false accusation fulfills Isaiah 53:7 — "he opened not his mouth." He will not dignify distorted testimony with a defense. But when the high priest invokes the name of the living God with the formal oath of adjuration, Jesus speaks. The question — "Are you the Christ, the Son of God?" — is the question of the entire Gospel, asked at last by the highest human authority in Israel. Jesus will answer it, and the answer will cost him everything. Begg notes that Jesus' silence before lies and his speech before truth is the model for Christian witness: we do not argue every accusation but we do confess every truth, whatever the cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven." Then the high priest tore his robes and said, "He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus confirms the title and immediately escalates it: combining Psalm 110:1 (seated at God's right hand) with Daniel 7:13 (coming on the clouds), he claims to be both the enthroned Lord of the universe and the cosmic judge before whom all nations will stand. This is not merely messianic — it is a claim to share the divine identity. The high priest's charge of blasphemy is, from his perspective, the only possible response. If Jesus is not who he claims, the charge is correct. If he is, the high priest has condemned the Son of God. The tearing of robes — the prescribed response to blasphemy — is itself a fulfillment of irony: the high priest, who should recognize the Messiah, renders the verdict that seals his own condemnation.

verseByVerse.quote: "What is your judgment?" They answered, "He deserves death."
verseByVerse.commentary: The verdict is unanimous and immediate. The predetermined conclusion is reached. The Son of God is condemned to death by the highest religious court of his own people. This is the climax of the rejection of Israel's leadership that Jesus has narrated throughout chapters 21–23. What they call justice is murder; what they call blasphemy is truth; what they call his death sentence is their own. Carson notes that the council's unanimous verdict fulfills not their justice but God's — because this death, unjustly imposed, is the very death that will atone for the sins of the world, including those who condemned him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they spit in his face and struck him. And some slapped him, saying, "Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The judicial dignity of the trial dissolves into violence and mockery. Spitting in the face was the most extreme form of contempt in Jewish culture (cf. Num. 12:14; Deut. 25:9). The demand to prophesy — to identify his unseen attacker — mocks his claim to messianic insight. But the supreme irony, which the mockers cannot perceive, is that this very moment — the striking, the humiliation — was prophesied in Isaiah 50:6: "I gave my back to those who strike." He is fulfilling the very prophecy they mock him for claiming. And the identity of those who struck him? He knows. He knows all of them. He will remember all of them at the judgment he has just described from Daniel 7.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And a servant girl came up to him and said, "You also were with Jesus the Galilean." But he denied it before them all, saying, "I do not know what you mean."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first denial. The accuser is not a soldier or an official but a servant girl — a socially powerless person. Peter who drew a sword in the garden cannot stand before a servant's question. His denial is not a reasoned theological recantation but a panicked, instinctive lie. "I do not know what you mean" — the evasion of someone buying time, hoping the moment will pass. Keller observes that this is how most denials of Christ happen: not in dramatic confrontations with power but in casual social situations where the cost of association suddenly feels too high and the instinct of self-preservation overcomes the will to confess.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, "This man was with Jesus of Nazareth." And again he denied it with an oath: "I do not know the man."
verseByVerse.commentary: The second denial escalates: now with an oath — a formal invocation of God as witness to the truth of what Peter is saying. Peter is swearing by God that he does not know Jesus. This is exactly the kind of oath-taking Jesus condemned in 5:33–37 as unnecessary for the truthful person. Worse, it is perjury before God. Each denial digs a deeper hole; the oath makes the lie more deliberate and the fall more catastrophic. Carson notes that the progressive escalation of Peter's denials — evasion, oath, cursing — mirrors a soul being dragged by fear from one compromise to the next, each step making the next easier.

verseByVerse.quote: After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, "Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you." Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know the man." And immediately the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third denial reaches its lowest point: invoking a curse on himself — calling down divine judgment if he is lying — while lying. Peter, who slept in Gethsemane while Jesus prayed, who fled at the arrest, now curses himself in the courtyard. And immediately — the rooster, the divinely appointed alarm. God's faithfulness to his word (v.34) and to Peter is shown precisely in the rooster's crow: the moment of exposure is also the moment of recall, and recall is the beginning of repentance. The cock's crow that announces Peter's failure is simultaneously the sound that will call him back. Sproul writes that this is what grace does: it refuses to let Peter sleep in his sin.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus, "Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Peter remembered" — this is the turning point. Memory of Christ's word, confronting his own failure, produces not despair but grief. The bitter weeping is genuine repentance — not Judas's remorse that leads to destruction but Peter's sorrow that leads to restoration (2 Cor. 7:10). He goes out — away from the courtyard, away from the scene of failure — and weeps. The chapter that began with the woman's extravagant love ends with the apostle's extravagant tears. Both are beautiful in different ways: her love anticipated his burial; his tears begin his restoration. Begg writes that bitter weeping before God is one of the most hopeful sounds in Scripture — it means the heart is not dead but alive to its own failure, and alive hearts can be healed.

26.theology: The cup of wrath and substitutionary atonement. The cup that Jesus prays might pass in Gethsemane and then drinks on the cross is the Old Testament cup of divine wrath — the concentrated judgment of God against human sin. That he drinks it “for many” (26:28) and “for the forgiveness of sins” is Matthew’s clearest statement of penal substitutionary atonement: Christ in the place of sinners, bearing the penalty that was theirs, so that the forgiveness that is his might become theirs. This is the heart of the gospel — not merely that God loves us (though he does) or that Jesus shows us how to live (though he does) but that the holy God, in the person of his Son, absorbed the full penalty for human sin so that justice and mercy could be simultaneously satisfied at the cross.
26.examples:
Then: The disciples slept in Gethsemane while Jesus prayed. They could not watch one hour. Their failure is not recorded to condemn them but to reveal the bankruptcy of human resolve — and to show that the cross was accomplished not by the strength of the disciples but by the obedience of the Son, alone, in the dark, sustained only by the Father.

Now: Every celebration of the Lord’s Supper is a proclamation of Gethsemane and the cross. The bread and cup carry the weight of that night — the betrayal, the agony, the submission, the arrest, the trial. To eat and drink worthily (1 Cor 11:27–29) is to remember not merely a past event but the present ground of our standing before God: his blood, poured out for many, for the forgiveness of sins. That includes every sin we brought to the table today.

27.title: The Crucifixion of the King
27.text: <sup>29</sup>and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>35</sup>And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. <sup>37</sup>And over his head they put the charge against him, which read, “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.” <sup>45</sup>Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. <sup>46</sup>And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>50</sup>And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit. <sup>51</sup>And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. <sup>54</sup>When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were afraid, and said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” <sup>60</sup>and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 is the centre of the universe. Everything in the Old Testament moves toward it; everything in the New Testament moves from it. The crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, is the event by which God reconciles a broken world to himself. Matthew narrates it with restraint — he does not linger on the physical agony of crucifixion — but saturates every scene with Old Testament allusion: Psalm 22 (the cry of dereliction, the dividing of garments, the mocking); Zechariah 11 (thirty pieces of silver); Isaiah 53 (numbered with transgressors, interceding for sinners).

The theological climax comes in three simultaneous signs at the moment of death: the tearing of the temple veil, the earthquake and split rocks, and the opening of tombs. The veil torn from top to bottom is God’s own act: the barrier between the holy and the profane is removed. The way into the presence of God is now open to all who come through the crucified King. The centurion’s confession — “Truly this man was the Son of God!” — is the Gentile answer to the question Jesus asked in chapter 16: spoken at the foot of the cross, by a soldier, at the moment of death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — The Trial before Pilate and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The morning trial before Pilate, the fate of Judas, and the crucifixion itself occupy the first two-thirds of chapter 27. Roman power and Jewish pressure combine to condemn an innocent man. The soldiers' mockery, the crowd's cry, the two robbers' derision — all these converge at Golgotha, where the Son of God is crucified between criminals and derided by passers-by.
verseByVerse.theology: The cross is simultaneously the greatest injustice and the greatest act of justice in human history: innocent condemned so that the guilty might go free, the righteous bearing the penalty of the unrighteous. The mockery at the cross — 'He saved others; he cannot save himself' — is the deepest irony of the gospel: he cannot save himself precisely because he is saving others. The way of the cross is the way of substitution; the Savior must not come down from the cross in order to save those for whom he hangs.
verseByVerse.examples: Stott's 'The Cross of Christ' is the definitive Reformed treatment of what the cross accomplishes. Sproul's 'The Truth of the Cross' is equally essential. Both emphasize that the atonement is not an accident but the eternal plan of the triune God, and the cross is not defeat but the decisive victory over sin, death, and the devil.

verseByVerse.quote: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. And they bound him and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor.
verseByVerse.commentary: The dawn consultation formalizes what the night trial determined. They bind Jesus — the one who bound no one but loosed the prisoners of sin — and deliver him to Pilate. The delivering over (paradidomi) is the same verb used of Judas's betrayal: the leaders hand Jesus over as Judas did, as the Father will in a deeper sense (Rom. 8:32). Pilate, the Roman governor, has the authority of crucifixion, which the Jewish council lacks under Roman jurisdiction. The machinery of two empires — religious and political — is conscripted to accomplish what the eternal counsel of the Trinity had determined before the foundation of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood." They said, "What is that to us? See to it yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary: Judas's change of mind (metamelomai — remorse, not metanoia — repentance) comes too late and is rejected by those who used him. "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood" — Judas confesses the truth. The leaders' response — "What is that to us?" — is chilling: they used him, got what they wanted, and now disclaim responsibility. But Judas's remorse does not lead to Christ but to self-destruction, which is the difference between godly sorrow and worldly sorrow (2 Cor. 7:10). He recognizes his sin but does not seek the Savior who could forgive it. Carson notes that Judas's tragedy is not that he sinned greater than Peter but that he did not seek the same grace Peter found.

verseByVerse.quote: And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and he went and hanged himself. But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, "It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money."
verseByVerse.commentary: Judas throws the silver into the temple — perhaps toward the sanctuary — as a futile act of rejection. Then he hangs himself. His death is recorded without embellishment; Matthew's theological point is already made. The priests' scrupulous concern about the legal status of blood money is devastating irony: they will not defile the treasury with money used to purchase innocent blood, yet they have just condemned innocent blood to death. Their legal fastidiousness is hypocrisy at its most refined — straining out the gnat of treasury regulations while swallowing the camel of judicial murder. Begg notes this as perhaps the starkest example in the Gospels of religion without conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took counsel and bought with them the potter's field as a burial place for strangers. Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary: The thirty pieces of silver buy a potter's field for the burial of strangers — the worthless earth of a potter's discard. The irony is that money used to buy the death of the Son of God ends up purchasing ground for the burial of those with no home and no name. The field is named for blood, and the name persists. Scripture is not silent on what the money bought: it bought both the Savior's betrayal and a piece of ground that testifies to that betrayal forever. Zechariah 11:13 and Jeremiah 32:7–9 converge in this detail, showing God's providential ordering of even the disposal of blood money.

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Matthew attributes the prophecy to Jeremiah (who purchased a field, Jer. 32) but the verbal details match Zechariah 11:12–13 more closely — a textual complexity that has generated extensive discussion. The most likely explanation is that Matthew is citing a combination of prophetic texts under the name of the major prophet, a Jewish convention. What matters theologically is the fulfillment itself: the thirty pieces, the potter's field, the sons of Israel — all these details were ordered by God centuries before and now converge in the purchase of a worthless field with the price of the priceless Son. Providence reaches into every detail of the Passion.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" Jesus said, "You have said so." And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before Pilate, the political question takes center stage: kingship. Jesus' answer — "You have said so" — neither denies the title nor embraces its political connotations. He is a king, but not the kind Pilate fears. His silence before the chief priests' accusations again fulfills Isaiah 53:7. Pilate is used to defendants who protest vigorously; this defendant's composure unsettles him. The King of kings stands before a provincial governor and gives him dignity even in trial. Carson notes that Jesus' silence before false accusation is not passivity but sovereignty — he is not defending himself because he has already determined to submit to what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate said to him, "Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?" But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary: Pilate's amazement at Jesus' silence is the response of a man who has never encountered someone who does not care about self-preservation in the normal way. Every accused person Pilate has tried has defended himself vigorously; this one is silent, and the silence itself is a kind of testimony. The governor's amazement will increase as the trial proceeds: he finds no guilt, his wife sends a warning, he washes his hands — and yet he still condemns. The amazement without action is the tragedy of Pilate: he recognized something extraordinary and did nothing about it. Keller notes that neutral acknowledgment of Jesus' unusual character is not the same as faith — Pilate amazed at Jesus is not Pilate believing in Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas.
verseByVerse.commentary: The custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover — attested in Roman and Jewish sources — becomes the occasion for the most dramatic substitution in human history. Barabbas ("son of the father") is described as notorious — a violent insurrectionist according to Mark and Luke. The crowd will be given the choice between the Son of the Father (in the deepest sense) and this earthly son of a father who bears the same Aramaic title by coincidence. The substitution is not metaphorical: Barabbas is the guilty man released because the innocent man takes his place. In Barabbas, every sinner can recognize himself — released because of the death of the one who replaced him.

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, "Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?" For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary: Pilate reads the situation accurately — the motivation is envy — and tries to use the Passover custom to release Jesus while satisfying the crowd. His political calculation is sincere if inadequate: he would prefer not to execute an innocent man. But political calculation is no substitute for moral courage. Knowing that Jesus is innocent and that the leaders acted from envy, Pilate still lacks the will to do what justice requires. Carson notes that Pilate's failure is not intellectual — he knows the truth — but volitional: he will not bear the personal cost of releasing Jesus against the establishment's wishes. Moral cowardice condemned the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, "Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream."
verseByVerse.commentary: A Gentile woman's dream — unsolicited, urgent, accurate — testifies to Jesus' righteousness at the moment of his condemnation. This echo of Pilate's wife joins the centurion's confession (v.54), the torn curtain (v.51), and the opened tombs (v.52) as non-Jewish witnesses to Jesus' true identity at the cross. God speaks through dreams (cf. 1:20; 2:12); the warning is real. Pilate's wife calls Jesus "that righteous man" — the verdict his own enemies cannot bring themselves to deny. Her testimony is ignored, the dream is dismissed, and the one she called righteous is condemned. The voice of righteousness is often silenced by those with political authority to silence it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor again said to them, "Which of the two do you want me to release for you?" And they said, "Barabbas."
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd that welcomed Jesus with hosannas on Palm Sunday now, under priestly manipulation, calls for his death. This is the terrifying power of religious and political leadership over crowds: the same people can be led to reverence or to murder depending on who is directing them. "They persuaded" — the verb suggests active, deliberate campaigning. The priests and elders work the crowd while Pilate sits on the judgment seat. By the time Pilate asks his question, the answer is already determined. MacArthur notes that this is how human tribunals often work: the verdict is reached before the evidence is weighed, and the deliberative process is theater masking predetermined conclusions.

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to them, "Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?" They all said, "Let him be crucified!" And he said, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Let him be crucified!"
verseByVerse.commentary: Pilate's question — "What shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?" — is the question every human being must answer. He cannot remain neutral; the prisoner must be released or crucified. His attempt at moral reasoning — "What evil has he done?" — is drowned out by the crowd's shouting. The escalation from "let him be crucified" to "shouted all the more" shows the psychology of mob justice: volume replaces argument, repetition replaces reason. Sproul notes that the crowd's response to Pilate's question about Jesus' evil is itself the answer to Pilate's question about their evil — this is what human sin looks like when given power over the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, "I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves." And all the people answered, "His blood be on us and on our children!"
verseByVerse.commentary: Pilate's hand-washing is a public performance of innocence that changes nothing morally — one cannot wash away the guilt of a deliberate injustice with water. The crowd's self-imprecation — "His blood be on us and on our children" — has been misused across centuries to justify anti-Semitism, a profound perversion of the text. Theologically, Christ's blood is indeed upon those who called for his death — but as the blood of atonement, not merely of condemnation. The same blood cried for in judgment is the blood that speaks forgiveness (Heb. 12:24). Calvin notes that thousands of Jerusalem's inhabitants who called for his death were among the first recipients of Pentecost's grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary: Scourging was Roman flogging with a flagellum — leather thongs embedded with bone or metal — often so severe that victims died before crucifixion. Matthew records it in a single clause; the restraint is more powerful than elaboration. Isaiah 53:5 — "with his stripes we are healed" — is being fulfilled in brutal physical reality. The release of Barabbas and the scourging of Jesus in the same sentence is the essence of substitutionary atonement compressed into one verse: the guilty goes free; the innocent bears the punishment. What happens to Barabbas is what happens to every sinner who is justified by Christ: released at the price of Another's suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor's headquarters, and they gathered the whole battalion before him. And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him,
verseByVerse.commentary: The battalion (cohort — up to six hundred soldiers) assembles for a spectacle of mockery. The stripping of Jesus — removing his garments — prefigures the later dividing of his clothes (v.35) and recalls the shaming of a condemned criminal. The scarlet robe (a soldier's cloak) is a parody of royal purple: they crown him as a mock king, not knowing he is the King. The irony that runs through the entire Passion narrative is most concentrated in the mocking: every form of honor given derisively — robe, crown, scepter, the title "King of the Jews" — is in fact true. They mock what they worship in ignorance. The soldiers crown the King of kings and call it comedy.

verseByVerse.quote: and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head.
verseByVerse.commentary: The crown of thorns recalls the curse of Genesis 3:18 — "thorns and thistles it shall bring forth" — pressed onto the head of the one who came to bear the curse so that the creation might be renewed. The reed is a scepter of contempt. The kneeling is a parody of worship that is also unwitting prophecy: one day every knee will bow before this King (Phil. 2:10) in genuine adoration. The striking of the head with the reed drives the thorns deeper. Stott writes that this scene, more than any other, shows the depth of human contempt for God: given the King in the flesh, humanity crowns him with thorns and calls it entertainment.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The mockery ends; the execution begins. His own clothes are returned — perhaps to identify the executed man publicly. He is led away. The movement from the Praetorium to Golgotha is the most significant walk in human history: the Son of God carrying (or attempting to carry) the cross toward the place where he will be offered as the sacrifice that ends all sacrifices. Every step is taken freely; every step fulfills Scripture; every step is an act of love for those who will benefit from what happens at the end of the walk. Keller writes that Jesus walks toward Golgotha as the only person in history who truly chose his own death for the salvation of others.

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. They compelled this man to carry his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary: Simon of Cyrene — a diaspora Jew from North Africa — is conscripted from the crowd to carry the cross. The physical detail suggests Jesus' condition after scourging: he could not carry it the full distance. The Roman soldiers have authority to compel anyone to carry a burden (cf. 5:41). Simon, an observer, becomes a participant — the first to carry Jesus' cross behind him (cf. 16:24). Mark 15:21 identifies him as the father of Alexander and Rufus, suggesting he became known in the early church community. An anonymous man pressed into service becomes an enduring image of cross-bearing discipleship: taking up the actual wood of the cross that Jesus carried.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull), they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it.
verseByVerse.commentary: Golgotha — "skull place" — is likely named for its rounded shape or for its use as an execution site. Wine mixed with gall (or myrrh, Mark 15:23) was offered as a mild anesthetic by women of Jerusalem as an act of mercy. Jesus tastes it and refuses. He will drink the cup his Father has given him (26:39, 42) fully conscious and fully present, not numbed by narcotic. The deliberate refusal of the painkiller shows that the cross is undergone with complete awareness — not a death partially anesthetized but the full bearing of wrath with every faculty engaged. This is love at its most costly: refusing the mercy of unconsciousness in order to be fully present to what he is accomplishing.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. Then they sat down and kept watch over him there.
verseByVerse.commentary: "When they had crucified him" — Matthew does not linger on the physical details, but what that phrase meant to a first-century audience — and what a preacher must convey to a modern congregation that does not know — is essential to grasping the weight of the atonement. Crucifixion was reserved for slaves and the worst class of criminals; Roman law legally exempted citizens from it. The condemned was stripped naked — part of the humiliation — and nailed or bound to the cross. Crucifixion victims were nailed through the wrists (the hands alone could not bear the weight), with the arms extended and slightly raised. A nail was driven through both feet onto a small wooden foot-rest. The design was engineered for prolonged agony: the weight of the body dragged down on the outstretched arms, making it progressively harder to breathe. To inhale, the victim had to push upward against the nail through the feet, raising the body just enough to fill the lungs — then sag down again. This cycle of push and sag, each breath purchased through the wound in the feet, could continue for hours or even days. Death came primarily by asphyxiation, exhaustion, or blood loss. When the Romans wanted to hasten death — as they would do that evening before the Passover Sabbath (John 19:31-32) — they broke the legs, making it impossible to push up to breathe; death followed within minutes. The whole apparatus was designed for maximum pain, maximum duration, and maximum public shame: the naked, exposed body displayed at eye level on a thoroughfare, stripped of every dignity. Cicero called it "the most cruel and horrifying of punishments" and thought even the word too vulgar for polite Latin conversation. That the apostles would preach a crucified Messiah — that the Son of God had died this death — was not merely theologically startling but socially scandalous in a way that is nearly impossible to recover today (1 Cor. 1:23). This is what Jesus submitted to willingly, for the forgiveness of sins. The dividing of garments by lot fulfills Psalm 22:18 exactly. The soldiers sit down and keep watch — the ordinary routine of an execution detail, unaware that above them the salvation of the world is being accomplished. The casualness of the lot-casting while the Son of God dies is not indifference to the moment but ignorance of it. Stott notes that the cross is simultaneously the most ordinary-looking event in the world and the most cosmically significant.

verseByVerse.quote: And over his head they put the charge against him, which read: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews." Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left.
verseByVerse.commentary: The titulus — the criminal charge posted above the condemned — reads as an insult but is in fact the most accurate theological statement on the cross. "King of the Jews" — Pilate will not change it (John 19:22): God uses even the governor's stubbornness to inscribe the truth above the cross. The two robbers on either side fulfill Isaiah 53:12 — "he was numbered with the transgressors." He is placed at the center, between criminals, as though he is the worst of them. But the center position also marks him as the one toward whom the thieves must orient: one will reject, one will receive (Luke 23:39–43). The cross is the ultimate point of decision for all who come near it.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross."
verseByVerse.commentary: The passerby mockery — wagging heads — fulfills Psalm 22:7: "All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads." The taunt about destroying and rebuilding the temple uses the distorted version from the false witnesses (26:61); what they mean as mockery Jesus has already explained as prophecy. "If you are the Son of God, come down" echoes the wilderness temptation (4:3, 6) — the devil's logic through human voices: prove your identity by using power to escape suffering. But the proof of his identity is precisely that he does not come down. He remains because love remains. He is the Son of God most powerfully when he stays on the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him."
verseByVerse.commentary: "He saved others; he cannot save himself" — the most theologically loaded taunt ever spoken, and its speakers do not know it. He saved others — healings, forgiveness, resurrections — all true. He cannot save himself — not because of lack of power but because of the nature of salvation: the Savior must not save himself in order to save others. Substitutionary atonement means he absorbs the curse that belongs to others; he cannot absorb it and escape it simultaneously. Stott calls this the deepest irony of the Passion: the mockers speak the truth of the atonement while meaning it as an insult. "Let him come down... and we will believe" — the final proof demanded. But the resurrection, not a descent, will be the sign given (cf. 12:39–40).

verseByVerse.quote: "He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.'" And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final taunt combines Psalm 22:8 exactly: "He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him." The Passion fulfills the very Psalm that begins with "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" What the mockers intend as disproof of God's delight in Jesus is actually the fulfillment of prophetic scripture about the suffering servant. The robbers join the reviling — at this point in the crucifixion, all human voices mock. Then Luke 23:39–43 shows one robber turn. But Matthew records the universal initial rejection to show the depth of the darkness before the light breaks. Even the dying call him a fraud — and he dies for them anyway.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–66 — The Death, the Burial, and the Guard at the Tomb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final section of chapter 27 moves from crucifixion to death to burial to the sealing of the tomb. The darkness, the cry of dereliction, the tearing of the curtain, the centurion's confession, and the faithful women form the climax of the Passion narrative. The burial by Joseph of Arimathea and the guard placed at the tomb set the stage for the resurrection.
verseByVerse.theology: The cry of dereliction — 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — is the theological center of the atonement. The Son, bearing the sin of the world, experiences the relational rupture of divine judgment: the Father turns his face from the sin-bearer. This is not the dissolution of the Trinity but the full weight of Godforsakenness that fallen sinners deserve, borne in the Son's person. The tearing of the curtain confirms that what Jesus accomplished at the cross opened access to God that the temple system symbolized but could not provide.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul's treatment of the cry of dereliction is essential: he argues this is real abandonment — not perceived abandonment — because the sin Jesus bore was real, and God's holiness requires that he not look on sin. Stott concurs: the darkness and the cry together reveal that the cross is God judging sin in the person of his own Son, the only one who could bear that judgment without being destroyed by it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?" that is, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Midday to mid-afternoon — three hours of darkness, as at the Egyptian plague (Exod. 10:22), signaling judgment and the withdrawal of the Creator's blessing from creation. Then the cry: Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic, shouted with a loud voice — not a whisper of despair but a full-voiced cry of anguished prayer to God. This is the cry of dereliction, the most theologically weighty sentence in the Gospels. The Son, bearing the sin of the world (2 Cor. 5:21), experiences the Godforsakenness that is the just consequence of sin. The Father has not ceased to love the Son, but the Son bearing sin experiences the full weight of divine judgment upon it. Sproul writes that this moment is the price of our forgiveness: not our Godforsakenness but his.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders, hearing it, said, "This man is calling Elijah." And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, and put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink.
verseByVerse.commentary: The mishearing of "Eli" as a call to Elijah — possible in the noise and confusion — results in a sponge of sour wine (posca, the common soldier's drink), lifted to his lips. This fulfills Psalm 69:21: "for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink." Some of the bystanders offer this as a gesture of minimal mercy; others wait to see if Elijah will come. The expectation of Elijah as an eschatological rescuer (Mal. 4:5) is still active in the crowd's imagination. But Elijah has already come in the person of John the Baptist (17:12–13). No rescue is coming from outside; the rescue is happening through the death itself.

verseByVerse.quote: But the others said, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd's expectation of an Elijah-rescue is both understandable and theologically mistaken. They are watching the wrong kind of rescue: they look for a visible, dramatic intervention from outside, while the invisible, cosmic work of redemption is accomplished in the dying of the one they watch. The crowd at the cross, like the disciples in Gethsemane, cannot comprehend what is happening in front of them. Their watching — "let us see" — is curiosity, not faith. Begg notes that proximity to the cross without comprehension of its meaning is the condition of many who stand near Christian worship and observe with interest but do not see what is actually happening.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Yielded up his spirit" — a deliberate, active yielding, not a passive collapse. Jesus dies as he has lived: in sovereign freedom. He said "no one takes my life from me; I lay it down of my own accord" (John 10:18), and the manner of his death confirms it. Even the loud cry is remarkable: crucifixion deaths typically involved the gradual failure of voice and breath as strength failed. His loud cry before death testifies to the voluntary nature of his surrender. He decides the moment. This is the King laying down his scepter, the High Priest offering the final sacrifice, the Lamb slain from before the foundation of the world completing the act for which he came. It is finished (John 19:30).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. And the tombs also were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised,
verseByVerse.commentary: Four cosmic signs testify to the significance of Jesus' death. The temple curtain — sixty feet high, four inches thick — torn from top to bottom (from God's side, not human hands) signals the abolition of the barrier between God and humanity (Heb. 10:19–20). Earthquake and split rocks are apocalyptic signs of divine presence (Ps. 68:8; Hab. 3:6). The opening of tombs and raising of saints is a proleptic sign of the general resurrection that Jesus' own resurrection will inaugurate. The physical creation responds to the death of its Creator with seismic testimony. Stott writes that the torn curtain is the theological headline of the crucifixion: access to God is now open, permanently and universally, to all who come through Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many. When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe and said, "Truly this was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary: The raised saints appear after the resurrection — Matthew notes the temporal sequence — as the firstfruits of the new creation harvest. Their appearance to many in Jerusalem is concrete, bodily testimony that death has been defeated. The centurion's confession — "Truly this was the Son of God" — is the Gentile soldier's recognition of what Israel's leaders denied. A Roman military officer, not a theologian, is the first to name the crucified one as Son of God in Matthew's narrative. Keller notes that this confession from the most unlikely source — a pagan soldier who just supervised an execution — is Matthew's signal that the gospel will leap every boundary of religion, ethnicity, and background.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him, among whom were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joseph and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples fled (26:56); the women remained. At the crucifixion, at the burial, and at the tomb, women are the faithful witnesses where the male disciples have scattered. Mary Magdalene — from whom seven demons were cast out (Luke 8:2) — and the other Marys have followed Jesus from Galilee, supporting his ministry out of their own means (Luke 8:3). Their presence "from a distance" shows they could not prevent what happened but refused to abandon him. Carson notes that this group of faithful women becomes the primary witness chain for the resurrection: they see him die, they see where he is buried, and they will be first to see him risen. God honors faithful presence even at a distance.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joseph of Arimathea — identified by John as a secret disciple for fear of the Jews (John 19:38) — steps forward at the most dangerous moment, when all others have hidden or fled. His act of courage is also an act of fulfillment: Isaiah 53:9 says "they made his grave... with a rich man in his death." Asking Pilate for the body required identifying oneself publicly as associated with a condemned man — a significant risk of personal and social consequence. The cross draws out courageous love from unexpected sources: a Cyrenean compelled to carry it, a rich man who risks his reputation to bury it. God provides for his Son's body even in death.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary: The burial is dignified, personal, and costly: Joseph's own new tomb, unused, cut from rock. Clean linen shroud — the ceremonial care given to the body of the condemned reflects Joseph's faith that this is no ordinary condemned man. The great stone rolled at the entrance seals the tomb. The very thoroughness of the burial — witnessed, sealed, guarded — becomes the evidence that the resurrection is not a case of mistaken death or a stolen body but a genuine emergence from a verifiably sealed tomb. What looks like the conclusive sealing of Jesus' story is actually the setting of the stage for its climax. Carson notes that every detail of the burial serves the resurrection's credibility.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two women keep vigil. They do not leave. They sit opposite the tomb — present, faithful, watching, even when there is nothing to do and no hope visible. Their faithful presence at the burial ensures that on resurrection morning they will know exactly where to go; they are not confused about which tomb. The feminine faithfulness that persisted through the crucifixion continues into burial. In the darkest moment of human history — the Son of God sealed in a tomb — these two women embody the posture of the church in every dark age: present, watching, waiting, not fully understanding, but refusing to leave. Begg writes that faithful presence, even when it accomplishes nothing immediately visible, is the form love takes when love cannot fix what has broken.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate and said, "Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The religious leaders approach Pilate on the Sabbath — a theological irony noted by commentators: these strict sabbatarians violate their own Sabbath sensibilities to approach a Gentile governor on the most sacred day of the week, out of fear of a dead man. They remember Jesus' resurrection prediction better than the disciples apparently did. They call him an "impostor" (planos — deceiver) even now, but their anxiety about his prediction reveals a lingering unease. Carson notes that sometimes those who oppose the gospel show by their precautions that they take its claims more seriously than they admit in public. Their haste to secure the tomb is a backhanded tribute to the power of Jesus' words.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead,' and the last fraud will be worse than the first." Pilate said to them, "You have a guard of soldiers. Go, make it as secure as you can."
verseByVerse.commentary: The irony of the leaders' request is total: their precautions against fraud become the most powerful attestation of the resurrection's reality. A Roman guard at a sealed tomb means the disciples could not have stolen the body without detection. The guard, the seal, the stone — all these human precautions against resurrection become, when the tomb is found empty, evidence that the resurrection was not accomplished by human hands. Pilate's words — "make it as secure as you can" — have a sardonic quality: no human security will contain the one who defeated death. As Sproul writes, the chief priests and Pilate together provide the most powerful inadvertent apologetic for the resurrection in history.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with the tomb sealed and guarded. The stone is immovable; the guard is professional; the seal is Roman authority. By every human calculation, the story is over. The impostor is dead, the disciples are scattered, the tomb is sealed, and the leaders are satisfied. This is history at its darkest point — and it is where God is most completely at work. The sealing of the tomb is the final human attempt to contain the Son of God; the resurrection on the third day is God's definitive answer to every human attempt to have the final word. Begg notes that sealed tombs do not stop the God who creates from nothing and raises from death — they only make the victory more undeniable when it comes.

27.theology: The atonement: the cross as the world’s turning point. Matthew 27 narrates the event that is the hinge of history. Reformed theology has always insisted on the objective reality of what happened at the cross: the wrath of God against sin was exhausted in the person of the Son; the legal debt of humanity was paid; the judgment that was ours was borne by him. This is not one theory among many — it is the heart of the apostolic proclamation. “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Cor 15:3). The tearing of the veil demonstrates it architecturally: the barrier is gone. The centurion’s confession demonstrates it personally: the cross reveals the Son of God. Every subsequent generation is invited to stand at the foot of the cross and make the centurion’s confession their own.
27.examples:
Then: The women who watched from a distance (v. 55), who followed him from Galilee, who served him, who would be the first to the tomb on Sunday morning — they stayed when the disciples fled. Love kept them at the cross when fear drove others away. The crucifixion was not the end of their faith; it was its most costly expression.

Now: The cross is the Christian’s only boast (Gal 6:14). Not our moral achievement, not our spiritual progress, not our theological sophistication — the cross of Christ crucified is the one thing on which salvation rests. Charles Spurgeon preached: “I have a great need for Christ; I have a great Christ for my need.” Matthew 27 is the ground of that confidence. The stone rolled over the tomb is the last attempt of human power to contain what cannot be contained.

28.title: He Is Risen — Go and Make Disciples
28.text: <sup>5</sup>But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. <sup>6</sup>He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay. <sup>7</sup>Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead.” <sup>9</sup>And behold, Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. <sup>17</sup>And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted. <sup>18</sup>And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. <sup>19</sup>Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, <sup>20</sup>teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
28.overview:
The Gospel of Matthew ends not with a conclusion but with a commission. The resurrection of Jesus is announced by an angel, confirmed by the empty tomb, and experienced in a personal encounter — the women grasp his feet and worship. Then comes the mountain in Galilee: the eleven, some worshipping and some still doubting, gathered around the risen Lord. And from the mountain — the place where Moses received the law, where Jesus gave the Sermon, where Peter heard “listen to him” — the final and greatest declaration is made: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

The Great Commission is the Matthew bookend that closes the Emmanuel bracket. In chapter 1, an angel announced “they shall call his name Emmanuel — God with us.” In chapter 28, the risen Lord promises “I am with you always, to the end of the age.” Emmanuel is still with us — not in a manger, not on a cross, but in the risen, enthroned, all-authoritative presence of the Son of God who goes with his people to the ends of the earth. The Gospel does not end; it is sent. The reader is commissioned. Every disciple who has read these twenty-eight chapters is addressed by the last three verses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Resurrection and the Great Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew's Gospel ends where the entire story has been moving: the empty tomb, the risen Jesus, and the commission that sends the church to the ends of the earth. The resurrection is not an appendix to the Gospel but its vindication and foundation. The Great Commission is not an isolated command but the risen King's declaration that all authority in heaven and on earth belongs to him — and his command to act on that authority by making disciples of all nations.
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection is the hinge of all Christian theology: without it, the cross is only a tragedy; with it, the cross is the decisive act of redemption whose efficacy is declared and guaranteed. The Great Commission rests on the authority of the risen Christ: 'all authority has been given to me' is the basis for 'therefore go.' The church's mission is not generated by human enthusiasm but by the royal decree of the enthroned King. And the promise — 'I am with you always, to the end of the age' — means the mission is never undertaken alone.
verseByVerse.examples: Carson on the Great Commission: 'make disciples' is the main verb; 'going,' 'baptizing,' and 'teaching' are the participles that describe how disciple-making happens. The mission is not merely evangelism (going) or initiation (baptizing) but the full formation of people in everything Jesus commanded. Keller notes that 'all nations' (panta ta ethne) is the fulfillment of the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 12:3) and the completion of the OT trajectory toward universal worship of the God of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it.
verseByVerse.commentary: The women who watched at the cross and sat opposite the burial return at the first possible moment — dawn on the first day. Their devotion is the thread connecting death and resurrection: the same faithful love that would not leave the cross arrives earliest at the tomb. The earthquake echoes the crucifixion's earthquake (27:51) — divine power shaking the earth at both death and resurrection. The angel rolls back the stone not to let Jesus out (he is already risen, v.6) but to let the witnesses in. The stone is moved for the women, not for Jesus. Sproul writes that the rolling away of the stone is a declaration to human witnesses, not a necessity for the risen Lord who passed through locked doors (John 20:19).

verseByVerse.quote: His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men.
verseByVerse.commentary: The angel's appearance mirrors the Transfiguration's glory (17:2) — lightning-bright, snow-white, overwhelming. The Roman guards — professional soldiers trained for violence and experienced with death — "became like dead men." The guardians of the sealed tomb, meant to prevent resurrection, are prostrated by the angel's presence. The irony is complete: those commissioned to prevent the resurrection are undone by the glory that accompanies it. The guards' terror is the appropriate human response to divine power breaking into the world. They will soon recover enough to accept bribes (v.11–15), but in this moment even professional hardness cannot withstand the glory of the resurrection morning.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to the women, "Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Do not be afraid" — the first resurrection word is an act of grace, as every angelic greeting of good news in Matthew has been (1:20; 2:10). The angel identifies Jesus by his shame — "who was crucified" — not by glory, because the resurrection does not erase the cross but vindicates it. "He has risen, as he said" — the resurrection is the confirmation that Jesus' own words were true. Every prediction, every claim, every teaching is now confirmed. "Come, see the place" — the empty tomb is not a rumor but a physical, inspectable fact. They are invited to verify it. Carson notes that the Christian proclamation always invites verification, not just belief: come and see.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and behold, he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you." So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Fear and great joy" — the two emotions coexist without contradiction. The resurrection is simultaneously awesome and wonderful, terrifying and exhilarating. They run — the urgency of the news propels them. The commission given to the women before the Great Commission is given to the eleven: go and tell. Women are the first evangelists of the resurrection, commissioned by an angel to proclaim to the apostles what the whole world will eventually need to hear. The direction — Galilee, where the ministry began — shows that the risen Lord does not abandon the disciples who fled but goes before them to the place of their calling and commission. Keller notes that grace always goes before: Jesus precedes his followers to Galilee as the shepherd goes before the flock.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, Jesus met them and said, "Greetings!" And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. Then Jesus said to them, "Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary: The risen Jesus meets the women before they reach the disciples — a gracious appearing to those who were faithful first. "Greetings" (chairete) — literally "rejoice" — the first word of the risen Christ is joy. They take hold of his feet: he is physically present, bodily risen, not a ghost or a vision. They worship him — the Greek proskuneo is the full prostration of worship given to God alone. Jesus calls the disciples "my brothers" — restoring the relational bond severed by their betrayal and flight. He does not call them "my disciples" or "the eleven" but brothers, signaling that the failure of Gethsemane and Golgotha has not permanently defined the relationship. Resurrection is the word of forgiveness and restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers,
verseByVerse.commentary: Matthew alone records the guard's report and the leaders' response. The priests and elders, confronted with eyewitness testimony of the resurrection from their own commissioned guards, respond not with faith but with bribery. The "sufficient sum" (hikana arguria — considerable money) purchases a lie rather than a truth. This is the final, most explicit example of the leaders' suppression of evidence about Jesus: first his teaching, then his miracles, then his resurrection is denied by those with the most to lose if it is true. Carson notes that their very willingness to pay large sums for a cover story implies they found the guards' testimony credible — you don't pay to suppress a story you don't fear is true.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "Tell people, 'His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.' And if this comes to the governor's ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble."
verseByVerse.commentary: The cover story is self-defeating: sleeping soldiers cannot testify to what happened while they slept. If they were asleep, they saw nothing; if they saw nothing, their testimony is worthless. The alternative explanation for the empty tomb requires the disciples — scattered, fearful, grieving, without a plan — to have overcome a trained Roman guard in the night and moved a sealed stone silently. The story collapses under examination. The leaders offer to manage Pilate, adding complicity to bribery. The entire cover-up apparatus deployed against the resurrection — guards, seal, stone, bribery, official story — is itself evidence of how desperately the establishment needed the tomb to stay sealed. It did not.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary: Matthew notes that the fabricated story was still circulating in his own day — confirming that he wrote to address it directly. The resurrection's opponents never claimed the tomb was occupied; they only disputed how it became empty. This is itself a concession to the central fact: the tomb was empty. The debate was always about explanation, not fact. The disciples' story — he is risen — requires a miracle. The leaders' story — the disciples stole him — requires improbable human conspiracy by frightened men who later died for the claim that he rose. Stott notes that the willingness of the apostles to die for the resurrection makes the theft theory psychologically impossible: people do not die for a lie they themselves manufactured.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Galilee appearance brings the disciples full circle — back to the region where they were first called, where the Sermon on the Mount was delivered, where most of the ministry happened. The mountain setting recalls the Transfiguration (17:1–9) and the Beatitudes (5:1). When they see him, they worship — and "some doubted." Matthew does not smooth over the doubt; it is part of the honest record. Carson suggests this is not the doubt of unbelief but of overwhelming wonder — some were temporarily paralyzed by the sheer impossibility of what stood before them. Keller notes that the Great Commission is given to a group that includes doubters: Jesus does not wait for perfect faith before commissioning his church. He meets them in their imperfect, awestruck, wondering state and sends them anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus came and said to them, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,"
verseByVerse.commentary: "All authority in heaven and on earth" — this is Daniel 7:14 fulfilled: the Son of Man receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom from the Ancient of Days. The authority is comprehensive (heaven and earth), current (given — the resurrection and exaltation have already accomplished this), and the basis for the commission ("therefore go"). The Great Commission flows from the reality of Christ's universal lordship, not from human enthusiasm. Baptism in the Trinitarian name — one name with three distinct persons — is the clearest Trinitarian formula in the Synoptic Gospels. To be baptized into this name is to be brought into the life and covenant of the triune God. Carson notes this is the richest theological statement in any commission Jesus gives his disciples.

verseByVerse.quote: "teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Great Commission includes not just evangelism but full formation: "teaching them to observe all that I have commanded." Matthew's Gospel — which has presented Jesus' teaching in five great discourses — is itself a resource for this teaching mission. The whole of Christ's teaching, preserved and proclaimed, is the content of disciple-making. And the commission ends where the Gospel of Matthew began: "Emmanuel, which means God with us" (1:23). The final promise — "I am with you always, to the end of the age" — is not a comfort added as an afterthought but the necessary condition for everything commanded. The church does not go in its own strength to make disciples of all nations; it goes in the presence of the risen King who has all authority. He goes with them. He goes with us. This is sufficient.

28.theology: The resurrection as the foundation of everything. Matthew 28 establishes the resurrection as the ground of mission, authority, and presence. Without the resurrection, the Great Commission has no basis (no authority), no confidence (no living Lord accompanying the missionaries), and no goal (no risen Christ to present to the nations). Reformed theology has always insisted that the resurrection is not a supplement to the cross but its necessary vindication: the cross without the resurrection is a tragedy; the resurrection without the cross is a mystery. Together they are the gospel: he died for our sins and was raised for our justification (Rom 4:25). The risen Christ on the Galilean mountain, commissioning doubting disciples with unlimited authority, is the culmination of the new genesis that began in Matthew 1:1. The biblos geneseos — the book of the new beginning — ends with the world opened to the word of the King.
28.examples:
Then: Eleven ordinary men — fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot — were commissioned to disciple all nations. They had no army, no empire, no money, no social status. They had a risen Lord with all authority and a promise of presence. Within a generation the gospel had reached Rome. Within three centuries the Roman Empire had been transformed. The mustard seed had become the tree.

Now: The Great Commission has not been rescinded or transferred. Every church, every believer, every generation stands in the Galilean company — some worshipping, some doubting, all commissioned. The command is threefold: go, baptize, teach. The ground is unchanging: all authority belongs to the risen Christ. The promise is absolute: I am with you always. This is enough. It has always been enough. Go.
